Vulnerability: Server-side fetch using untrusted user input
Impact: - Trigger internal services to execute code- Compromise CI/CD, metadata, or container environment
Detection: - Log HTTP requests to internal IPs- WAF blocks to private/internal IP ranges- Monitor for unusual outgoing requests
Remediation: - Block SSRF to internal/private ranges- Enforce domain allowlists- Use internal services authentication- Segregate services via network/firewall- Do not expose Docker API or Jenkins publicly- Sanitize and validate URL inputs

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: RCE via Expression Language (EL) Injection
output:
Many Java-based frameworks like Apache Struts, JSP, Spring, or JSF use Expression Language (EL) to dynamically evaluate user inputs (e.g., ${param.name}). If user inputs are embedded unsafely into EL expressions without proper validation, an attacker can inject malicious expressions. These get evaluated and executed on the server side, potentially resulting in remote code execution.
Vulnerability: Unsafe Expression Language Evaluation
Impact: - Full server takeover- File system access- OS command execution- Data theft or malware install
Detection: - Monitor logs for ${ patterns- Use static code analysis- Log all inputs into EL fields- Monitor for suspicious parameters
Remediation: - Never interpolate raw user input into EL expressions- Escape using fn:escapeXml()- Disable class/method access- Use newer frameworks that don’t evaluate EL by default- Apply server-side validation and input restrictions

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via Parsers attack: RCE via Misconfigured YAML / JSON Parsers
output:
Applications that parse user-controlled YAML or JSON input with unsafe deserialization logic are vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE). Some YAML parsers like PyYAML (Python), ruamel.yaml, or unsafe eval() usage in JavaScript can be tricked into running code by an attacker. This happens when the app loads input using unsafe functions like yaml.load() (not safe_load) or evaluates JSON in JavaScript using eval() instead of JSON.parse().
Vulnerability: Unsafe deserialization via YAML or JSON
Impact: - Arbitrary OS command execution- Full server compromise- Sensitive data exposure- Reverse shell possibilities
Detection: - Static code analysis- Logging YAML/JSON input fields- Detect object tags like !!python/object/apply: or misuse of eval() in JS
Remediation: - Use safe_load() or json.loads() instead of unsafe alternatives- Do not allow arbitrary object resolution- Validate inputs strictly- Avoid eval() or any code execution from external data- Keep parsers updated with security patches

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via SSI attack: RCE via Server-Side Includes (SSI)
output:
Server-Side Includes (SSI) is a feature used by web servers (like Apache) to include dynamic content in HTML pages. If SSI is enabled and the server does not filter or sanitize uploaded files, an attacker can upload a file containing SSI directives (e.g. <!--#exec-->) and trick the server into executing OS commands. This can lead to full remote code execution.
Vulnerability: Server executes unsafe SSI directives
Impact: - OS command execution- Access to internal files- Reverse shell- Full system compromise
Detection: - Monitor for .shtml files with <!--#exec in content- Review upload folders- Look for unknown file types in webroot
Remediation: - Disable SSI processing entirely if not needed- Only allow specific file extensions (e.g. .jpg, .png) in uploads- Sanitize and rename uploaded files- Store uploads outside webroot (so they can’t be executed)- Use Web Application Firewalls (WAF) to block known SSI patterns- Log and monitor execution of uncommon files- Train devs and testers to recognize SSI attacks

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via File Paths attack: RCE via Path Injection
output:
AI or backend systems allow users to submit filenames or paths to open files, read logs, or fetch code. If the path is used unsafely in a command or eval context, RCE becomes possible.
Vulnerability: Path passed directly into eval or shell
Impact: Remote Code Execution, Data Theft, Full Takeover
Detection: Monitor unusual file paths in logs; alert on use of shell metacharacters (;, &&, backticks) or external network calls
Remediation: Never pass user-supplied paths to system functions; sanitize/whitelist paths; disable shell=True; use secure file resolvers

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: RCE via Database Features (xp_cmdshell / LOAD_FILE / UDF)
output:
Some database systems like Microsoft SQL Server or MySQL allow execution of operating system commands directly using features like xp_cmdshell (SQL Server), LOAD_FILE() or custom user-defined functions (UDFs). If a web application allows SQL Injection or database-level access, an attacker can abuse these features to run shell commands — achieving full Remote Code Execution (RCE).
Vulnerability: SQL Injection → OS command execution
Impact: - Full server compromise- Reverse shell- Arbitrary file read/write- Malware upload
Detection: - Monitor for xp_cmdshell, LOAD_FILE() usage- Check for UDFs being created- Look at logins that run OS commands- WAF logs with SQLi patterns
Remediation: - Disable dangerous DB features (xp_cmdshell, UDFs)- Use parameterized queries only- Enforce least privilege DB users- Sanitize all user input- Keep DB updated with patches

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Upload Web Shell (RCE)
output:
A web shell is a small malicious file (usually .php, .asp, .jsp, etc.) uploaded to a web server via an insecure file upload form. Once uploaded, the attacker accesses it through the browser to run system commands remotely. If the application fails to validate file type, extension, or content, the attacker can gain full Remote Code Execution, perform privilege escalation, or drop malware.
Vulnerability: Insecure File Upload → Web Shell Upload
Impact: - Full server compromise- File system access- Remote shell- Malware upload / persistence
Detection: - Look for .php, .jsp, .asp files in upload folders- Review logs for strange upload activity- Use WAF to block shell keywords like <?php system()
Remediation: - Validate file content type (server-side)- Rename files on upload (random UUIDs)- Store files outside webroot- Block executable extensions- Use allowlist file types- Monitor uploads via antivirus/WAF

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Upload .htaccess + Shell (Apache Servers)
output:
When a web application prevents .php file uploads (to stop shell access), attackers can still upload a .htaccess file that changes how the server interprets file types. Apache allows .htaccess to override server behavior in the current directory. By uploading a shell script with a fake extension (like .jpg) and an .htaccess file that tells Apache to treat .jpg files as PHP, the attacker can run code remotely, bypassing restrictions.
Vulnerability: Apache misconfiguration + Insecure Upload
Impact: - Full server takeover- Arbitrary command execution- Shell access with any file type
Detection: - Detect .htaccess files in user upload dirs- Monitor access to unexpected .jpg with PHP behavior- Scan file contents using antivirus/WAF
Remediation: - Disable .htaccess override (AllowOverride None)- Store files outside document root- Remove execution permissions- Validate both MIME and content type- Use random file renaming

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Bypass MIME Type Checks
output:
Many web apps check uploaded files using the MIME type (e.g., image/jpeg) to prevent file upload attacks. However, this check can be bypassed by modifying the HTTP request headers or using fake content headers, allowing attackers to upload executable files like .php disguised as images or text. Once uploaded, these files can be executed to achieve Remote Code Execution.
Vulnerability: MIME Type Spoofing in Uploads
Impact: - Remote shell access- System control- File manipulation- Malware deployment
Detection: - Monitor uploads with fake MIME types- Look for .php, .jsp in upload paths- Use antivirus/WAF to scan uploads
Remediation: - Validate MIME on server side (finfo_file() in PHP)- Check magic bytes- Block .php, .phtml extensions- Store files outside webroot- Rename uploaded files

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Extension Bypass (Double Extension Trick)
output:
Many file upload systems block files based on their file extension, e.g., .php is not allowed, but .jpg or .txt is. The double extension trick involves renaming the shell to something like shell.php.jpg or shell.php;.jpg, which may bypass extension filters. If the server interprets the file based on the first extension or allows execution regardless of the name, this results in full Remote Code Execution.
Vulnerability: Extension filtering based on filename only
Impact: - RCE via disguised shell- Full web server compromise- Malware delivery- Privilege escalation
Detection: - Monitor uploads with multiple extensions- Look for filenames like .php.jpg, .php;.png- Use antivirus/WAF to scan uploads
Remediation: - Use server-side MIME detection- Validate extension and file content- Rename uploaded files (UUID)- Store uploads outside of web root- Disallow execution in upload directories

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Magic Byte Evasion
output:
Many secure applications check file content using magic bytes — the first few bytes that identify file type (like \xFF\xD8\xFF for JPEG). Magic byte evasion involves crafting a malicious file (like a .php web shell) with fake headers or real image headers prepended. This fools the content scanner into thinking it's an image while the server still executes it as PHP — leading to remote code execution when the file is accessed.
Vulnerability: Magic Byte Evasion on Upload Filter
Impact: - Full RCE via file upload- Executable code inside non-executable types- Access to internal system
Detection: - Use tools like YARA or antivirus to scan full file- Check for executable content beyond magic bytes- Monitor unexpected .php in uploads
Remediation: - Check entire file content using finfo_file()- Restrict .php execution in upload directories- Rename uploaded files with .txt or UUID- Use MIME + magic byte + extension checks

instruction: Describe the Input Validation Bypass / RCE Prep attack: Client-Side Validation Bypass
output:
Many web applications use JavaScript in the browser to validate forms (like upload size, filename, allowed extensions). However, this client-side validation can be bypassed using tools like Burp Suite, browser dev tools, or curl. If the server doesn’t re-validate the input, attackers can upload malicious content (like PHP shells) or inject XSS/SQL. This is a common weakness exploited before achieving other attacks like Web Shell RCE.
Vulnerability: Missing server-side input validation
Impact: - RCE via upload- XSS or SQLi injection- Complete business logic bypass
Detection: - Monitor for .php, .exe or dangerous extensions in upload folders- Check logs for bypass attempts- Enable WAF rules
Remediation: - NEVER trust client-side validation- Always validate filename, extension, and content on the server- Use MIME + magic byte + extension + size checks- Sanitize filenames and user input completely

instruction: Describe the Cross‑Site Scripting (XSS) attack: SVG/XSS Payload Upload
output:
Allows uploading of SVG files that include inline JavaScript. Once uploaded and viewed in-browser, the script runs, leading to cookie theft, account compromise, or further chaining to RCE via CSRF or session hijacking.
Vulnerability: Lack of SVG sanitization
Impact: — Cookie theft— Session hijacking— Client-side compromise that can lead to server compromise
Detection: — Monitor uploads for inline <script> tags in SVGs— CSP violation reports— AV scanning of uploaded files
Remediation: — Sanitize or strip <script> and event attributes— Convert SVGs to sanitized formats (PNG)— Serve SVGs as attachments, not inline— Implement strong CSP: script-src 'none'— Use SVG sanitizers like SVGO or DOMPurify

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via Polyglot File attack: Polyglot File Upload (Image + Script)
output:
A polyglot file is crafted to serve as a valid image (e.g., PNG/JPEG) while also containing valid script code (PHP, JavaScript, etc.). If a site allows image uploads and does minimal validation, this file can be interpreted as both an image and code. When the server stores it with a .php or processes it, the script executes—leading to full remote code execution or client-side XSS.
Vulnerability: Lack of content & extension validation
Impact: Full server compromiseReverse shellData theft or malware
Detection: Monitor uploads for mixed headers/scriptsUse YARA/antivirus for embedded PHPScan for unexpected file types
Remediation: Validate extension, MIME, magic bytes, image processing server-sideRename files, store outside web root, disable PHP execution in upload dirsUse antivirus scan pipeline

instruction: Describe the Unauthorized File Overwrite / DoS / RCE attack: Overwrite Sensitive Files
output:
If an application lets you upload files without validating the filename or path, an attacker can overwrite important server files—even .htaccess, .env, or PHP scripts. This can disable security, break functionality, or grant remote code execution.
Vulnerability: Insecure file upload allows unauthorized overwrite
Impact: - Disables security (.htaccess)- Denial-of-Service- Full RCE via overwritten scripts
Detection: - Monitor uploads targeting filenames like .htaccess, config.php- File integrity monitoring- Unexpected timestamp/size changes
Remediation: - Reject uploads matching restricted filenames- Clean filenames (randomize/UUDI‑based)- Store uploads outside web root- Avoid executable permissions in upload dirs- Validate and sanitize user-supplied names

instruction: Describe the Denial of Service (DoS) via Uploads attack: DoS via Large File Upload
output:
Many web apps allow users to upload files (e.g., profile pictures, documents) without enforcing file size limits or memory/time constraints. If attackers upload gigabyte-sized files, they can exhaust server memory, disk, or network bandwidth, causing the server to hang, crash, or go offline.
Vulnerability: Missing upload size/memory validation
Impact: - Full server crash- Resource exhaustion (RAM, disk, CPU)- Temporary or persistent downtime
Detection: - Monitor server logs for large requests- Check disk space usage in /uploads/- Use alerting (Zabbix, Prometheus) on disk/memory spikes
Remediation: - Set upload_max_filesize and post_max_size in PHP- Implement rate limiting (e.g., 5 uploads/hour/IP)- Reject files over 5MB- Use Content-Length headers for early checks- Move uploads to cloud (S3, etc.) or background processing

instruction: Describe the Arbitrary File Overwrite / RCE attack: Zip Slip (Path Traversal via ZIP Upload)
output:
Zip Slip is a path traversal vulnerability triggered during ZIP file extraction. If a web application allows users to upload ZIP archives and extracts them without validating or sanitizing the file paths inside, attackers can include files like ../../../../var/www/html/shell.php. This causes the system to extract files outside the intended directory—overwriting sensitive files or placing web shells, leading to Remote Code Execution (RCE) or full system compromise.
Vulnerability: Path traversal inside ZIP filename entries
Impact: - Overwrite system files- Inject persistent shells- Break access controls- Achieve full RCE
Detection: - Monitor logs for uploaded ZIPs- Track extracted files outside intended directory- Look for unexpected writes via zip-related operations
Remediation: - Validate ZIP contents before extraction- Sanitize and canonicalize paths- Use extraction libraries that prevent traversal (like safezip, zip-slip-check)- Extract to sandboxed directory with no write access to webroot- Reject ZIP entries with ../, backslashes, or absolute paths

instruction: Describe the Race Condition / TOCTOU (Time-of-Check Time-of-Use) attack: Race Condition / TOCTOU Attack
output:
TOCTOU is a type of race condition where a program checks for a condition (e.g., file permissions, file existence) and then acts on it. If an attacker can change the state between check and use, they can exploit this window to trick the application. Example: a program checks a file for security, then opens it. The attacker quickly swaps the file with a malicious one right before the "use" step. This is common in temporary file handling, permission escalations, symlink attacks, and file uploads.
Vulnerability: TOCTOU Race Condition
Impact: - Sensitive file exposure- Privilege escalation- Possible RCE
Detection: - Use audit logs to track symlink and file replacement- Monitor for abnormal file access patterns
Remediation: - Use atomic operations (e.g., open before check)- Don’t rely on file paths after validation- Lock files during access- Avoid symlink in secure operations

instruction: Describe the Broken Access Control / IDOR attack: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
output:
Many web apps allow users to access resources via predictable IDs (e.g., /user/1001). If proper access control is not enforced on the server, attackers can manipulate the ID and view, edit, or delete other users' data. For example, if logged in as user 1001, changing the ID to 1002 in the URL might show another user's profile or invoice.
Vulnerability: Insecure Object References
Impact: - Exposure of PII- Account takeover- Unauthorized modifications
Detection: - Monitor logs for unusual ID access- Detect sequential object access attempts- Alert on unauthorized access patterns
Remediation: - Implement server-side access control checks- Use UUIDs instead of sequential IDs- Apply Access Control Matrix for sensitive operations- Always verify ownership before serving content

instruction: Describe the Authorization Bypass / Enumeration attack: Force Browsing (Unprotected Endpoints)
output:
Force Browsing is an attack where a user manually or automatically discovers hidden, unlinked, or unprotected web pages or APIs by guessing URLs or using tools. If a web developer forgets to secure pages like /admin, /logs, /config, /backup.zip, or /staging-dashboard, an attacker can simply type these URLs and access sensitive features or data — even without login. This commonly occurs when devs rely only on frontend menus to hide pages instead of implementing server-side access control checks. This attack is simple and often overlooked.
Vulnerability: Broken / Missing Access Control
Impact: - Unauthorized admin access- Info exposure (logs, config, source)- Business logic abuse
Detection: - Monitor logs for sequential brute-forcing- Check web server logs for high 404/200 patterns- Watch for scans from tools like Gobuster
Remediation: - Enforce access control server-side on every endpoint- Remove unused/legacy/debug endpoints- Monitor server logs and block brute-forcing IPs- Use WAF or access token authentication for APIs

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Role Manipulation attack: Privilege Escalation via Role Tampering
output:
In many web applications, the user's role (e.g., user, admin) is stored in a client-side session token or form field. If the server fails to validate and enforce role-based access strictly, a malicious user can manipulate the role value (e.g., change "role":"user" to "role":"admin") in the token, cookie, or request body. If the server trusts that value blindly, the attacker gains unauthorized admin-level access. This type of attack is often successful in insecure JWT tokens, hidden form fields, local storage, or API requests.
Vulnerability: Insecure Role Validation
Impact: - Full admin access- User data exposure- System compromise
Detection: - Monitor unusual role changes in logs- Track users accessing restricted endpoints- Alert on role mismatch activity
Remediation: - NEVER trust client-side role info- Validate role server-side using sessions or databases- Sign and verify all tokens properly- Implement RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) backend

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation (Vertical) attack: Vertical Privilege Escalation
output:
Vertical Privilege Escalation occurs when a lower-privileged user (like a “customer” or “viewer”) can perform actions reserved for higher-privileged users (like “admin” or “manager”). This happens due to poor authorization enforcement on the server side. For example, a normal user should not be able to access /admin/delete_user, but if the server doesn’t verify their role properly, they might gain access by directly visiting the URL or tampering with the request. This often occurs in role-based systems without strict backend controls or when client-side logic is used to hide admin functionality.
Vulnerability: Insecure Role Authorization
Impact: - Admin data exposure- User deletion- Configuration tampering
Detection: - Audit logs for unauthorized use of admin endpoints- Monitor user role vs endpoint access frequency- Alerts for low-privilege users hitting sensitive APIs
Remediation: - Implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) on server- Authorize every endpoint based on user’s session/role- NEVER trust client input for role or permissions- Hide and protect admin APIs- Log all access attempts and alert on abuse

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation (Horizontal) attack: Horizontal Privilege Escalation
output:
Horizontal privilege escalation happens when a user gains access to another user’s data or functions by changing something simple, like a user ID or username in the URL or request. For example, user A is allowed to view their profile at /user/profile/101. But by changing the URL to /user/profile/102, they may view user B’s private info. This vulnerability occurs when the server fails to verify ownership of the resource being accessed. It is different from vertical privilege escalation (which is about gaining higher-level access). Horizontal privilege escalation is accessing peer-level data that you shouldn’t have access to.
Vulnerability: Broken Object-Level Authorization
Impact: - Unauthorized access to peer data- Privacy violations- GDPR & legal risks
Detection: - Log analysis: check user ID mismatch in access logs- Monitor high request patterns to user-based endpoints- Alert when user accesses others’ records
Remediation: - Enforce server-side authorization per object (user ID)- Match session user with resource ownership- Use access control libraries or middleware- NEVER rely on client-side hiding or trust alone

instruction: Describe the Input Manipulation / Business Logic Bypass / Client-side Trust Exploit attack: Parameter Pollution / Hidden Field Tampering
output:
Many web apps rely on hidden input fields in forms (like price, discount, role, user_id) or assume fixed parameters (e.g., one per field). Attackers can manipulate hidden fields or add duplicate parameters to confuse the server or override intended logic. For example, changing <input type="hidden" name="price" value="100"> to 1 can result in product price manipulation, or submitting duplicate parameters like price=100&price=1 may cause pollution, depending on how the backend handles duplicates. If the server uses the first or last occurrence or merges values, it may lead to authorization bypass, discount abuse, or logic flaw exploitation.
Vulnerability: Hidden Field Tampering / Parameter Pollution
Impact: - Modify product price- Switch user IDs- Abuse hidden roles or discounts- Bypass logic conditions
Detection: - Server logs with mismatched pricing data- Detect duplicate parameters in request logs- Unexpected values for price, user, role
Remediation: - NEVER trust client-side values (even hidden fields)- Always validate/recalculate values server-side- Sanitize/strip duplicate parameters- Use secure backend logic for prices, roles, etc.

instruction: Describe the Insecure Method-Level Access Control (REST) attack: Unauthorized API Method Access (REST Abuse)
output:
REST APIs expose different HTTP methods (like GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) to interact with server resources. Sometimes, developers forget to restrict access to certain methods for regular users. For example, a normal user might be allowed to GET /api/users/123, but should NOT be allowed to DELETE /api/users/123. If the server doesn’t properly validate user roles and HTTP method access, attackers can abuse exposed methods (like DELETE or PUT) to modify or delete data they shouldn’t have access to. This is especially dangerous in systems where frontend hides functionality but backend still accepts powerful methods. This is common in APIs built using Express, Flask, Laravel, etc.
Vulnerability: Insecure Method Access / Missing Access Control
Impact: - Unauthorized deletion of users or records- Data tampering- System compromise via method override
Detection: - Audit logs for abnormal use of dangerous methods (DELETE, PUT)- Monitor which roles use which methods- API rate and role tracking systems
Remediation: - Enforce method-based access control (e.g., RBAC for DELETE/PUT)- Use allowlist for HTTP methods per role- Never trust frontend restrictions- Validate permissions on server for every method and action

instruction: Describe the Function/Feature-Level Access Bypass attack: Missing Function Level Access Control
output:
Web applications often expose different functions (or features) for different types of users: e.g., users vs admins. When a user logs in, only the buttons or links for allowed functions are shown (e.g., “Edit Profile” for user, “Manage Users” for admin). However, if the backend fails to enforce proper access control, and simply relies on frontend logic (like hiding buttons), a normal user can directly access the backend URL of an admin function (e.g., /admin/deleteUser?id=5). This attack occurs when functions exist but access checks are missing, allowing any logged-in user to access restricted features by crafting URLs or API calls manually.
Vulnerability: Missing function-level access validation
Impact: - Admin features accessed by normal users- Unauthorized actions like delete/edit roles- Data compromise and account escalation
Detection: - Monitor logs for normal users accessing admin routes- Alert on abnormal role activity- Check HTTP method usage by unauthorized users
Remediation: - Implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)- Backend must verify user permissions for every feature- Do not rely only on UI to restrict functionality- Use access control middleware or decorators

instruction: Describe the Authentication Bypass / Privilege Escalation attack: JWT or Cookie Manipulation (Fake Privileges)
output:
Many web applications use cookies or JWT (JSON Web Tokens) to store user information like email, user ID, or roles ("role": "user"). When the server doesn't properly verify or sign these values (or uses insecure algorithms like none), an attacker can decode, change, and re-encode the token to gain admin access or impersonate another user. For example, if the server blindly trusts role=admin in a cookie or token without validation, a regular user can change it and perform admin actions. This is common in systems using self-made auth, weak JWT signing, or cookies storing role-based access values.
Vulnerability: JWT Tampering / Insecure Cookie Trust
Impact: - Unauthorized access to admin functions- Impersonating users- Data leaks or deletion
Detection: - Log user roles against request paths- Alert if role=admin seen in unsigned/unexpected tokens- Check JWT header for insecure algorithms
Remediation: - Always sign JWTs with strong secret keys (HS256, RS256)- Reject unsigned or alg=none tokens- Validate user roles server-side, not just from the token- Use HttpOnly, Secure flags for cookies

instruction: Describe the Path Traversal / Directory Traversal attack: Unrestricted File Access via Path Manipulation
output:
Many web applications accept a filename or path as a parameter to read files from the server (e.g., view?file=report.pdf). If developers do not sanitize the input, attackers can manipulate the path (e.g., ../../../../etc/passwd) to access sensitive files outside the intended directory. This is known as path traversal. In many real apps, a user can download/view files, and developers use the file path directly from user input. This allows attackers to access internal server files (e.g., config, passwd, SSH keys). When combined with file upload, attackers can read uploaded shell files too.
Vulnerability: Improper Input Validation on File Paths
Impact: - Leakage of config, credentials, environment variables- Remote shell access or backdoor- Full system compromise
Detection: - Monitor logs for repeated "../"- Use File Access Auditing- Track non-whitelisted file paths
Remediation: - Normalize and sanitize file paths- Use whitelisting for file names- Never accept raw user file paths- Use static directories and filename maps (e.g., file_id=23)

instruction: Describe the Abuse of Rate Limiting / Access-Control Controls attack: Rate-Limited / Access-Controlled Resource Abuse
output:
Some web applications implement rate limits (e.g., 5 OTPs per minute) or access controls (like limiting profile views or downloads). These controls are often enforced client-side or poorly server-side, and attackers can bypass or abuse them using tools that automate repeated requests. For example, by rotating IPs, tweaking headers, or using scripts, an attacker can send thousands of OTP requests, brute-force a password, or download sensitive data in bulk. Common abuse includes brute-force login, API scraping, coupon fraud, OTP bomb, or DoS using uncontrolled resources.
Vulnerability: Missing or weak server-side rate-limiting / access control
Impact: - Mass OTP flooding- Automated API scraping- Brute-force login- Data scraping- Resource exhaustion
Detection: - Analyze server logs for high-frequency requests- Track requests per IP, user-agent- Monitor spikes in OTPs/emails/downloads
Remediation: - Enforce server-side rate limiting using Redis, NGINX, or API gateway- Track per-IP, per-token, per-user- Add captcha or challenge after X attempts- Use 429 Too Many Requests headers

instruction: Describe the Tenant Isolation Bypass / Access Control attack: Multi-Tenant Bypass
output:
In multi-tenant applications, a single app is used by multiple companies or groups (called "tenants"), and each tenant’s users should only see their own data. If access controls are weak, a user from Tenant A can view, modify, or delete data from Tenant B — by guessing or changing the tenant ID in URLs, headers, or APIs. For example, a finance dashboard URL like /tenant/1234/invoices can be changed to /tenant/9999/invoices. If the app doesn’t check ownership, this bypasses tenant isolation and leaks sensitive data across organizations.
Vulnerability: Insecure Tenant Isolation / Missing Authorization Logic
Impact: - Data leakage across organizations- Unauthorized edits or deletions- Compliance violations (e.g., GDPR)- Loss of trust / brand damage
Detection: - Monitor API logs for cross-tenant access- Track mismatches between user ID and tenant ID- Use correlation IDs for requests by tenant
Remediation: - Never trust tenant or org ID from client- Check that the authenticated user belongs to the tenant on the server- Use middleware that binds session to tenant- Avoid exposing internal tenant IDs in URLs or forms

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover via CNAME Hijack attack: CNAME to Unclaimed GitHub Repo Takeover
output:
A company points a subdomain (e.g., blog.company.com) to a GitHub Pages repo (e.g., username.github.io) using a CNAME record. If that GitHub repo is deleted but the CNAME still exists, an attacker can recreate the repo and claim the subdomain, gaining full control over blog.company.com.
Vulnerability: DNS misconfiguration and unclaimed repo
Impact: - Full control over company's subdomain- Phishing, malware injection, brand defacement- Can bypass company domain protections
Detection: - Use subjack, nuclei, or online DNS checkers- Look for GitHub Pages 404 pages- Scan with tools for takeover patterns
Remediation: - Remove CNAME records that point to deleted repos- Monitor DNS records regularly- Use DNS hosting monitoring tools- Use hosted zone ownership checks in CI/CD- GitHub now shows CNAME conflicts — fix quickly

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover via CNAME Hijack (Heroku) attack: CNAME to Unclaimed Heroku App Takeover
output:
A company configures a subdomain (like app.company.com) to point to a Heroku-hosted app (like myapp.herokuapp.com). If the Heroku app is deleted but the DNS record (CNAME) still points to it, an attacker can create a new Heroku app using the same name (myapp) and control the content of app.company.com.
Vulnerability: Orphaned DNS records + unclaimed Heroku apps
Impact: - Full subdomain control- Deface company site- Launch phishing/malware from trusted domain- Can affect email security if domain uses SPF/DKIM
Detection: - Use subjack, nuclei, or online DNS + Heroku checkers- Monitor for "No such app" on sub.domain.com and original Heroku app
Remediation: - Regularly audit DNS records for decommissioned apps- Remove DNS records when Heroku apps are deleted- Use automation to alert when a Heroku app is down or removed- Use wildcard disallow DNS or hosting protections

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover via AWS S3 Bucket attack: Unclaimed AWS S3 Bucket Subdomain Takeover
output:
A company hosts a static website using an Amazon S3 bucket and maps a subdomain (e.g., media.company.com) to it via a CNAME DNS record. If the bucket is deleted but the DNS record remains, an attacker can create an S3 bucket with the same name and take over the subdomain, serving malicious files from a trusted company subdomain.
Vulnerability: CNAME to deleted (unclaimed) AWS S3 bucket
Impact: - Full control over trusted subdomain- Hosting malware, phishing, fake pages- Breaking CDN / JS or CSS integrity if linked assets
Detection: - Look for DNS CNAME to s3.amazonaws.com domains- Check error messages like NoSuchBucket, 404, or 403 Access Denied from AWS- Use tools like subjack, nuclei, Amass
Remediation: - Remove DNS entries for deleted buckets- Use bucket ownership verification before CNAME mapping- Monitor DNS and S3 regularly- Enable cloud posture tools (like AWS Config, GuardDuty)- Use CI/CD to check for orphaned buckets before deploy

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover via CNAME → Azure Blob/Web Apps attack: Unclaimed Azure Blob/Web App Subdomain Takeover
output:
A company maps a subdomain like assets.company.com or portal.company.com to an Azure Blob storage container or an Azure App Service (Web App) using a CNAME DNS record. If the Azure resource is deleted (but DNS is not updated), an attacker can create a resource with the same name and take over the subdomain to host malicious content.
Vulnerability: Dangling DNS to deleted Azure resource (App or Blob)
Impact: - Full control of trusted subdomain- Host phishing/malware under valid domain- Impact branding, reputation, and even email security (SPF, DKIM)
Detection: - Use DNS tools to check CNAMEs- Use subjack, nuclei for automated detection- Watch for Azure-branded error pages or 404s with Azure headers
Remediation: - Delete DNS records for removed Azure services- Monitor subdomains regularly- Require domain validation before Azure mapping- Automate detection with nuclei, securitytrails, or Azure Defender

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover (CNAME → Fastly Misconfig) attack: Subdomain Takeover via Fastly CDN
output:
When a company uses Fastly CDN to serve static or dynamic content (like cdn.company.com or static.company.com), they configure a CNAME DNS record to point to a Fastly-hosted service (e.g., global.ssl.fastly.net). If they delete the Fastly service but forget to remove the DNS record, anyone can create a Fastly account and claim that domain, taking full control of the subdomain.
Vulnerability: DNS points to deleted Fastly service (unclaimed subdomain)
Impact: - Complete control over company subdomain- Host malicious scripts, phishing, fake login pages- Compromise third-party CDN-linked apps/scripts
Detection: - Check CNAME record → Fastly- Visit domain → look for “Fastly Unknown Domain”- Run subjack, nuclei, or dnsx for automation
Remediation: - Remove DNS records pointing to unused Fastly services- Monitor CNAME records and expired services- Use Fastly domain verification (via TLS cert validation / ownership proof)- Alert security teams on DNS + CDN mismatches

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover (Custom Domain Hijack) attack: Subdomain Takeover via Bitbucket Pages
output:
A company points a subdomain (e.g., blog.company.com) to a Bitbucket Pages repo (username.bitbucket.io) using a CNAME DNS record. If the Bitbucket repo or Pages service is deleted and DNS still points there, an attacker can recreate the repo or Pages service with that username and take over blog.company.com, serving custom content.
Vulnerability: Dangling DNS + deleted Bitbucket Pages resource
Impact: • Full control of trusted subdomain• Hosting phishing, malware, defacement• Inject malicious scripts in web pages using the domain
Detection: • Detect CNAME → Bitbucket Pages• View 404 repo/page• Use subjack, nuclei, or manual checks to flag dangling DNS
Remediation: • Remove DNS records for deleted Pages/Repos• Monitor subdomains and DNS CNAMEs regularly• Use CI/CD or DNS-change alerts• Require custom domain verification before use

instruction: Describe the Subdomain Takeover via Expired Domain attack: Subdomain Forwarding to Expired Domains
output:
A subdomain (e.g., api.example.com) points via DNS (CNAME or redirect) to a domain that has expired or is unregistered. An attacker registers that domain and takes over the subdomain.
Vulnerability: DNS forwarding to unregistered/expired domain
Impact: Phishing, Session Hijacking, Credential Theft
Detection: Monitor DNS records for expired CNAMES; detect DNS resolution failures; alert on new IP bound to subdomain
Remediation: Reclaim/disable all unused subdomains; monitor DNS; avoid CNAME to third-party domains; use asset inventory tools

instruction: Describe the Wildcard CNAME Misconfiguration Leading to Takeover attack: Wildcard CNAME Subdomain Takeover
output:
A domain is configured with a wildcard CNAME record (*.company.com) pointing to an external target (like origin.example.com). If the external target becomes expired or removed, every subdomain under company.com (for example, hidden.company.com, mail.company.com) suddenly resolves to a dangling host. An attacker can claim the target (origin.example.com) and gain control of all subsubdomains without needing individual misconfigurations.
Vulnerability: Wildcard CNAME pointing to an expired or unclaimed target
Impact: - Broad takeover of every subdomain- Large-scale phishing, malware, and brand compromise- No need to hunt down individual vulnerable subdomains
Detection: - DNS wildcard scanning tools- WHOIS monitoring for external hostnames- Detect unresolved targets behind wildcard entries
Remediation: - Eliminate wildcard CNAMEs unless necessary- Ensure external hosts are live and monitored- Alert on target expiration or host accessibility changes

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect / URL Manipulation attack: Basic Redirect via URL Parameter
output:
A web app allows users to specify a destination URL via a parameter like returnUrl or redirect. For example: https://app.company.com/login?returnUrl=https://app.company.com/dashboard. If the parameter is not validated, an attacker can modify it to https://malicious.site, causing users to be redirected to an attacker-controlled site after login—leading to phishing or malware delivery.
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation on redirect parameter
Impact: • Enables phishing or malware via trusted domain• Social engineering becomes more convincing• Potential credential theft, reputation loss
Detection: • Try redirect URL tampering• Burp/ZAP scans for open redirect• Code scan for unvalidated Location headers
Remediation: • Validate redirect params with whitelist or allow only relative paths• Use static code analyzers to detect redirects• Show confirmation page before redirecting externally

instruction: Describe the Redirect Manipulation via Relative Paths attack: Relative Path Redirect Abuse
output:
A web application accepts a URL parameter (e.g., redirect) and assumes only safe, internal paths are passed—such as /home, /settings. The server blindly concatenates this parameter and performs a redirect. If an attacker passes a crafted value like //evil.com or /\evil.com, they can redirect victims to external malicious domains, bypassing basic validation.
Vulnerability: Improper validation of user-controlled redirect paths
Impact: • Aids phishing via trusted domains• Malware or credential harvesting upon redirect• Circumvents simple validation logic
Detection: • Manually try //evil.com style redirects• Proxy tools to analyze Location headers• Find all redirects in code lacking host checks
Remediation: • Whitelist internal paths only• Use proper URL parsing and host validation• Alert and confirm on external redirects

instruction: Describe the URL Validation Bypass via Alternate Protocols attack: Protocol-Based Bypass
output:
A web application attempts to restrict redirects to internal domains by checking only the protocol (e.g. allowing only https://company.com) and not validating or filtering other protocols like javascript:, data:, or file:. Attackers can craft payloads such as javascript:alert(1) or use double encoding to bypass checks, leading to XSS, phishing, or Open Redirect.
Vulnerability: Inadequate URL validation allowing unsafe protocols
Impact: • Reflected XSS, data theft, malware injection• Phishing using legitimate domain• Session token exfiltration
Detection: • Manual tests with JS/data URL• Burp/ZAP scanners detect open redirects/XSS• Static code analysis flags unsafe protocol acceptance
Remediation: • Enforce whitelists and parsing• Use frameworks that auto-validate URLs• Escape URIs, validate only relative paths

instruction: Describe the Input Validation Bypass (XSS/SQL Injection) attack: Bypass via Obfuscation
output:
A web application attempts to filter dangerous inputs (e.g., <script>, ' OR 1=1) using naive pattern matching. Attackers encode or rearrange payloads—like using HTML entities (<script>), Unicode escapes, string concatenation (<scr + ipt>), mixed casing, or SQL comments—to bypass filters and execute malicious actions.
Vulnerability: Improper input filtering allowing obfuscation
Impact: • Persistent/Reflected XSS → data theft- Malware injection, session hijacking- Brand trust loss, site defacement
Detection: • Send obfuscated variants (entities, mixed case)- Burp/ZAP fuzzing- Code scanning for naive filter code
Remediation: • Use context-aware escaping- Normalize before validation- Use whitelist-based filtering- Avoid unsafe custom sanitizers

instruction: Describe the Unsafe JS Redirect attack: Redirect via JavaScript location
output:
A web application uses JavaScript to redirect users based on a URL parameter, e.g., <script>location.href = params.dest;</script>. If this parameter isn’t validated or sanitized, attackers can craft malicious links that redirect users under a trusted domain to arbitrary external URLs—enabling phishing or malware distribution.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated redirect targets in JS without sanitization
Impact: • Phishing, malware spread via trusted domain- XSS via javascript: payload- Brand trust and session security compromised
Detection: • Manually test behavior with malicious dest= arguments- Use scanner to detect dynamic redirects- Code review for unsafe location=... usage
Remediation: • Limit allowed destinations via whitelist- Do server-side mapping of parameters- Validate and encode input, restrict to same origin

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect (HTML Meta-Based) attack: Redirect via Meta Refresh Tag
output:
Some web apps use the <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=..."> tag to redirect users to another page. If the URL is taken directly from user input (e.g., ?url=https://evil.com) and not properly validated, attackers can use the trusted domain to redirect victims to malicious websites (like phishing or malware pages), abusing user trust and browser behavior.
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation for redirect destinations
Impact: - Phishing and social engineering- Credential theft- Malware delivery- Brand damage via trust abuse
Detection: - Change url= to attacker-controlled value- Use proxy to test full redirects- Scan HTML code for meta-refresh with URL variables
Remediation: - Whitelist allowed redirect destinations- Avoid passing URLs as parameters directly- Provide exit-warning page before external redirects

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect (via HTTP 3xx Location) attack: Redirect via 3xx HTTP Headers
output:
Some web applications redirect users to different pages using HTTP 3xx responses (like 301 or 302). If a user-provided parameter (like ?next=, ?url=, or ?redirect=) is used directly in the HTTP Location header without validation, attackers can craft URLs that make the browser first request a legitimate site, but then silently redirect to a malicious one.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated redirect in HTTP Location header
Impact: - Phishing via redirect- User credential theft- Reputation loss- Redirection to malware or scam pages
Detection: - Change redirect params to external domains- Inspect HTTP response Location: header- Proxy-based intercept and log
Remediation: - Whitelist paths only- Block external domains- Use mapping IDs not raw URLs- Add redirect confirmation screen

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect via OAuth attack: Redirect in OAuth Flows
output:
During OAuth authentication, the redirect_uri tells the identity provider where to send the user after login. If this redirect_uri is not validated, attackers can supply malicious domains. After successful login, users are redirected to attacker-controlled sites with tokens or sensitive data. This breaks the trust in the OAuth flow and can lead to session hijacking, phishing, or account compromise.
Vulnerability: Improper redirect_uri validation in OAuth flow
Impact: - Credential/token leakage- Account takeover- Session hijacking- Loss of trust in login system
Detection: - Modify redirect_uri manually or via proxy- Look for unvalidated redirects in traffic- Use logging + URL inspection in security monitoring tools
Remediation: - Whitelist redirect URIs- Validate input strictly- Avoid relying solely on client parameters- Use state and CSRF tokens for protection

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect (Unvalidated Input) attack: Redirect via Referer or returnTo Param
output:
Many web apps include a returnTo, next, or Referer parameter to redirect users after login or logout. If these values are not validated or sanitized, an attacker can provide a malicious external URL. The server will redirect users to that URL, thinking it's a trusted part of the application. This can result in phishing, token leakage, or malicious redirection from a trusted domain.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized user-controlled redirect parameters
Impact: - Phishing- User redirection to malicious websites- Token/session leakage- Loss of user trust- Security audits fail for redirection flaws
Detection: - Manual testing of returnTo or Referer values- Proxying requests via Burp- Source code audit- Automated scanners like OWASP ZAP or Nikto
Remediation: - Whitelist allowed paths- Ignore or sanitize Referer header- Never accept full external URLs from client- Confirm redirection visually for user if unsure

instruction: Describe the Multi-Step Open-Redirect (Chaining) attack: Chained Redirects (Redirect to Redirect)
output:
A web app redirects a user via an internal endpoint, which then redirects again based on an unvalidated parameter. Attackers exploit this chain to hide malicious targets behind multiple trusted-looking URLs. Users see only the first trusted domain before being forwarded through a second, potentially malicious domain—making detection difficult and phishing more convincing.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated redirect parameters across chained endpoints
Impact: - Phishing through trusted URL chains- Malware or unwanted content delivery- Detect evasion via multi-step redirect
Detection: - cURL/Inspector to follow chain- Burp/ZAP scanner tracks multiple 3xx responses- Code audit for multi-header redirect patterns
Remediation: - Validate URLs across all steps- Avoid redirect chaining or map IDs- Confirm redirection to external targets

instruction: Describe the Open Redirect via Email Link attack: Password Reset Poisoning
output:
Many web applications allow password reset through a link sent via email. If the application includes user-controllable parameters like next=, redirect=, or Referer in the reset link, attackers can inject a malicious URL that gets embedded in the reset email. When users click it, they are redirected to the attacker’s site, which mimics the original app to steal passwords or other info.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated user input in redirect parameters inside email URLs
Impact: - Phishing via real reset flow- Account Hijacking- Credential Theft
Detection: - Check reset email for external links- Intercept and alter next= param in Burp- Code inspection of email link builder
Remediation: - Remove external redirect support- Use whitelist of allowed internal paths- Don’t allow user input in reset URLs

instruction: Describe the Cache Poisoning / Header Injection attack: Cache Poisoning via Host Header
output:
Some websites and CDNs (like Fastly, Cloudflare, NGINX) cache responses to speed up performance. If they use the Host header without proper validation, attackers can inject a fake domain. If that response gets cached, future visitors will get the poisoned version — redirecting them or showing malicious content. This is dangerous when caching layers trust headers too much.
Vulnerability: Cache key misconfiguration, untrusted Host header
Impact: - Users redirected to malicious domains- Phishing, fake login pages, malware- Brand abuse, SEO poisoning
Detection: - Send requests with modified Host- Analyze HTML for reflected value- Check cache behavior and response headers
Remediation: - Sanitize Host header- Set Vary: Host or strict cache keys- Avoid using Host in HTML or redirect links

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Host header attack: SSRF via Host Header
output:
Web apps or APIs sometimes use the Host header to route internal requests or to form URLs that backend services fetch. If that header isn't validated, attackers can inject arbitrary internal domains or IPs (e.g., 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels), forcing the server to fetch sensitive data from internal services and return it—breaking network boundaries.
Vulnerability: Host header injection leads to SSRF when used to build backend fetch URLs
Impact: Data exfiltration of internal resources, metadata, admin access, full compromise
Detection: Manual injection + Burp, scanning tools, server logs monitoring
Remediation: Whitelist hosts/IPs, don't trust Host for URLs, block internal IP requests

instruction: Describe the HTTP Host Header Routing Bypass attack: Bypass Virtual Host Routing
output:
Web servers often route requests based on the Host header (e.g., vhost.example.com). If an application doesn’t strictly validate that header, attackers can supply unexpected hostnames or IP addresses to access internal or otherwise-inaccessible virtual hosts—potentially revealing admin panels or hidden tenants.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated Host header leads to virtual host bypass
Impact: - Access unauthorized admin/content- Tenant data leaks- Privilege escalation
Detection: - Testing with custom Host headers via curl/Burp- Code audits for Host reliance- Automated scanning for host splitting
Remediation: - Strict host validation in server configs- Reject unknown Host headers- Enforce HTTPS+cert reuse per host

instruction: Describe the Open Redirection via Host Header attack: Open Redirect via Host Header
output:
Some web applications use the HTTP Host header to build redirect URLs. If this header isn't validated, attackers can send requests with a malicious Host value. The server will then redirect victims to attacker-controlled domains, even though the initial request came from a trusted domain.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated Host header used in redirect response
Impact: • Victims sent to phishing/evil sites- Brand trust eroded- Possible follow-up attacks
Detection: • Modify Host header manually and check response- Proxy-carried tests with scanning tools- Audit code for misuse of Host in redirects
Remediation: • Use fixed domains in redirect- Whitelist expected Host values- Reject or error on unexpected Host- Avoid dynamic Host-based redirects

instruction: Describe the Reflected XSS via HTTP Host header attack: Cross‑Site Scripting (Reflected) via Host Header
output:
An AI assistant or LLM backend returns the Host header in responses (e.g., links, prompts), allowing attackers to inject JavaScript via a malicious custom Host, which executes in victims' browsers.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized/reflected Host header use
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, prompt manipulation
Detection: Scan for Host echo in HTML/JSON; use automated XSS detectors; inspect DevTools
Remediation: Whitelist valid hostnames; HTML-encode header values; use Content Security Policy (CSP); fix prompt UI to use canonical domain

instruction: Describe the CSRF Token Bypass / Host Header Attack attack: Host Header Based CSRF Token Bypass
output:
Many web apps validate CSRF tokens based on the Host header to prevent cross-site requests. But if this value is not properly verified, an attacker can trick the application into generating valid CSRF tokens for attacker-controlled domains, thereby bypassing CSRF protections. This is possible when tokens are bound to a hostname without enforcing strict origin validation.
Vulnerability: Trusting user-supplied Host header for CSRF validation
Impact: - CSRF protections bypassed- Account takeover- Data tampering- Forged user actions (like changing email or password)
Detection: - Monitor Host headers for unexpected domains- Analyze logs for CSRF token generation with wrong hosts
Remediation: - Enforce strict origin and referer checks- Bind CSRF tokens to session, not host headers- Whitelist allowed domains- Validate Host headers before trusting- Use SameSite cookies to reduce CSRF attack surface

instruction: Describe the Identity Impersonation / Social Engineering attack: Email Spoofing / Notification Hijack
output:
A web app or mail system sends emails to users (e.g., password reset, invoices). If the system does not enforce SPF, DKIM, or DMARC, an attacker can spoof the sender address, making it seem like the email came from a legitimate source. They use this to send fake alerts, reset links, or invoices to users, tricking them into visiting phishing sites or downloading malware.
Vulnerability: Lack of authentication for email origin / poor email server config
Impact: - Users may click fake password reset links- Financial loss from phishing- Reputation damage- Credential harvesting- Notification system hijack
Detection: - Check DMARC, SPF, DKIM configs- Monitor bounced messages with spoofed headers- Analyze unusual email volume or alerts from postmasters
Remediation: - Use strict DMARC policy (reject)- Implement SPF + DKIM records- Don't send user-controllable inputs in email bodies or headers- Validate all from headers before sending- Use rate-limiting on notification endpoints- Require email confirmation on changes

instruction: Describe the UI Redress Attack (Clickjacking) attack: Basic iFrame-Based Clickjacking
output:
Clickjacking is a technique where an attacker loads a legitimate web page (e.g., a banking site) inside a hidden iFrame on their malicious site, and tricks the user into clicking buttons they cannot see—like “Transfer,” “Buy,” or “Allow.” This lets attackers trick users into taking actions they didn’t intend.
Vulnerability: Lack of X-Frame-Options or CSP headers
Impact: - Tricking users to unknowingly perform actions- Account deletion, purchases, privacy breach- Bypassing user intent
Detection: - Use browser dev tools to check for iFrames- Use Burp or DevTools to inspect headers (e.g., X-Frame-Options)- Test if site allows being framed
Remediation: - Add X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN to HTTP response headers- Use CSP (Content Security Policy): frame-ancestors 'none'- Confirm critical actions with re-auth or CAPTCHA

instruction: Describe the UI Redress / Clickjacking attack: Likejacking (Social Media Hijack)
output:
Likejacking is a type of clickjacking attack that tricks users into clicking "Like" or "Follow" buttons for Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, etc. without realizing it. The attacker hides a social media widget (like button) under a fake "Play video" or "Claim prize" button on their website to hijack likes or followers.
Vulnerability: Invisible iFrames overlaid on visible content
Impact: - Force user to like/follow social media pages- Increase likes/followers dishonestly- Bypass genuine user consent
Detection: - Use browser developer tools to inspect if hidden social buttons are being layered- Facebook security tools may detect abuse patterns
Remediation: - Use X-Frame-Options: DENY to block framing- Require click confirmation for social actions- Use CAPTCHA or click validation- Educate users not to click suspicious buttons

instruction: Describe the UI Redress (Clickjacking) attack: Cursor Spoofing / Click Offset
output:
Cursor spoofing is a UI deception attack where a fake cursor is displayed to the user, while the real cursor is offset or hidden, tricking users into clicking hidden buttons (e.g., "Buy", "Like", "Confirm") without realizing. This misleads users into unintended actions.
Vulnerability: Insecure UI interaction via styling
Impact: - Misleads user into clicking something harmful- May result in account deletion, forced likes, purchases, or confirmation of actions unknowingly
Detection: - Check site for custom cursor styles + "cursor: none"- Use browser dev tools to detect JavaScript offset scripts- Manual UI testing for mouse position tricks
Remediation: - Never hide real cursor for critical actions- Use double confirmation for sensitive actions- Disable external iframe embeds unless needed- Use CSP and anti-clickjacking headers

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking (UI Redress) attack: Transparent Layer Overlay Attack
output:
A transparent HTML element is placed over a visible and enticing button (like "Play" or "Download"). When the user clicks on the visible button, they're actually clicking the invisible button behind it. The attacker tricks the user into submitting a form, liking a page, or making a transaction unintentionally.
Vulnerability: Transparent UI Layers (CSS)
Impact: - Unauthorized actions (e.g., liking pages, deleting account)- High risk on financial, admin, or social accounts
Detection: - Use browser dev tools to inspect page layers- Check for opacity: 0, z-index, and pointer-events settings
Remediation: - Use X-Frame-Options: DENY header- Use frame-busting JavaScript to prevent page embedding- Require click confirmations on sensitive actions

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking + CSRF (Chained) attack: Clickjacking + CSRF Combo Attack
output:
A combo attack where an attacker embeds a legitimate website inside an invisible iframe and then tricks the user into clicking something (like "Delete Account" or "Change Email"). The click is passed to the embedded iframe, which sends a CSRF request to the real app behind the scenes, performing an action without the user realizing it.
Vulnerability: Clickjacking + Missing CSRF Protections
Impact: - Unauthorized actions like password/email change- Can lead to full account hijack- No user awareness – looks harmless
Detection: - Use dev tools to inspect iframe, opacity, and check request logs- Monitor unexpected state changes after user visits external pages
Remediation: - Use SameSite cookies- Implement X-Frame-Options- Add CSRF tokens in forms- Require re-authentication for critical actions

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking (Advanced Type) attack: Drag-and-Drop Clickjacking
output:
An attacker builds a malicious webpage using drag-and-drop elements (e.g., emojis or images) and overlays them above legitimate iframe controls (e.g., email deletion, fund transfer, etc.). When the victim drags and drops the element, the action is passed to the target app in the background without victim realizing it.
Vulnerability: Lack of frame-busting headers
Impact: - Delete or modify sensitive data- Trick users into dragging files to delete or submit forms- Fully invisible and hard to detect
Detection: - Check for X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy headers- Observe UI click events over iframe overlays
Remediation: - Always use X-Frame-Options: DENY- Use Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'- Disable drag-based triggers without confirmation

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking (Advanced) attack: File Upload Clickjacking
output:
The attacker tricks the user into thinking they are uploading a file (e.g., resume, document) to a trusted platform. However, behind the visible button is an invisible iframe of a sensitive or malicious file upload form. The user unknowingly uploads a private or malicious file to a sensitive app.
Vulnerability: Iframe Overlay with File Action
Impact: - Private file uploads to wrong app- Upload malware to admin system- Bypass upload validation using visual deception
Detection: - Use browser dev tools → Elements tab → inspect for iframe overlays- Log upload origins and compare with user page session
Remediation: - Use X-Frame-Options: DENY or CSP frame-ancestors 'none'- Require CSRF tokens or confirm uploads- Disable drag/upload via iframe overlays

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking (UI Redress) attack: Like/Favorite/Subscribe Clickjacking
output:
The attacker tricks a user into clicking a “Like”, “Subscribe”, or “Favorite” button on a social media or video platform like YouTube, Facebook, etc., by overlaying it behind an innocent-looking image or game.
Vulnerability: Frame Injection / UI Redress
Impact: - Forces users to subscribe/follow without consent- Manipulates social engagement- Can cause brand damage or spam attacks
Detection: - Inspect page using browser DevTools and check for invisible iframes- Monitor sudden spikes in engagement/subscriptions
Remediation: - Use X-Frame-Options: DENY- Use Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'- Confirm user intent with modal popups (not just 1 click)

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking + OAuth Abuse attack: Clickjacking in OAuth Flows
output:
The attacker tricks a user into clicking a button inside a hidden OAuth authorization page (such as Google or Facebook), where clicking authorizes the attacker’s app to gain access to the user’s profile or data without clear consent.
Vulnerability: UI Redress + OAuth Abuse
Impact: - Users may unknowingly give apps access to private profile info- Used in phishing, scam apps, impersonation, etc.
Detection: - Look for OAuth consent pages being loaded in iframe or from untrusted domains- Check browser CSP/X-Frame headers
Remediation: - Use X-Frame-Options: DENY or Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'- OAuth providers should block iframe rendering- Educate users with explicit permission prompts

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking (UI Redress) attack: Invisible CAPTCHA Clickjacking
output:
A malicious site tricks users into clicking a "Submit" or "Verify" button that is actually an invisible reCAPTCHA checkbox (or submit form protected by CAPTCHA) of another website embedded in an invisible iframe, thereby bypassing human verification checks.
Vulnerability: Lack of X-Frame-Options or CSP
Impact: CAPTCHA bypass, account creation abuse, fake signup form completions, bot avoidance mechanisms defeated
Detection: - Use DevTools > Network to check if CAPTCHA is embedded in iframe- Inspect form behavior during interaction
Remediation: - Add X-Frame-Options: DENY or Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' headers- Use JavaScript-based click detection- Block iframe embedding from 3rd-party domains

instruction: Describe the Clickjacking / UI Redressing attack: Clickjacking with Popups (Window Redressing)
output:
An attacker opens a popup window (or new browser window) that looks like a secure login or system notification. They then overlay this popup with a fake, visually similar element. The victim believes they’re interacting with a secure window, but are unknowingly clicking attacker-controlled buttons or inputs.
Vulnerability: No X-Frame-Options, lack of popup content integrity checks
Impact: Login hijacking, session takeover, fraudulent clicks, account access
Detection: - Manual analysis of popup behavior- Browser dev tools to inspect unexpected overlays or style changes- Look for tampered or dynamic DOM injections
Remediation: - Block popup window content modification via CSP and proper origin checks- Use frame-ancestors, sandbox, or verify opener integrity- Apply UI integrity checks on popups (JavaScript guards, referrer checks)

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Mapping attack: External Port Scanning (Classic)
output:
An attacker uses a port scanner from an external (outside the network) machine to find open, closed, or filtered ports on a public IP. This helps them identify what services (like SSH, FTP, web servers) are running and potentially exploitable.
Vulnerability: Open ports & exposed services
Impact: Attackers can find weak services like outdated SSH, open FTP, or unprotected databases
Detection: - IDS/IPS may flag Nmap scanning- Network logs show unusual port sweeps- Firewalls with logging
Remediation: - Use firewalls to block unused ports- Disable services you don't need- Enable IDS (Snort, Suricata)- Restrict IP ranges that can access specific services (e.g., SSH)

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack: Web-Based Port Scanning via SSRF
output:
A web app allows users to fetch URLs (e.g., import images, test webhooks, or check URLs) but fails to restrict internal IP access. An attacker abuses this to make the app scan internal or external ports by observing response time, HTTP codes, or errors from the server.
Vulnerability: SSRF → Internal Network Scanning
Impact: Attacker may discover internal DBs, admin panels, cloud metadata services (AWS, GCP)
Detection: - Web server logs- Web application firewalls- Monitor for unexpected internal IP access
Remediation: - Whitelist allowed domains in fetchers- Block internal IP ranges in SSRF endpoints- Use metadata API protection headers (AWS: Metadata-Flavor: Google)

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Browser Scam attack: JavaScript-Based Port Scanning (Client-Side)
output: An attacker embeds JavaScript code into a malicious or compromised website that attempts to connect to a series of IP:port combinations using hidden or

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Browser Scan attack: WebSocket-Based Port Scanning via Browser
output:
An attacker embeds JavaScript in a malicious web page that tries to connect to a list of ports on a target (like localhost or internal IPs) using WebSocket connections. Based on connection success or failure (via onopen / onerror events), they can determine which ports are open. This allows them to scan local or internal networks just by tricking a user into opening a browser page.
Vulnerability: WebSocket not restricted by CORS policy+ browsers allow connections to local ports
Impact: - Attackers can detect internal services like WebSocket APIs- Used for further targeted attacks based on service fingerprinting
Detection: - Monitor dev console or unusual network calls- Network firewalls may show attempts to internal ports
Remediation: - Disable access to internal services from browser- Implement strict Content Security Policy (CSP)- Use browser extensions that prevent unsolicited scripts

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Port Scanning via XXE attack: Port Scanning via XML External Entity (XXE) Payload
output:
An attacker exploits an XXE vulnerability in a web application that parses XML files. By injecting a specially crafted XML document with an external entity referencing internal network addresses (like http://127.0.0.1:22), the attacker can check which ports are open or closed on the internal network. This uses the application's own server to perform the scan, bypassing firewall restrictions and giving insight into private/internal systems.
Vulnerability: Improper XML parser configuration allowing external entity expansion
Impact: - Internal services exposed (e.g., databases, Redis, internal APIs)- Attackers gain internal visibility and plan lateral movement
Detection: - Monitor XML traffic- Detect unusual outbound HTTP requests in logs- Use application-level firewalls or WAFs
Remediation: - Disable external entity parsing in XML parsers- Use secure XML libraries (lxml, defusedxml) in Python, Java, PHP- Validate and sanitize all uploaded files

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution / Recon attack: Command Injection for Port Scanning (Ping Scan)
output:
The attacker finds a vulnerable parameter (e.g., form field or query string) that is not properly sanitized and allows command injection. They inject OS commands like ping, nc, or timeout into this parameter. By doing so, they can scan internal or external ports via the vulnerable server. This gives the attacker visibility into services running inside the network, even those not publicly exposed.
Vulnerability: Input not sanitized before OS command execution
Impact: - Allows internal reconnaissance- Gain visibility of open ports- Lateral movement possible from web app
Detection: - Monitor logs for abnormal shell usage- Use AppSec tools to test for unsafe functions like os.system()
Remediation: - Always sanitize input- Use subprocess with shell=False- Avoid direct command execution from user input- Use WAF to block unusual query patterns

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Port Discovery via DNS attack: DNS-Based Blind Port Scanning via SSRF
output:
An attacker uses a blind Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability to force a web server to connect to various internal ports. The attacker cannot directly observe the result (hence "blind"), but each connection attempt triggers a DNS request to an attacker-controlled domain, revealing the result indirectly. This allows port scanning of internal networks from the outside, even if the server is protected by firewalls.
Vulnerability: Server-Side Request Forgery (Blind SSRF + DNS Leaks)
Impact: - Internal services are mapped via DNS-based indirect signals- Firewalls bypassed due to internal resolution- Enables lateral movement or exploitation
Detection: - Monitor unusual DNS queries- Use DNS logging tools (e.g., Cloudflare, Akamai, firewall logs)- WAFs can detect unusual url= patterns
Remediation: - Block access to internal IPs in SSRF endpoints- Use allowlists (not blocklists)- Validate URL schemes strictly (http, https only)- Use DNS egress filtering to block untrusted domains

instruction: Describe the Covert Recon via Latency Measurement attack: Timing-Based Blind Port Scanning (via SSRF or RCE)
output:
This technique exploits an SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) or RCE (Remote Command Execution) vulnerability to scan internal ports without visible output. Instead of looking for direct responses, the attacker sends requests to different ports and measures the time delay in the server’s response. If a port is open, the server may take longer to respond due to connection timeout. This technique is useful when DNS logs or HTTP responses are unavailable, and only timing differences indicate success.
Vulnerability: SSRF or RCE allowing external connections or command execution
Impact: - Reveals open ports/services- Firewall bypass via internal timing- Enables deeper internal enumeration
Detection: - Log monitoring with time analysis- WAF can detect abnormal delays or SSRF parameters- Endpoint monitoring with EDR tools
Remediation: - Block SSRF/RCE using secure coding practices- Validate all input and URLs- Use metadata proxies with firewall rules- Disable unnecessary internal services

instruction: Describe the Stealth Recon / Firewall Bypass attack: Firewall Evasion Port Scanning
output:
An ethical tester wants to scan ports on a system behind a restrictive firewall that blocks standard scan tools. By tweaking scanning behavior—changing packet timing, splitting packets, randomizing port order, or using fragmented and stealthy techniques—they can identify open ports without triggering alerts. This simulates how attackers bypass defenses.
Vulnerability: Firewall packet filtering / IDS not evading stealth scans
Impact: - Reveals internal open ports- Attackers can bypass firewall detection- Enables deeper infiltration
Detection: - Monitor IDS/IPS alert logs- Analyze firewall events- Look for scanned IP/port patterns
Remediation: - Configure application-layer firewalls- Enforce strict egress/ingress packet filtering- Use IDS with anomaly detection

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Information Disclosure attack: HTTP Banner Grabbing (Web Server)
output:
An attacker or ethical tester sends simple HTTP requests to a web server to identify the server software, version, or other sensitive metadata. This is done through HTTP headers returned by the server. This information can be used in the next phase of an attack (e.g., to exploit version-specific vulnerabilities).
Vulnerability: Information disclosure via HTTP headers
Impact: - Identifies server version & type- Helps attacker plan version-specific attacks- Can lead to exploit or RCE attempts
Detection: - Use logging tools like Splunk, ELK, or Fail2Ban- Monitor for unexpected curl / telnet access patterns
Remediation: - Remove Server header in configs (ServerTokens Prod, ServerSignature Off)- Use reverse proxies (e.g., Nginx stripping headers)- Keep servers up to date

instruction: Describe the Passive Recon / Fingerprinting attack: HTTPS Banner Grabbing (TLS Fingerprinting)
output:
HTTPS servers use TLS (Transport Layer Security) to encrypt traffic. But when you connect to a server, before encryption begins, the TLS handshake shares metadata like supported ciphers, server certificates, and protocol versions. Tools can analyze this handshake and infer the type, version, and OS of the server (e.g., Nginx on Ubuntu). This is called TLS fingerprinting. No hacking—just passive detection.
Vulnerability: Metadata leakage in TLS handshake
Impact: - Reveals web server type, certificate, OS info- Helps in planning future attacks (e.g., outdated TLS or weak cipher use)
Detection: - Monitor TLS handshake analysis with IDS- Use SIEM (like Splunk) to flag excessive TLS fingerprinting
Remediation: - Use minimal info in TLS certs- Disable outdated protocols (e.g., TLS 1.0)- Use reverse proxies that hide server details

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Fingerprinting attack: FTP Banner Grabbing
output:
An attacker or penetration tester connects to an FTP server (File Transfer Protocol) to retrieve banner information like the FTP server software name, version, and operating system. This info helps identify vulnerabilities in outdated software. The banner is usually revealed immediately when you connect, even without logging in.
Vulnerability: Information disclosure via service greeting banners
Impact: - Identifies FTP server version- Enables targeted vulnerability scanning- Risk of full exploit via known CVEs
Detection: - Monitor port 21 access logs- Use IDS/IPS to track FTP banner grabbing attempts
Remediation: - Disable banner (in vsftpd.conf: ftpd_banner=)- Update FTP software regularly- Restrict anonymous access and whitelist IPs

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Fingerprinting attack: SSH Banner Grabbing
output:
When a user connects to an SSH server (on port 22), the server automatically sends a banner with details like OpenSSH version and sometimes the underlying OS. This is sent before login, so attackers or pentesters can use it to identify vulnerable software versions without needing credentials.
Vulnerability: Information disclosure via SSH protocol handshake
Impact: - Reveals software name & version- Helps attacker find version-specific exploits- May expose outdated vulnerable software
Detection: - Monitor connection attempts on port 22- Use fail2ban, UFW, or SSH logs to detect scans or banners reads
Remediation: - Suppress or modify banner:In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set:Banner noneDebianBanner noThen sudo systemctl restart ssh- Keep OpenSSH updated

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Fingerprinting attack: SMTP Banner Grabbing
output:
SMTP servers (used for sending email) run on port 25, 465, or 587. When a connection is made, they respond with a banner message showing the mail server type, version, and sometimes hostname. This information can help attackers identify software versions and plan targeted attacks, especially if the server runs an old or vulnerable version of Postfix, Exim, etc.
Vulnerability: Information leakage in banner greeting
Impact: - Reveals SMTP software and version- Helps attackers find known exploits- Risk of targeted vulnerability scanning
Detection: - Monitor port 25 connection attempts- Use SIEM tools (Splunk, ELK) to detect unusual SMTP probing
Remediation: - Suppress or modify banner in config:For Postfix: smtpd_banner = $myhostname ESMTP- Always keep SMTP server software updated

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Fingerprinting attack: DNS Service Banner Grabbing
output:
When you connect to a DNS server (usually on UDP or TCP port 53), you can send a simple query. Some misconfigured DNS servers may include version info, software details (like BIND 9.16, dnsmasq, etc.), or operating system fingerprints in their responses or in the version.bind record under the special CHAOS class. Attackers or pentesters use this to map DNS infrastructure.
Vulnerability: Information disclosure via DNS version banners
Impact: - Reveals DNS software name & version- Allows attacker to look up known vulnerabilities in that version
Detection: - Monitor DNS query logs for version.bind or CHAOS class queries- Use IDS tools to flag unusual DNS requests
Remediation: - Configure DNS to disable version responses:For BIND:options { version "Not Disclosed"; };- Block CHAOS class queries with firewall or app layer rules

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance / Fingerprinting attack: Custom Web App Headers
output:
Many custom-built or CMS-based web applications include unique HTTP response headers such as X-Powered-By, Server, X-CMS-Engine, or others. These headers can unintentionally reveal backend software, programming language (like PHP), server types, or even internal details. Attackers or ethical hackers can use simple tools to detect these headers and determine if they expose sensitive system info.
Vulnerability: Overexposed HTTP headers revealing stack info
Impact: - Exposes backend frameworks- May reveal outdated PHP/Node.js versions- Enables targeted attacks
Detection: - Monitor HTTP logs for user agents like curl/nmap- Use WAF or SIEM to flag banner enumeration
