Vulnerability: Windows Task Scheduler allows creating tasks to execute arbitrary codeRun level can be set to highest privileges without strong restrictions
Impact: - Persistent reverse shell- Local privilege escalation- Full code execution on every logon- Bypass antivirus with proxy EXEs
Detection: - Monitor new scheduled tasks (Event ID 4698)- Use Autoruns to audit scheduled jobs- Look for unknown payloads in \Tasks\ or %Public% folders- Use EDR rules for schtasks.exe abuse
Remediation: - Restrict schtasks.exe to admins only- Monitor creation of tasks with high privileges- Remove unused or unknown scheduled jobs- Use AppLocker / WDAC to block untrusted EXEs

instruction: Describe the Persistence + Privilege Escalation via Task Abuse attack: Modify Existing Task to Run Malicious Payload
output:
This simulation explores how an attacker can locate an existing scheduled task (created by the system or software), and modify it to point to a malicious payload instead of the original program. It abuses the fact that task actions (like .exe, .bat, .vbs) can be changed via CLI if the attacker has permission, resulting in stealthy persistence or privilege escalation.
Vulnerability: Task modification not monitoredLack of integrity check on task action pathPermissions on task not restricted
Impact: - Full privilege escalation- Stealthy reverse shell- Persistent backdoor with legit task name- Low AV detection rate if task was already trusted
Detection: - Enable Task Scheduler logging- Monitor Event IDs 4698 (register), 4700 (change), 4701 (disable)- Use EDR to detect changes to schtasks.exe arguments
Remediation: - Restrict task modification to SYSTEM/admin- Monitor schtasks.exe usage- Use AppLocker to block payload paths- Remove unneeded scheduled tasks- Harden permissions on existing tasks

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation + Persistence via Task File Abuse attack: Hijack Writable Scheduled Task Files
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with limited privileges can escalate by modifying the file contents (e.g., action .bat, .exe, .vbs) of an existing scheduled task — if that file is world-writable or write-accessible. When the task is next triggered, it executes the attacker's malicious payload with the privilege level of the task owner (e.g., SYSTEM or admin). Common in misconfigured software and IT automation environments.
Vulnerability: Scheduled tasks referencing writable filesImproper ACLs on task-linked resources
Impact: - SYSTEM privilege escalation- Stealthy persistence via existing task- Bypasses UAC and many EDRs- Used in ransomware + APT kits
Detection: - Use accesschk to audit tasks and their linked files- Monitor task folders and contents for changes- Event ID 4698, 4700 (task mod), and 4688 (process creation)
Remediation: - Apply strict ACLs on all task-linked files/scripts- Avoid referencing files in writable paths- Use Code Integrity / AppLocker- Regularly audit task configuration

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Task Misconfiguration attack: Leverage User-Level Tasks with Elevated Privileges
output:
This simulation shows how attackers can leverage user-created scheduled tasks that are configured to run with elevated privileges (e.g., SYSTEM or admin) but are modifiable or executable by the user. These tasks are often created by installers or IT scripts and may not enforce proper permissions. A local user can hijack such tasks to run malicious payloads at higher privilege levels without needing admin credentials.
Vulnerability: Scheduled tasks that run elevated but reference user-writable files or are user-creatable
Impact: - SYSTEM privilege escalation- Stealthy execution without alerting UAC- Used in ransomware, malware loaders- Persistence across reboots
Detection: - Use accesschk.exe to check task and file permissions- Review Windows Event ID 4698, 4700, 106- Monitor for modifications in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks and user temp folders
Remediation: - Ensure least privilege when creating tasks- Avoid Run with highest privileges if unnecessary- Use signed executables/scripts- Audit tasks regularly and monitor for new/changed entries

instruction: Describe the Persistence via Scheduled Task Abuse attack: Use Scheduled Tasks for Persistence
output:
Attackers commonly use Windows Task Scheduler to maintain persistence on a system. By creating a new scheduled task that launches a malicious binary at logon, startup, or a timed interval, malware ensures re-execution even after reboot. This method is stealthy and often blends into legitimate background tasks. It's widely used in APT campaigns, red teaming, and malware implants.
Vulnerability: Abusable task creation permissionsNo restrictions on who can create scheduled tasks
Impact: - Persistence across reboots/logons- Stealthy malware execution- Evasion of AV & user detection
Detection: - Monitor task creation events (Event ID 4698)- Use Autoruns/Sysinternals to scan for unusual tasks- Look for unsigned/unknown task paths
Remediation: - Limit who can create tasks- Monitor registry/task scheduler- Enable AppLocker or whitelisting- Use EDR for behavioral analysis

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Task COM Hijack attack: Abuse Task Scheduler COM Interface
output:
This simulation shows how an attacker can abuse the Task Scheduler COM interface (via Schedule.Service) to programmatically create or modify scheduled tasks, bypassing command-line logging or EDR detection. It allows stealthy creation of persistent or privilege-escalated tasks using Windows scripting (PowerShell or JScript) without using schtasks.exe or visible shell commands.
Vulnerability: Schedule.Service COM object lacks sufficient telemetryAV/EDR may not detect PowerShell COM usage
Impact: - Covert task creation- Evade schtasks command-line monitoring- Persist after reboot
Detection: - Monitor PowerShell event logs (4104, 4688)- Use Sysmon for COM object instantiation- Watch for suspicious task descriptions
Remediation: - Limit script-based COM creation- Enable script block logging- Use AppLocker to block PowerShell COM misuse

instruction: Describe the UAC Bypass via Auto-elevated Task Abuse attack: Bypass UAC via Scheduled Task
output:
This simulation shows how an attacker can bypass UAC (User Account Control) by leveraging auto-elevated scheduled tasks that already run with high integrity level. Many system-defined tasks in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks can be hijacked if permissions are misconfigured or if they're auto-elevated without a consent prompt. The attacker creates/modifies a scheduled task or executes one via command line or COM API to elevate privileges without triggering a UAC prompt.
Vulnerability: Auto-elevated scheduled task without secure action pathWritable path or arguments
Impact: - Full local privilege escalation- UAC bypass with no popup- Attacker gains SYSTEM/Administrator context
Detection: - Monitor usage of schtasks.exe or COM Scheduler API- Enable logging for task registration and execution (Event ID 4698, 4700)- Detect unsigned payloads executed by system tasks
Remediation: - Set UAC to “Always Notify” (value 2)- Avoid using scheduled tasks with “Run with highest privileges” for user-controlled tasks- Use AppLocker / Defender Application Control- Harden permissions on all task files and actions

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via Scheduled Tasks attack: Cron Job Injection
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with limited access on a Linux machine can escalate privileges by injecting a malicious command into a world-writable cron file, abusing misconfigured cron jobs, or placing a malicious script in directories executed by root-owned cron tasks. This is a common privilege escalation technique when Linux administrators use poor permission policies or leave writable cron paths exposed.
Vulnerability: Writable cron files or scriptsMisconfigured file permissionsImproper validation of scheduled tasks
Impact: - Attacker escalates to root- Can maintain persistence- Potential lateral movement or full takeover
Detection: - Monitor changes in /etc/cron*- Audit file permissions- Use auditd or pspy to detect unauthorized cron executions
Remediation: - Set strict permissions on all cron files and scripts- Use chown root:root and chmod 600 for cron tasks- Monitor cron job execution with logging and alerting

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via Cron Script Injection attack: Inject Payload into Writable Cron Script
output:
This scenario demonstrates how an attacker with low privileges can gain root access by modifying a writable cron-executed script. If a script executed by root via cron is found to be writable by any user, an attacker can append malicious commands to it (e.g., reverse shell), and gain elevated privileges once the cron job runs. This is a common misconfiguration in Linux systems where automation scripts are not properly protected.
Vulnerability: Root-owned script is writable by low-privileged user and executed on schedule
Impact: - Root-level code execution- Shell access- Full host compromise- Optional persistence mechanism
Detection: - Monitor cron execution and file changes- Use auditd, inotify, pspy- Watch for cron-based reverse shell behavior in logs
Remediation: - Set strict file permissions:chmod 700 and chown root:root for root scripts- Avoid world-writable cron scripts- Centralize script management and auditing

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via Crontab Injection attack: Writable Cron File (Root’s Crontab)
output:
This attack leverages misconfigured permissions on root’s crontab file or related files. If any cron job configuration file (e.g., /var/spool/cron/root or /etc/crontab) is writable by a non-root user, attackers can inject malicious commands or payloads. The cron daemon will execute them as root, giving the attacker elevated privileges or persistence.
Vulnerability: Crontab file owned by root is world/group-writable or misconfigured
Impact: - Attacker gains persistent root shell- Can run arbitrary code as root every minute- Privilege escalation
Detection: - Monitor crontab entries- Use auditd or inotify to track changes to /var/spool/cron/root- Monitor for reverse shell behavior in logs
Remediation: - Set proper permissions: chmod 600- Only root should own and write cron files- Monitor cron directories regularly- Use file integrity monitoring (FIM)

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Env Variable Manipulation attack: Hijack Environment Variable in Cron Job
output:
Many cron jobs use environment variables (e.g., PATH, SHELL, MAILTO) at the top of the crontab. If an attacker can edit a user's crontab (or trick the system into running it), they can set a malicious environment variable (like PATH) to point to a directory with a malicious binary, tricking the cron job to run their payload as root or a privileged user.
Vulnerability: Cron using insecure or attacker-controlled environment variables
Impact: - Malicious script execution- Escalation to root (if cron runs as root)- Data overwrite or exfil
Detection: - Monitor cron files for unusual env variables- Check PATH integrity before job runs- Use FIM on /etc/crontab and /var/spool/cron
Remediation: - Never include untrusted paths in cron environment- Set PATH to known safe defaults- Do not run critical cron jobs as root unnecessarily

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via File Hijacking attack: Hijack Log or Temp File Referenced by Cron Script
output:
In this scenario, a cron job run as root references a temporary file or log file (e.g., /tmp/task.log) that is world-writable or improperly permissioned. An attacker can replace or symlink the file to a malicious script or system file (like /etc/shadow). On next cron run, the root process overwrites it or executes unintended code, leading to privilege escalation or data corruption.
Vulnerability: Writable log or temp file used in root-owned cron job
Impact: - File overwrite as root- Full privilege escalation- Shadow file deletion or replacement
Detection: - Monitor cron job output- Use auditd or Sysmon for Linux- Detect symlink to protected files
Remediation: - Use mktemp with safe perms- Never write to world-writable paths- Validate log file paths- Use logrotate with correct perms

instruction: Describe the Persistence / Privilege Abuse via Cron attack: Create Malicious Cron Job in User Crontab
output:
In this attack, an adversary compromises a non-root user account and leverages the user's crontab to create a malicious scheduled task. The cron job ensures automatic execution of a payload, allowing the attacker to maintain persistence, re-establish access, or run arbitrary commands at specific intervals. This is a simple yet powerful method for stealthy persistence using native OS features.
Vulnerability: User-level cron access without validation or integrity checking
Impact: - Persistent backdoor access- Remote shell every minute- Recon/Enum/Data Theft possibilities
Detection: - Monitor user crontab entries- Enable auditd to track crontab -e usage- Review /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ changes
Remediation: - Disable cron for low-privilege users- Audit crontab usage- Alert on suspicious job contents- Use AppArmor/SELinux for script restrictions

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Persistence via Cron attack: Abuse World-Writable /etc/cron.d/
output:
If the directory /etc/cron.d/ is world-writable (chmod 777 or chmod o+w), attackers can place malicious job files that the cron daemon executes with root privileges. This attack exploits misconfigured file permissions, common in poorly hardened Linux systems, allowing any local user to escalate privileges or maintain stealthy persistence using native system cron features.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured directory permissions allowing global write access to /etc/cron.d/
Impact: - Root privilege escalation- System backdoor- Arbitrary command execution as root
Detection: - Monitor file integrity of /etc/cron.d/- Use auditd to track file writes- Alert on new files owned by non-root users
Remediation: - Restrict write permissions to /etc/cron.d/- Run chmod o-w /etc/cron.d- Implement tripwire, aide, or similar integrity checkers- Use AppArmor/SELinux to limit cron jobs

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via File Replace attack: Replace sethc.exe with cmd.exe (Classic)
output:
This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit access to the Windows System32 directory to replace sethc.exe (Sticky Keys) with cmd.exe. Once replaced, pressing Shift key 5 times at the login screen launches a SYSTEM-level command prompt without logging in, bypassing authentication. This exploit is often used on locked systems with physical access or bootable USBs.
Vulnerability: Weak physical securitySticky Keys enabledWrite access to System32 via boot media
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level shell without credentials- Add users- Change passwords- Enable backdoors
Detection: - Monitor for abnormal use of cmd.exe or sethc.exe at logon screen- Integrity check on System32 files- Audit login screen interactions
Remediation: - Disable Sticky Keys from login screen- Use full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Restrict BIOS boot options- Enable UEFI password- Monitor & block bootable media

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via File Replace attack: Replace Utility Manager (utilman.exe)
output:
This simulation demonstrates how attackers can exploit access to the Windows System32 directory to replace utilman.exe (Utility Manager) with cmd.exe. Utility Manager can be launched from the login screen via Windows + U shortcut. Once replaced, pressing this combo will trigger a SYSTEM-level command prompt, granting full access without logging in. Used in physical access or bootable USB scenarios.
Vulnerability: Physical access to System32Unrestricted file operationsEase of Access apps run as SYSTEM
Impact: - SYSTEM-level shell at login- Full user control- Add or reset passwords- Activate services like RDP
Detection: - Integrity monitoring on System32 binaries- Event log (ID 4688) for cmd.exe at login- Forensics for file modification timestamps
Remediation: - Disable Ease of Access tools on login screen- Use BitLocker for full disk encryption- Enable UEFI password- Restrict boot from USB / CD-ROM

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via File Replacement attack: Replace Alternate Accessibility Binaries
output:
This simulation demonstrates how attackers can escalate privileges by replacing alternate accessibility binaries (e.g., osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe) in C:\Windows\System32 with cmd.exe. These tools run with SYSTEM privileges at the login screen via Ease of Access or keyboard shortcuts. This allows full shell access without credentials — often used in red teaming or physical access post-exploitation.
Vulnerability: Accessibility binaries run as SYSTEMNo file integrity protection or BitLocker
Impact: - Full SYSTEM shell at login screen- Create admin users- Reset credentials- Enable RDP
Detection: - Detect changes to osk.exe, narrator.exe, etc.- Monitor for SYSTEM cmd.exe launch during login- Use File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) tools
Remediation: - Block USB boot or password protect BIOS- Enable full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Remove Ease of Access from login screen- Monitor System32 file changes

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (Offline Bypass) attack: Bypass via Live CD / Bootable USB
output:
This simulation showcases how an attacker can bypass Windows authentication entirely by booting from a Live CD or bootable USB (e.g., Kali Linux, WinPE) and accessing the NTFS partition of the system. From there, the attacker can reset local passwords, extract sensitive files (like SAM hashes), or replace system binaries (like cmd.exe, utilman.exe, sethc.exe). This is extremely effective where BitLocker or BIOS-level protections are not enforced.
Vulnerability: - No BIOS password- No USB boot restrictions- No disk encryption- Writable filesystem
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level access- Local password reset- User creation- Credential theft- Offline data exfiltration
Detection: - Monitor boot logs- Look for unexpected password resets- Check registry audit trails- Use forensic analysis tools
Remediation: - Enforce BIOS password- Disable USB boot- Enable full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Monitor registry and login changes- Use tamper-proof endpoint controls

instruction: Describe the Remote Local Privilege Escalation (RDP) attack: Sticky Keys RDP Bypass (Remote)
output:
This scenario shows how attackers who have RDP access to a Windows machine (often with limited or guest credentials) can gain SYSTEM-level access by triggering the sticky keys backdoor (sethc.exe). If cmd.exe has previously been swapped in place of sethc.exe, even low-privileged RDP users can spawn a SYSTEM shell at the login screen without physical access. Commonly abused in persistent or multi-session environments, such as corporate RDP servers, jump boxes, or VMs.
Vulnerability: Misuse of accessibility featuresUnprotected binary modificationInsecure RDP configurations
Impact: SYSTEM-level access remotelyAdmin account creationDomain-wide escalation (if reused creds)
Detection: Monitor for sticky keys launches (sethc.exe), audit System32 file integrity, track RDP session events
Remediation: Enable AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC)Protect accessibility binaries with permissionsEnforce MFA on RDPDisable unused RDP access

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (Linux) attack: Run Known Exploitable SUID Binary with Shell Spawn
output:
This simulation shows how attackers can exploit known vulnerable SUID binaries (e.g., vim, less, find, cp, etc. with SUID bit set) to gain root access. The attacker, starting as a limited user, finds these binaries using find or linpeas, and uses known abuse techniques from GTFOBins to escalate privileges by spawning a root shell (/bin/sh or /bin/bash). Very common in misconfigured or old Linux systems.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured SUID binariesImproper privilege management
Impact: Root-level shellFull system takeoverPossible persistence setup
Detection: File integrity tools (AIDE)Audit SUID binaries regularlyMonitor for abnormal uid=0 activity
Remediation: Remove unnecessary SUID bitsUse AppArmor/SELinux to restrict executionPatch or replace misconfigured binaries

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (Manual SUID) attack: Write Custom SUID C Shell Binary
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker or insider with write access to a directory or permission to execute a compiled binary with root ownership and SUID set, can compile a malicious C binary that spawns a shell (/bin/bash). Once executed, the attacker gains root shell access even from an unprivileged user. This simulates real misconfigurations where devs leave testing SUID binaries or attackers plant one. Common in weak hardened Linux systems.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured dev environmentSUID binary creation without audit
Impact: Full root shell access from local userSystem compromisePersistence setup
Detection: Scan for SUID files using find / -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -la {} \; regularlyAudit new binaries in sensitive paths
Remediation: Remove unnecessary SUID permissionsUse AppArmor or SELinux to deny executionDisallow gcc in production environments

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via SUID Misuse attack: SUID Binary Allows Arbitrary Command Execution
output:
This lab simulates how a user can gain root access by exploiting a vulnerable SUID binary that either improperly uses system(), or takes input without sanitization, allowing execution of arbitrary commands as root. These binaries are often overlooked in audits. This vulnerability is often found in homegrown admin scripts, legacy testing tools, or custom-built C programs left on production systems.
Vulnerability: Insecure use of system callsPoor input sanitization in SUID binaries
Impact: Root shell access from local userUnauthorized system modification
Detection: - Monitor for unusual SUID binaries- Use lsof, auditd, or AppArmor profiles- Check for strange user input passed to shell commands
Remediation: - Audit custom SUID binaries- Avoid using system() with user input- Remove SUID from unnecessary files- Use sudo with whitelist configuration instead

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via Shared Object Injection attack: LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH Injection
output:
This simulation showcases how a local attacker can abuse environment variables like LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH to load a malicious shared object (.so) before the target binary loads its real library. If the binary is not protected (e.g., not setuid-root or lacks sanitization), attackers can escalate privileges or hijack execution, especially in scripts or misconfigured cron jobs.
Vulnerability: Unsafe use of LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATHBinary does not sanitize environment variables
Impact: - Execute malicious code as root- Bypass intended restrictions- Full local privilege escalation
Detection: - Monitor use of LD_PRELOAD- Detect shared object injection with auditd, ps, or custom watchdogs
Remediation: - Strip SUID binaries of environment vars (secure_exec)- Use static linking for critical tools- Do not run SUID-root scripts that respect LD_PRELOAD

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via PATH Hijack attack: PATH Variable Manipulation (Unsafe System Calls)
output:
This simulation explores how an attacker can exploit a poorly written script or binary that uses relative system calls (e.g., system("cp file /tmp/")) without full paths. If the script runs with elevated privileges and the attacker can manipulate $PATH, they can replace the called command (e.g., cp) with a malicious version that spawns a root shell. This is a common misconfiguration in custom scripts and backup utilities.
Vulnerability: Unquoted/unqualified system calls in privileged scriptAttacker-controlled PATH
Impact: - Execute arbitrary code as root- Persistent privilege escalation- Lateral movement
Detection: - Use auditd to log execs- Check sudo scripts and cron jobs for unqualified calls
Remediation: - Always use absolute paths in privileged scripts (e.g., /bin/cp)- Sanitize environment vars- Avoid system() where possible

instruction: Describe the SUID abuse / Local shell attack: Python SUID Reverse Shell
output:
On a CTF or misconfigured system, /usr/bin/python is SUID-root. Attackers can leverage it to spawn a root shell and escalate privileges.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured SUID-root permissions on python binary
Impact: Full root shell obtained; attacker can access entire OS.
Detection: Monitor creation/use of SUID binaries; audit sudo/SUID files.
Remediation: Remove SUID bit from /usr/bin/python (chmod u‑s); restrict privileged binaries; implement least privilege.

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (SUID/BOF) attack: Exploit Custom SUID Binary via Buffer Overflow / File Overwrite
output:
A custom SUID binary written in C is installed with root ownership and SUID permission. Due to improper input validation (e.g., gets() or strcpy()), a classic buffer overflow is possible. This can be exploited to gain root shell, overwrite files, or hijack execution flow (e.g., overwrite return address to point to system("/bin/sh")). Common in old Linux apps and CTF machines.
Vulnerability: Buffer Overflow in SUID binaryImproper input validation (strcpy, gets)
Impact: Root shell executionFile overwritePrivilege escalation
Detection: • Use auditd to monitor SUID execs• Use gdb core dumps• Monitor /var/log/syslog for segfaults
Remediation: • Avoid SUID binaries unless essential• Use secure functions (fgets, snprintf)• Enable stack protection, ASLR, PIE• Regularly audit SUID files (find / -perm -4000)

instruction: Describe the Path Hijacking / File Execution Hijack attack: Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program.exe
output:
When Windows services or scheduled tasks use unquoted paths with spaces (e.g., "C:\Program Files\Example Service\service.exe"), Windows will look for the first matching executable in the split path (e.g., C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\Example.exe). An attacker with low privilege and write access to C:\ can drop a malicious executable named Program.exe, which runs with SYSTEM privileges when the service starts. Common on misconfigured Windows systems.
Vulnerability: Unquoted service path with spacesWritable C:\ drive for low-priv user
Impact: Full SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shellPersistence setup
Detection: - Event logs: 7045 (Service install), 4697 (Service start)- Use Sysmon to monitor unexpected EXE in C:\
Remediation: - Always quote paths in Windows service configs- Remove write permissions from C:\ for Users- Use GPO to enforce restricted paths

instruction: Describe the Path Hijacking via Intermediate Executable attack: Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program Files\Some.exe
output:
Similar to the C:\Program.exe attack, this technique targets unquoted Windows service paths with intermediate folders having spaces. If a service is configured like "C:\Program Files\Some Folder\AppService.exe" and the attacker has write access to C:\Program Files\, they can drop a malicious file like Some.exe. When the system attempts to start the service, it may launch Some.exe instead of the correct binary due to how Windows handles path parsing. This results in SYSTEM-level execution of the attacker's EXE.
Vulnerability: Unquoted service pathWritable intermediate directoryImproper file hierarchy configuration
Impact: SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shell or backdoorPersistence installation
Detection: • Use Sysinternals Process Monitor (procmon)• Enable auditing on folder/EXE creation• Monitor service binary paths regularly
Remediation: • Always quote service paths• Prevent write access to C:\Program Files\ for non-admins• Enforce folder ACLs via GPO• Regular audit via wmic/sc qc

instruction: Describe the Path Hijacking via Writable Directory attack: Writable Directory Within Path
output:
In this technique, attackers exploit a writable directory that appears in the system %PATH% environment variable. When a privileged process or user runs a command without specifying a full path, Windows will search each directory in %PATH% for that binary. If a lower-privileged user can drop a malicious EXE (e.g., net.exe, whoami.exe) in one of these writable directories, and the process prioritizes it, the attacker’s binary is executed with higher privileges (e.g., SYSTEM).
Vulnerability: Writable PATH directoryCommand execution without full binary pathNo integrity checking
Impact: Full SYSTEM privilegeReverse shell or local adminCode execution during service/scheduled task/script runs
Detection: • Enable audit logging• Monitor %PATH% environment• Use Sysmon or EDR to detect rogue binaries• Review folder-level permissions regularly
Remediation: • Never include user-writable directories in %PATH%• Use full paths in scripts and configs• Lock down folder ACLs in %PATH%• Use AppLocker or allowlists

instruction: Describe the Path Hijacking via Unquoted Service Path with Space attack: Path Injection via Space in Custom Service Paths
output:
This attack abuses custom Windows services registered with unquoted executable paths containing spaces (e.g., "C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe"). When the service starts, Windows attempts to parse the path incorrectly and may execute a malicious binary placed at an intermediate path, such as C:\Apps\My.exe. This allows a low-privileged attacker with write access to the directory to escalate privileges to SYSTEM, as the service is executed under elevated context.
Vulnerability: Unquoted service path with intermediate spaceNo input validationWritable intermediate directory
Impact: Full SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shellPersistence backdoor
Detection: • Monitor service execution paths• Sysmon/Procmon for unusual binary execution• Check for unexpected EXEs in common app folders
Remediation: • Always quote binary paths in Windows services• Lock directory permissions where services are installed• Regular audit using wmic, sc, accesschk, GPO• Use AppLocker / Defender Application Control

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution over WinRM (PowerShell) attack: Remote PowerShell Execution via Evil-WinRM
output:
This attack demonstrates how an attacker with valid credentials (typically obtained via credential dumping or phishing) can use Evil-WinRM, a post-exploitation tool, to gain a remote PowerShell session on a Windows machine. It abuses Windows Remote Management (WinRM), which is often enabled on domain-joined machines for administrative purposes. If WinRM is exposed and a local or domain admin account is known, attackers can achieve remote SYSTEM-level code execution.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured or exposed WinRM serviceValid credentialsWeak endpoint protection
Impact: Remote PowerShell accessCode execution as SYSTEMDomain persistenceLateral movement
Detection: - Monitor for Evil-WinRM usage- Analyze logs for 5985/5986 activity- Review remote PowerShell audit events (event IDs 4100–4104)- Use EDRs to flag unusual scripts
Remediation: - Disable WinRM where not needed- Use strong auth (Kerberos, 2FA)- Use Just Enough Admin (JEA)- Monitor and restrict lateral movement- Apply PowerShell logging and constrained language mode

instruction: Describe the Credential Abuse / Network Pivoting attack: Lateral Movement Using Stolen Hashes (Pass-the-Hash)
output:
This simulation showcases how attackers can perform lateral movement inside a Windows Active Directory network using NTLM password hashes instead of plaintext passwords. This is known as Pass-the-Hash (PtH). If the attacker compromises a system and dumps password hashes using tools like Mimikatz, they can use those hashes to access other systems that accept NTLM authentication, effectively bypassing the need for passwords.
Vulnerability: NTLM authentication enabledPrivilege reuseWeak hash protection (no LSA hardening)
Impact: Lateral movementAdmin shellFull network takeoverRemote code execution
Detection: - Monitor logon events- Detect NTLM login attempts across hosts- Use EDR to flag tools like Mimikatz- SIEM with lateral auth pattern rules
Remediation: - Disable NTLM where possible- Use LSA protection- Implement tiered admin accounts- Audit logins and sessions- Apply credential guard and EDR solutions

instruction: Describe the Legitimate Feature Abuse / Remote Code Execution attack: Remote Execution with PowerShell Remoting (Built-In)
output:
This attack demonstrates how PowerShell Remoting, a legitimate Windows feature (WinRM), can be abused to execute commands on remote domain-joined Windows systems without needing to drop any binaries. Attackers often use this method during lateral movement, especially post-credential theft. If WinRM is enabled and the attacker has valid credentials, they can remotely execute commands over HTTP(S), fully fileless.
Vulnerability: Overexposed WinRMDefault config allows domain authUnrestricted access to remote execution
Impact: Remote code executionFileless payload deliveryLateral movement across network
Detection: • Review PowerShell logs• Monitor 5985/5986 traffic• Correlate logon + remote execution events• Use SIEM to detect unusual PSRemoting patterns
Remediation: • Restrict WinRM access via GPO / IP ACLs• Disable for non-admin users• Use Just Enough Admin (JEA)• Enforce full script-block logging• Implement strong EDR rules

instruction: Describe the Remote Command Execution / Credential Abuse attack: Abuse Misconfigured WinRM with Weak Credentials
output:
This scenario demonstrates how an attacker abuses Windows Remote Management (WinRM) where WinRM is enabled, and a domain/local account with weak credentials is available. If WinRM is not properly restricted (e.g., open to all IPs or LAN), and credentials are easily guessed or harvested, attackers can gain remote shell access, execute payloads, pivot to other systems, or dump further credentials.
Vulnerability: WinRM exposed + weak credentialsNo network ACLsDefault config allows remote auth
Impact: - Full remote code execution- Credential dumping- Lateral movement & persistence
Detection: - Monitor WinRM logs- Failed/successful logon attempts- Unexpected logon times or from new IPs
Remediation: - Disable WinRM if not used- Enforce strong passwords- Restrict WinRM via GPO/network ACLs- Use PowerShell logging and alerting

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution / Persistence attack: Drop Backdoor Payload via WinRM
output:
This attack simulates how an adversary with valid credentials (gained via phishing, dump, or brute-force) can use Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to drop and execute a malicious payload (e.g., backdoor reverse shell or C2 beacon) directly on the target system. Misconfigured WinRM or poor access controls allow attackers to abuse legitimate management features for persistent access.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured WinRM accessWeak credentialsNo endpoint monitoring or EDRWinRM port open internally
Impact: • Full remote access with Meterpreter• Drop of persistent backdoors• Total takeover of Windows host• Possible lateral movement and domain compromise
Detection: • Monitor WinRM logs• Alert on EXE transfers• Analyze PowerShell logs• IDS alerts for beaconing traffic to attacker
Remediation: • Restrict WinRM to trusted IPs• Disable WinRM if unused• Use strong passwords & rotate creds• Deploy EDR to detect evil-winrm use• Segment network + logging

instruction: Describe the Lateral Movement using Built-in Protocol attack: Abuse Domain Admin Privileges to Pivot via WinRM
output:
This simulation explores how a threat actor, once in possession of domain admin credentials, can use WinRM (Windows Remote Management) to perform lateral movement, drop payloads, and execute remote PowerShell commands across multiple domain-joined systems. It leverages legitimate admin privileges and misconfigured WinRM or no endpoint protection, making it a stealthy post-exploitation technique. Often used in real-world APT attacks, internal red team operations, or malware propagation campaigns.
Vulnerability: Abuse of legitimate WinRM configurationInsufficient endpoint loggingFlat network with no segmentationOver-permissioned domain accounts
Impact: • Complete lateral movement from single entry point• Spread of malware or backdoors across environment• Full control of systems via PowerShell• Dumping of hashes, tokens, and secrets remotely
Detection: • Monitor Event IDs: 4688, 4624, 4104, 4648• Look for unusual WinRM sessions• Use EDR to flag Evil-WinRM strings or beaconing• Detect tools like mimikatz in memory• Network IDS for port 5985/5986 internal traffic
Remediation: • Restrict DA usage to jump hosts• Disable WinRM unless needed• Enforce LAPS and password rotation• Apply host segmentation (no flat trust)• PowerShell ScriptBlock and Transcription Logging• Apply Just-Enough-Administration (JEA)

instruction: Describe the Remote Reconnaissance / Info Leak attack: Remote Enumeration via WinRM
output:
This simulation demonstrates how attackers or red teamers can use Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to remotely enumerate system information, user accounts, group memberships, installed software, patches, running services, and other sensitive data without needing direct shell access or exploits. This technique leverages legit administrative access and can often bypass detection when WinRM is permitted internally. It is commonly used for privilege escalation, lateral movement prep, and AD recon.
Vulnerability: WinRM exposed internallyOver-permissioned usersLack of PowerShell loggingAbsence of endpoint behavior analysis tools
Impact: - Leakage of critical host information- Identification of high-value domain targets- Silent recon without triggering AV- Staging for further lateral movement
Detection: - PowerShell Event ID 4104 (ScriptBlock Logging)- Security Log ID 4624 (Logon Type 3)- Monitor WinRM connection logs- EDR detections on mass enumeration patterns- Correlation of recon tool execution
Remediation: - Enable full PowerShell logging- Restrict WinRM to management hosts- Block unnecessary lateral communication- Use Just Enough Admin (JEA) on endpoints- Monitor for recon patterns in logs- Deploy EDR with script detection

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution / Shell Access attack: Reverse Shell via Encoded PowerShell Payload
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can leverage built-in Windows tools like powershell.exe to establish a reverse shell using an encoded command. Encoding allows the payload to bypass simple input filters and AV detections. This is often used in phishing payloads, web shell post-exploitation, and lateral movement in enterprise Windows environments.
Vulnerability: Abuse of PowerShell for Remote Code Execution using Encoded Payload
Impact: Full remote shell access to the target system; potential privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or lateral movement
Detection: - Monitor for PowerShell using EncodedCommand in command-line arguments - Use PowerShell logging (ScriptBlock & Module logging) - SIEM alerting for suspicious Base64 payloads - Detect outbound traffic to unknown IPs on uncommon ports
Remediation: - Block PowerShell for standard users via AppLocker or WDAC - Disable PowerShell v2 - Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode - Use Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions- Train users on phishing and suspicious scripts

instruction: Describe the Persistence / Privilege Escalation via Service Hijack attack: Binary Replacement in Auto-Started Services
output:
In this scenario, an attacker abuses weak permissions on a Windows service binary path. If the service is set to auto-start and its executable path is writable by non-admin users, an attacker can replace the binary with a malicious payload. On system boot or manual service start, the malicious binary runs with elevated (SYSTEM) privileges. This attack is useful for persistence and privilege escalation.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured service binary path, Writable by non-admin users, Auto-starting with SYSTEM
Impact: SYSTEM-level reverse shell Full OS takeover Persistence across reboots
Detection: - Monitor file changes in service binary locations - Use tools like Sysmon - Procmon can detect binary tampering - Event Viewer logs 7036 (service start/stop)
Remediation: - Enforce NTFS permissions - Remove write access for Users - Use icacls to audit paths - Monitor services that run as SYSTEM - Use AppLocker or WDAC to block unsigned binaries

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Code Execution attack: DLL Hijacking in Writable Folders
output:
This simulation shows how attackers exploit applications that load DLL files from directories with weak permissions. If a user can place a malicious DLL in a writable folder and the application loads DLLs by relative path (without full path hardcoded), the attacker’s DLL can get executed automatically when the app or service runs. This technique abuses DLL search order behavior in Windows.
Vulnerability: DLL Search Order HijackWritable folder for standard userMissing or relative DLL path loading
Impact: Reverse shell with elevated privilegesPersistence via auto-runBypassing AppLocker (if DLL is unsigned)
Detection: - Use Process Monitor to detect DLL loading anomalies- Check Event Viewer logs- Monitor file writes to program folders- Enable DLL loading audit policies
Remediation: - Restrict folder write permissions- Use full paths in LoadLibrary- Sign all custom DLLs- Enable Safe DLL Search Mode- Use AppLocker to restrict DLL execution

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Persistence attack: Hijack Startup Entries or Scripts
output:
This attack simulates how an attacker can gain persistence or elevated code execution by hijacking startup entries or scripts (like .bat, .vbs, .ps1) that automatically execute at user login or system boot. This commonly involves modifying registry keys, startup folders, scheduled task scripts, or even login initialization files (e.g., init.bat, GPO logon scripts).
Vulnerability: Startup folder / Registry key points to writable scripts or pathsNo integrity or signature checksInsecure file permissions
Impact: Full persistenceAuto-execution of attacker payloadsAdmin/SYSTEM-level shell if service is elevatedCredential theft, C2 beacon, lateral movement
Detection: - Monitor changes to startup folders and registry Run keys- Enable Sysmon event logs for process creations- Use Windows Defender ATP or Sysinternals Autoruns- Detect unsigned script executions at boot/login
Remediation: - Lock down folder/script permissions- Use code signing- Monitor registry keys via Group Policy- Use AppLocker to restrict unapproved script execution

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Execution Hijack attack: Writable in PATH → Drop Trojan Binary
output:
This simulation covers a real-world technique where attackers find writable directories in the system’s %PATH% variable and drop a trojan binary with the same name as a legitimate tool (e.g., python.exe, net.exe, curl.exe). When any user or scheduled process calls that binary name without the full path, Windows uses its path search order — executing the attacker's binary first if it’s in an earlier or equal path. This enables stealthy privilege escalation or persistence, especially when the original binary is trusted by security products.
Vulnerability: Writable folder in PATHNo binary path hardcodingScript uses command name (not full path)
Impact: - Full code execution- Lateral movement- Remote access- Stealthy persistence- Execution under trusted binary name
Detection: - Monitor PATH variable for new/writable entries<br- Use AppLocker / WDAC- Detect duplicate binary names in multiple PATHs- Hash check on launched binaries- Use Sysmon for process creation logs
Remediation: - Lock down permissions on all PATH folders- Avoid adding writable folders to PATH- Call binaries using full path in all scripts- Monitor environment variable changes via GPO- Implement signed binary enforcement

instruction: Describe the Persistence / Social Engineering attack: Persistence via Shortcut Hijack
output:
This simulation shows how an attacker can achieve stealthy persistence by modifying existing shortcut (.lnk) files — often on the Desktop, Start Menu, or Startup folders. These shortcuts normally point to legitimate programs, but if a shortcut is writable, the attacker can change it to first execute malicious code, and then launch the legitimate app to avoid user suspicion. This method works well in multi-user systems where users trust shortcuts and don’t verify their properties.
Vulnerability: Writable .lnk files in user-accessible pathsStartup folder permissionsMissing shortcut signing or validation
Impact: - Stealthy code execution- Persistence across reboots- User-triggered execution- Lateral movement vector- Minimal antivirus detection
Detection: - Monitor changes to .lnk files- Check shortcut hashes or signatures- Use Windows Defender’s Controlled Folder Access- Use Sysmon with Event ID 1 + command line filters
Remediation: - Lock down Desktop, Startup folder permissions- Disable public Desktop if unused- Prevent COM access to WScript from user accounts- Educate users not to trust shortcut icons blindly

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Execution Hijack attack: Linux: Abuse of Writable /usr/local/bin/
output:
On misconfigured Linux systems, if a user has write access to /usr/local/bin/, an attacker can place a malicious executable with the same name as a trusted system binary (e.g., ls, nano, git). Since /usr/local/bin/ is usually early in the $PATH, the system may execute the attacker's binary before the real one. This allows attackers to hijack command execution, perform privilege escalation (if triggered by privileged processes), or establish persistence.
Vulnerability: Writable directory in $PATHUnsanitized command executionNo binary path hardcodingUsers run commands by name
Impact: - Full user or root shell- Stealthy execution- Hijack frequently used binaries- Elevation via cron or scheduled tasks
Detection: - Monitor and alert on world-writable PATH directories- Use auditd or inotify for file drops in /usr/local/bin- Log all command execution and match binary hashes- Use AppArmor or SELinux
Remediation: - Set /usr/local/bin permissions to root:root 755- Remove world/group write bits- Enforce full-path execution in scripts- Monitor cron or PATH abuse- Use signed binaries only where possible

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation / Persistence attack: Hijack Group Policy Scripts in Domain
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with write access to Group Policy logon scripts in a domain can hijack GPO-based login or startup behavior to run malicious payloads. These GPO scripts often run with user or even SYSTEM privileges during logon or startup. If GPO scripts reside on a writable network share (e.g., \\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Policies\...) and lack ACL enforcement, an attacker can modify them to include reverse shells or persistent backdoors. This is especially dangerous if applied domain-wide or to privileged OU objects.
Vulnerability: Weak ACLs on SYSVOLWritable GPO scriptsLack of script signingImproper OU delegationNo GPO change auditing
Impact: - Domain-wide persistence- Remote code execution- Privilege escalation to domain admin if applied to privileged users- Stealthy and trusted method- Difficult to detect without strong auditing
Detection: - Enable auditing on SYSVOL- Monitor file changes to GPO script folders- Use Sysmon Event ID 1 + command line filters- Enable GPO change alerts in SIEM- Check login behavior for anomalies
Remediation: - Lock down GPO script folder ACLs- Only allow Domain Admins to edit scripts- Use signed PowerShell scripts- Avoid using login/startup scripts if not needed- Regularly review SYSVOL for unauthorized changes

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation attack: Dirty COW – Copy-on-Write Exploit
output:
Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) is a well-known Linux kernel vulnerability that allows an unprivileged local attacker to escalate privileges to root by exploiting a race condition in the copy-on-write (COW) mechanism of memory management. This attack allows overwriting of read-only memory mappings, such as /etc/passwd, by exploiting madvise() and ptrace or threads, without proper permissions. This simulation walks through a controlled lab scenario to demonstrate full exploitation on a vulnerable Linux kernel (e.g., 2.6.22 - 3.x/4.x), showing how a normal user can gain full root shell.
Vulnerability: Race condition in copy-on-write (COW) memory mappingAllowed unprivileged memory overwrite via madvise()
Impact: - Full root access from normal user- Total system takeover- Can be automated or persistent- Works even without sudo- Stealthy in many logging environments
Detection: - Kernel-level logging for memory violations (rare)- Tripwire to monitor /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow changes- Check auditd logs for unusual privilege changes- Use Sysmon for Linux to monitor execution flow
Remediation: - Patch kernel immediately (apt upgrade, yum update)- Set /etc as read-only (if immutable system)- Use LSMs like AppArmor or SELinux- Monitor system file changes- Do not allow shell access to unknown users

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation / File Tampering attack: Dirty Pipe – Overwrite Read-Only Files
output:
Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) is a severe Linux kernel vulnerability that allows local users to overwrite read-only or root-owned files, even without having write permissions. It leverages a flaw in the Linux pipe buffer flag handling, allowing attackers to inject data into files like /etc/passwd or system binaries, gaining root shell. This is similar to Dirty COW but more powerful on newer kernels (5.8–5.16.11). This simulation shows a step-by-step lab to escalate privileges by editing /etc/passwd to add a root-level user.
Vulnerability: Linux Kernel Pipe Buffer Flag Mishandling (CVE-2022-0847)Write to read-only filesBypass traditional access controls
Impact: - Full root shell- Backdoor user creation- Tampering of protected configs- Kernel-layer stealth file overwrite- Persistence through modified binaries or passwd entries
Detection: - Monitor for unauthorized changes to /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow- Audit file integrity using Tripwire or AIDE- Review kernel logs for memory anomalies (though stealthy)- Use Sysmon for Linux or auditd rules- Run vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS)
Remediation: - Apply kernel patches (5.16.11+)- Update via apt update && apt upgrade- Use grsecurity or SELinux policies- Restrict shell access- Monitor sensitive file integrity using tools like aide

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation attack: OverlayFS Exploit (CVE-2021-3493)
output:
This simulation demonstrates a privilege escalation vulnerability in Ubuntu's patched OverlayFS module, introduced by Canonical and affecting several Ubuntu versions (including 20.04 and 21.04). By abusing the Linux OverlayFS filesystem and mounting it improperly, unprivileged users can create unauthorized entries in sensitive directories and gain elevated privileges. The flaw lies in how user namespaces allow mounting of OverlayFS without proper capability checks. The attacker can overwrite or inject content into protected locations such as /etc or escalate to root by placing and executing crafted binaries.
Vulnerability: CVE-2021-3493Improper OverlayFS mount privilege checks in Ubuntu-patched kernelUser namespace bypass
Impact: - Root access from regular user- Full control of system binaries- Persistence installation possible- Affects Ubuntu kernels < 5.11
Detection: - Monitor OverlayFS mount usage- Detect suspicious mount/unmount operations- Check for unexpected setuid binaries- Use auditd for exec/mount tracing
Remediation: - Upgrade to patched kernel (Ubuntu 5.11.0-27+)- Disable unprivileged user namespaces if not needed- Use AppArmor or SELinux- Monitor binary modifications

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) attack: Dirty Cred – Kernel Credential Exploit
output:
Dirty Cred (CVE-2022-2586) is a kernel-level LPE vulnerability affecting Linux 5.8+ (notably 5.10 LTS). It enables unprivileged users to reuse credential structures from privileged processes by exploiting a use-after-free vulnerability in the Netfilter subsystem (nf_tables). Unlike traditional LPEs, it doesn't overwrite system files — instead, it hijacks credential pointers to impersonate root users. Dirty Cred is stealthy, doesn’t touch disk, and bypasses traditional file monitoring solutions, making it ideal for red team persistence or container escape.
Vulnerability: Use-after-free in nf_tables allows kernel memory reuseHijacks freed cred pointer
Impact: - Root access from any unprivileged user- Bypasses sudo/su- No file or config overwrite- Works inside containers (host kernel)
Detection: - Monitor kernel logs and auditd for unusual Netfilter access- Use eBPF tools like tracee or bpftrace to track memory corruption- Detect abnormal UID switches- Enable SELinux/AppArmor
Remediation: - Upgrade Linux Kernel to patched version (≥ 5.10.102)- Apply vendor security patches- Restrict access to nf_tables if unused- Disable unprivileged user namespaces if not needed

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation attack: Stack Clash (glibc Bug)
output:
Qualys-discovered Stack Clash (CVE‑2017‑1000364 and related CVEs) affects Linux, BSD, Solaris. Glibc allows the stack to expand past guard pages by growing downward and colliding (“clashing”) with adjacent memory regions (heap, mapped sections). Attackers exploit this to overwrite memory, hijack return addresses, and escalate to root.
Vulnerability: Inadequate glibc guard-page size (4 KB too small)Stack‑heap/mmap clash exploits memory overlap
Impact: ➤ Root shell from unprivileged user➤ Full takeover without code signing➤ Works in containers or local shells➤ No file-system modifications
Detection: ✅ Audit abnormal stack allocations, monitor ulimit usage✅ Capture process crashes or memory corruption via syslog✅ Use eBPF to detect guard page skips✅ Monitor for root shells from unusual binaries
Remediation: ✅ Update to fixed kernels (≥ 4.11.6 or distro patches)✅ Recompile glibc with -fstack-check or enable larger guard-pages ✅ Harden ulimit for untrusted users✅ Use AppArmor/SELinux to confine suid binaries | #StackClash #CVE20171000364 #glibcBug #LocalExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #QualysResearch #PoC #LinuxKernelExploit | Qualys Blog (blog.qualys.com), CVE-DB, Debian DSA (debian.org)

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation to Root attack: CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit) – pkexec Local Root
output:
A critical vulnerability in the pkexec utility (part of polkit) allows any unprivileged local user to gain full root access on Linux. This bug has existed since 2009 and affects nearly every major Linux distribution.
Vulnerability: Out-of-bounds write in pkexec
Impact: Full root access for local users
Detection: Monitor /var/log/auth.log for abnormal pkexec calls; detect use of unprivileged users gaining UID 0
Remediation: Update polkit package to version 0.120 or later; apply OS security patches; restrict local shell access

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation attack: Writable Policy Files (.rules) Abuse
output:
In certain misconfigured Linux systems, the .rules files used by Polkit or udev under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ are world-writable or user-writable. Attackers with limited access can exploit this misconfiguration to insert malicious rules that escalate privileges without user interaction, allowing root-level command execution or persistence.
Vulnerability: Writable .rules files under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ allowing unauthorized modification
Impact: Root-level access via crafted .rules file without passwordPotential for full system takeover and persistence
Detection: Monitor .rules file changes using auditctl, inotifywait, or tripwireCorrelate with authentication bypass in journalctl or auth.log
Remediation: Remove world-writable permissions:chmod 644 <file> and chown root:root <file>Implement file integrity monitoring (e.g., AIDE, Tripwire)Restrict user write permissionsUpdate Polkit or udev to patched version

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Policy Abuse attack: Bypass via Misconfigured Polkit Policy (pkla)
output:
Linux systems that run ML workloads often rely on background services (e.g., JupyterHub, Dask, systemd units). If the PolicyKit (Polkit) system is misconfigured using .pkla files, it can unintentionally allow non-root users to execute root-level actions like restarting services or editing configurations.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured Polkit .pkla rules
Impact: Root-level control of ML pipelines or system services
Detection: Check for wildcard policies in .pkla files; monitor journalctl for service control by non-admins
Remediation: Use polkitd's modern JavaScript rules; remove legacy .pkla; restrict identities to specific, trusted usernames

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) attack: Abusing GUI Applications using pkexec
output:
This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can abuse GUI-based Linux applications that internally invoke pkexec (e.g., gparted, synaptic, gnome-disks) to escalate privileges. When these GUI apps use pkexec for privilege elevation but do not properly validate the environment, attackers may inject commands, overwrite binaries, or hijack execution using insecure graphical prompts or insecure environment propagation (e.g., through XDG_SESSION_ID, DISPLAY, or GDK_BACKEND). The attack allows GUI-based privilege escalation from an unprivileged user session.
Vulnerability: GUI applications that invoke pkexec without proper environment validation
Impact: - Local user gains root through GUI path manipulation- GUI app escalates injected binary
Detection: - Monitor GUI pkexec invocations- Log pkexec usage with environment variables- Detect DISPLAY, PATH, and XDG_SESSION_ID abuse
Remediation: - Avoid calling pkexec without full binary paths- Use PolicyKit rules to restrict GUI apps- Harden GUI session isolation and X11 access permissions

instruction: Describe the Remote Command Execution (RCE) attack: Remote Command Execution via wmic (CMD)
output:
This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can leverage wmic (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) to remotely execute commands on another Windows system, typically within the same domain or workgroup, using valid credentials. This method is commonly used in lateral movement post-compromise, or as part of remote admin tasks abused by threat actors in environments with weak endpoint monitoring.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted WMIC remote access with valid credentials
Impact: Remote command executionLateral movementInitial foothold or post-exploitation
Detection: - Monitor WMIC usage logs- Enable PowerShell and WMI logging- Alert on suspicious process call create events
Remediation: - Disable WMIC via GPO if not needed- Restrict remote WMI usage via firewall- Use EDR to monitor child processes from wmic.exe

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Remote Execution via PowerShell + WMI
output:
This technique showcases how an attacker can remotely execute commands on a Windows system using PowerShell in combination with WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation). This method is often used in lateral movement during post-exploitation, leveraging valid credentials and WMI classes like Win32_Process to execute commands remotely via Invoke-WmiMethod.

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) attack: Lateral Movement via Metasploit WMI
output:
This technique demonstrates how attackers can perform lateral movement within a Windows network using Metasploit Framework and WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation). The attacker leverages valid credentials or an existing Meterpreter session to remotely execute commands or payloads on a target machine. It is commonly used in post-exploitation to silently pivot to other machines.

Impact: Full remote control of lateral targetPrivilege escalation or remote persistence
Detection: • WMI Logs: Windows Event ID 5857–5861• PowerShell logs if WMI calls PowerShell• Network logs of RPC/DCOM• Metasploit session tracking
Remediation: • Disable or restrict WMI access• Apply firewalls to limit RPC/WMI to trusted sources• Implement LAPS and credential hygiene• Monitor WMI child process creation

instruction: Describe the Persistence (WMI Event Trigger) attack: WMI Persistence via Event Subscription
output:
This technique demonstrates how an attacker can establish persistence on a Windows system by creating a WMI permanent event subscription. This allows code execution to occur in response to a specific system event (e.g., user logon). Since these subscriptions reside in the WMI repository and do not rely on files or registry keys, they are stealthy and resilient across reboots.
Vulnerability: Abusable WMI namespaces + unrestricted consumer access
Impact: - Code execution on every logon- Fileless persistence- Evades common AV scans
Detection: - Use Sysmon to monitor process creation- WMI logging (Event ID 5861, 5860)- Autoruns → WMI tab- WMI Explorer or Get-WmiObject inspections
Remediation: - Enable WMI logging- Audit creation of __EventFilter and CommandLineEventConsumer- Use WMI hardening and restrict namespaces- Deploy Sysinternals Autoruns for auditing

instruction: Describe the Reconnaissance (Local + Remote) attack: WMI Enumeration for Reconnaissance
output:
WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) can be used by attackers to enumerate detailed system information such as user accounts, running processes, installed software, startup items, and more — without needing admin privileges. This technique is commonly used during post-exploitation or lateral movement to silently gather host intelligence. Can be used locally or remotely (via DCOM/WMI).
Vulnerability: Unrestricted WMI namespaces + exposed WinRM/WMI DCOM services
Impact: - Silent system profiling- AV evasion- Preparation for privilege escalation or lateral movement
Detection: - Enable WMI auditing- Monitor Event IDs 5861, 5860- Monitor excessive WMI queries via Sysmon (Event ID 1)- Track anomalous process creations tied to wmic.exe or powershell.exe
Remediation: - Restrict WMI and DCOM usage to administrators- Enable logging for WMI queries- Implement AppLocker policies to restrict script usage- Use EDR to monitor suspicious PowerShell/WMI usage

instruction: Describe the Execution + Defense Evasion attack: WMI + PowerShell Remoting for Evasion
output:
Attackers leverage WMI combined with PowerShell Remoting to execute commands or scripts without writing files to disk, allowing stealthy post-exploitation or lateral movement. This method abuses legitimate Windows services and communication channels, often bypassing basic antivirus and EDR detection because it avoids typical execution indicators like file drops or direct binary execution.
Vulnerability: Abuse of native remote execution channels (WMI, WinRM)In-memory execution avoids detection on disk
Impact: - Silent command execution- In-memory payloads- Antivirus evasion- No disk-based artifacts
Detection: - Enable PowerShell logging (Module, ScriptBlock Logging)- Monitor Event ID 4104 (PowerShell)- Use Sysmon to detect process creation (ID 1)- Detect WMI process creation via Event ID 4688 or 5861
Remediation: - Disable unnecessary remote access (WinRM, WMI)- Enforce JEA (Just Enough Administration)- Use constrained language mode- Implement strict logging and SIEM alerts

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via COM Hijack attack: Juicy Potato – CLSID Abuse
output:
This technique exploits a Windows COM server misconfiguration combined with a SeImpersonatePrivilege to spawn a process with SYSTEM-level access. The Juicy Potato exploit abuses DCOM activation and CLSIDs to force the system to impersonate a privileged token and assign it to the attacker's process. It is highly effective on default-configured Windows Server and Desktop environments pre-Windows 10 1803.
Vulnerability: COM server misconfiguration + SeImpersonatePrivilege
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level privilege escalation- Attackers can disable AV, create users, steal hashes
Detection: - Monitor usage of known CLSIDs in COM logs- Look for JuicyPotato.exe execution- Monitor process tokens and abnormal impersonation events
Remediation: - Patch or upgrade OS to Windows 10 1803+- Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from non-admins- Use AppLocker to block exploit binaries

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Token Spoofing attack: Rogue Potato – Modern Bypass for Juicy
output:
This exploit targets Windows Server and newer Windows 10+ (1809+) systems where Juicy Potato is patched. Rogue Potato leverages a local HTTP COM server and NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM impersonation via RPC abuse. It tricks the system into connecting to the attacker's local TCP listener instead of a real named pipe, enabling SYSTEM token impersonation and privilege escalation without needing a named pipe.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Windows RPC + COM interactionExploitable SeImpersonatePrivilege token
Impact: Full SYSTEM privilege escalationComplete control over systemAdmin backdoor creation
Detection: - Monitor creation of new SYSTEM processes- Detect RPC server binding on unusual ports- Audit use of SeImpersonatePrivilege
Remediation: - Remove or restrict SeImpersonatePrivilege- Block custom COM objects via AppLocker or WDAC- Monitor event logs for COM service abuse

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Print Spooler Abuse attack: PrintSpoofer – Abuse Print Spooler API
output:
PrintSpoofer is a Windows privilege escalation technique that exploits the Print Spooler service by abusing SeImpersonatePrivilege. It uses a named pipe trick to impersonate SYSTEM, bypassing patched legacy exploits (e.g., Juicy Potato). This works on systems where the Print Spooler is enabled and the user has the impersonation privilege. Common in enterprise environments with misconfigured services.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Print Spooler impersonation pipe + SeImpersonatePrivilege
Impact: - SYSTEM-level shell access- Full administrative control- Potential for persistence/backdoors
Detection: - Detect creation of named pipes by unprivileged users- Monitor for cmd.exe or unknown binaries launched under SYSTEM- Review Print Spooler logs and anomalies
Remediation: - Disable Print Spooler if not required: Stop-Service -Name Spooler- Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from low-priv accounts- Use AppLocker/WDAC to block unapproved binaries

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Named Pipe Impersonation attack: GodPotato – 2023 Token Impersonation Bypass
output:
GodPotato is a modern bypass of previous *Potato family exploits like JuicyPotato and RoguePotato. It leverages token impersonation over named pipes using NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM services triggered via DCOM, without relying on deprecated CLSIDs or hardcoded service behaviors. GodPotato is particularly dangerous because it functions on fully patched Windows 10/11 and Server 2016–2022 under specific privilege conditions.
Vulnerability: Named pipe impersonation using DCOM-triggered privileged service
Impact: Full SYSTEM shellAdmin user creationPersistence installationData exfiltration
Detection: - Monitor pipe impersonation activity- Alert on unexpected SYSTEM shell launches from user-level contexts- Use ETW or Sysmon for named pipe access tracking
Remediation: - Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from low-privileged accounts- Apply AppLocker or WDAC to prevent execution of unsigned binaries- Harden DCOM access rights- Monitor creation of unknown named pipes

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Access Token Abuse attack: Token Impersonation with Meterpreter
output:
This technique involves abusing impersonation tokens obtained during a Meterpreter session to escalate privileges. When a target has services or users logged in with high privileges (e.g., SYSTEM or domain admin), Meterpreter can steal and impersonate these tokens, allowing attackers to operate with those privileges without needing credentials or triggering alerts.
Vulnerability: Insecure token handlingExposed privileged sessionsImpersonable access tokens
Impact: Full SYSTEM or Domain Admin accessHash dumpingAdmin account creationCommand execution under SYSTEM context
Detection: - Enable Windows Auditing- Detect suspicious privilege escalation via Sysmon Event ID 1/10- Monitor for unusual getuid, incognito, or token impersonation activity
Remediation: - Use LSASS protection- Logoff inactive admin sessions- Restrict SeImpersonatePrivilege to trusted users- Use Credential Guard / LSA Protection

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Launch Daemons attack: Writable .plist Files in /Library/LaunchDaemons
output:
This technique exploits misconfigured permissions on .plist files within /Library/LaunchDaemons. If a user can modify these property list files, they can configure a launch daemon to execute arbitrary code as root during system boot or load time. Since launch daemons run with elevated privileges, a writable .plist file can be abused to gain persistent root access.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured file permissionsWritable .plist loaded as root
Impact: Full root privilege escalationPersistent backdoorPrivilege manipulation without kernel exploitation
Detection: - Monitor .plist file modifications- Use auditd or fs_usage- Track unauthorized launchctl load attempts
Remediation: - Ensure proper permissions: only root writable- Disable unneeded daemons- Monitor LaunchDaemons directory- Use macOS SIP and JAMF policies

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via New Launch Daemon attack: Creating a New Malicious Launch Daemon
output:
This attack simulates an adversary creating a new malicious LaunchDaemon in /Library/LaunchDaemons/ on macOS to execute arbitrary commands as root during system startup. This is possible when the attacker already has write access (e.g., via privilege escalation, sudo, or poorly configured permissions). The daemon ensures persistence and can run malicious payloads with root privileges upon reboot or manually triggered loading.
Vulnerability: LaunchDaemons executing root-level scripts through crafted or rogue .plist files
Impact: Persistent root-level executionBypasses TCC & SIP controlsSystem compromise upon reboot
Detection: - Monitor /Library/LaunchDaemons/ for unauthorized .plist- Use endpoint monitoring tools- Log alert on suspicious daemon loading
Remediation: - Restrict write access to /Library/LaunchDaemons/- Audit LaunchDaemon loads- Enforce system integrity protection (SIP)- Harden sudo policies

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Binary Replacement attack: Hijacking an Existing Daemon Executable
output:
This attack demonstrates how an adversary with write permissions to an existing daemon's binary (e.g., due to misconfigured file ownership or improper permissions) can replace the legitimate executable with a malicious payload. Once the daemon is started or restarted (manually or via system reboot), the malicious binary executes with elevated privileges (typically root), enabling privilege escalation or persistent backdoor access.
Vulnerability: Writable daemon executable paths due to improper file permissions
Impact: Root privilege escalationBackdoor persistenceArbitrary code execution as root
Detection: - Monitor changes in system daemon binaries using tripwire, aide, or auditd- Use systemctl status logs and diff binaries- Check for unauthorized service behavior via journald (journalctl)
Remediation: - Enforce correct file permissions (chmod 755)- Ensure daemon executables are owned by root and immutable if possible- Audit system services and binary paths regularly- Apply principle of least privilege

instruction: Describe the User-Level Persistence (macOS) attack: Using Launch Agents for Persistence
output:
This technique allows an attacker to maintain persistence on macOS systems by creating a Launch Agent plist file in the user's ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ directory. These Launch Agents are loaded automatically at user login and can execute any script or binary without needing root privileges.
Vulnerability: Abuse of LaunchAgents for autostart execution
Impact: Enables persistent access without root, stealthy post-exploitation foothold
Detection: Monitor ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ for new or unknown plist files, audit user login items, check for loaded agents via launchctl list
Remediation: Disable LaunchAgents in monitored environments, restrict write permissions, monitor plist changes, use EDR to flag suspicious agents

instruction: Describe the Credential Dumping via Registry Export attack: Dump Using Built-in reg save Command
output:
On Windows systems, sensitive credential data like SAM (Security Account Manager), SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives are stored in the registry. If an attacker has administrative privileges or SYSTEM-level access, they can use the built-in reg save command to dump these hives for offline credential extraction using tools like Mimikatz or secretsdump.py. This technique does not require external tools and can be performed using default Windows utilities.
Vulnerability: Abuse of reg save command to extract sensitive registry hives
Impact: Offline password hash extraction, NTLM reuse, lateral movement, privilege escalation
Detection: Monitor process activity for suspicious use of reg.exe targeting SAM/SYSTEM, EDR alerts on hive access, check for unauthorized file creation in temp/system paths
Remediation: Restrict local admin access, enable LSA protection, use Credential Guard, audit and alert on registry hive access, block reg.exe via AppLocker

instruction: Describe the Credential Dumping via Offline Registry Access attack: Offline Dump from C:\Windows\System32\Config
output:
When an attacker gains physical access to a Windows system (or has a mounted disk image), they can extract critical registry hives — SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY — directly from C:\Windows\System32\Config, bypassing live system protections. These files store sensitive credential data like password hashes and can be used for offline credential dumping using tools like secretsdump.py or Mimikatz. This method is stealthier than live dumping and works even if the OS is not running.
Vulnerability: Registry hive files are world-readable when accessed offline from disk
Impact: Complete credential compromise including local admin, NTLM, and cached secrets
Detection: Monitor access to physical disksAudit logs for offline registry access attemptsBitLocker alerts on unauthorized boot device use
Remediation: Enable full-disk encryption (BitLocker)Use BIOS passwordDisable boot from USBRestrict physical accessEncrypt backups and drive images

instruction: Describe the Credential Dumping (Live) attack: Mimikatz Live Dump (Local SYSTEM)
output:
This attack involves using the Mimikatz tool to extract plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and other secrets from the memory of the lsass.exe process while the Windows machine is running. The attacker must have SYSTEM-level privileges on the local machine. Often used post-exploitation after privilege escalation to extract local and domain credentials for lateral movement.
Vulnerability: Access to LSASS process memory with SYSTEM privileges
Impact: Exposure of all cached credentials on the system, including domain admin, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM hashes
Detection: - Monitor lsass.exe access (Event ID 4663)- Use Sysmon for parent-child process monitoring- Alert on usage of mimikatz.exe or related tools
Remediation: - Enable Credential Guard- Use EDR with LSASS protection- Harden LSASS using RunAsPPL- Limit local admin access- Disable WDigest

instruction: Describe the Credential Dumping (Offline SAM Extraction) attack: Metasploit SAM Dump Module
output:
This attack uses the post/windows/gather/hashdump module in Metasploit to dump credentials from the Windows Security Account Manager (SAM) database. It requires a valid meterpreter session with SYSTEM privileges, often obtained after initial exploitation or privilege escalation. The extracted NTLM hashes can be cracked offline or used in pass-the-hash attacks.
Vulnerability: Insecure storage of password hashes in SAM database accessible with SYSTEM privileges
Impact: Full compromise of local user accounts; potential domain admin hash exposure on workstations
Detection: - Monitor for use of Meterpreter or suspicious access to SAM- EDR tools that flag hashdump behavior- Log event ID 4624, 4672, and LSASS access attempts
Remediation: - Apply LSASS protections- Use Credential Guard- Limit local admin access- Enable logging and detection for post-exploitation tools- Patch known exploits used for initial access

instruction: Describe the Credential Dumping via Remote NTDS.dit & SAM Extraction attack: secretsdump.py (Impacket)
output:
This scenario demonstrates how attackers can use Impacket’s secretsdump.py to remotely extract password hashes from the NTDS.dit file (Active Directory) or SAM/LSA secrets from Windows systems. This does not require remote code execution — only valid credentials (e.g., admin account) and network access to the target. The hashes can then be cracked offline or abused using pass-the-hash.
Vulnerability: Weak protection of credential secrets over SMB and access via admin creds
Impact: Exposure of domain/local user hashes; offline cracking or direct abuse via pass-the-hash
Detection: - Monitor SMB connections- Alert on unusual use of built-in accounts- SIEM logs (Windows Event IDs 4624, 4648)- Detect secretsdump tool strings with EDR
Remediation: - Disable SMBv1- Limit admin access- Enable LAPS for local account management- Use strong passwords and monitor SMB share access- Segment network & implement firewall rules

instruction: Describe the Credential Harvesting via Registry Access attack: Direct Registry Read via PowerShell
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with local or remote access can use PowerShell to read sensitive registry hives directly from a Windows system. Common targets include SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives for credential data, and Run/RunOnce keys for persistence mechanisms. This technique is used in post-exploitation for privilege escalation or credential dumping.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted access to sensitive registry keys via PowerShell by privileged users
Impact: Exposure of user credentials (NTLM hashes), persistence mechanisms, or user behavior insights
Detection: - Monitor reg save, reg export, and PowerShell logging (Event ID 4104)- SIEM rules for access to SAM/SYSTEM paths- EDR alerts for access to sensitive registry hives
Remediation: - Apply least privilege access- Block access to registry via AppLocker or GPO- Enable PowerShell logging and transcription- Harden Volume Shadow Copy access- Enable Credential Guard on endpoints

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Linux Capabilities attack: Check for Misconfigured Capabilities
output:
This simulation explores how attackers can enumerate and exploit misconfigured file capabilities in Linux systems. Linux capabilities break down root privileges into discrete units and assign them to binaries. If a binary has inappropriate capabilities (e.g., cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin), a user may escalate to root or perform unauthorized actions. Common abuses include assigning capabilities to interpreters like Python or Bash.
