Vulnerability: Misconfigured or excessive Linux capabilities on user-controlled binaries
Impact: Local privilege escalationBypass of file system restrictionsRoot shell access via user binaries
Detection: - Monitor file capabilities using getcap regularly- Audit for sensitive capabilities (cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin)- Log capability changes
Remediation: - Restrict usage of setcap to root-only- Remove unnecessary capabilities- Monitor with file integrity tools (e.g., AIDE)- Avoid giving interpreters elevated capabilities

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation attack: Privilege Escalation via cap_setuid on Custom Binary
output:
This scenario explores how an attacker can escalate privileges by abusing a custom binary with the cap_setuid+ep capability. If a binary owned by a low-privileged user is granted this capability, it can set its UID to 0 and spawn a root shell. This attack is especially dangerous in development or CI/CD environments where developers or automation scripts have permission to modify binaries and assign capabilities.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Linux capabilities (cap_setuid) on user-modifiable binaries
Impact: - Local root shell- Full system control- Container escape (in some contexts)
Detection: - Use getcap -r / to scan files with dangerous capabilities- Monitor for non-root users assigning capabilities- Check for world-writable binaries with elevated caps
Remediation: - Remove unnecessary cap_setuid assignments- Limit setcap usage to root only- Apply file integrity monitoring (AIDE, tripwire)- Harden CI/CD policies to prevent automated capability assignment

instruction: Describe the Unauthorized File Read attack: Read /etc/shadow via cap_dac_read_search
output:
This scenario simulates an attacker leveraging a binary with the cap_dac_read_search capability to bypass traditional UNIX file permission checks and access sensitive system files like /etc/shadow, which normally requires root access. If the binary is user-controlled or misconfigured, it can be abused to extract password hashes for offline cracking. This capability allows read access regardless of DAC (Discretionary Access Control) restrictions.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured cap_dac_read_search allowing bypass of file read permissions
Impact: - Leakage of /etc/shadow hashes- Offline brute-force or password cracking- Lateral movement via credential reuse
Detection: - Use getcap -r / to enumerate binaries with cap_dac_read_search- Monitor for unexpected read access to restricted files- Check file audit logs (auditd)
Remediation: - Never assign cap_dac_read_search to user-modifiable binaries- Use file integrity monitoring- Enforce strict capability audit policies- Use AppArmor/SELinux to restrict sensitive file reads

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation & Takeover attack: Full System Compromise via cap_sys_admin
output:
This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with access to a binary containing the cap_sys_admin Linux capability can escalate privileges to root, mount filesystems, escape containers, access arbitrary files, and manipulate kernel namespaces. This capability is referred to as "the new root" due to its wide-ranging system control powers. It is often accidentally left assigned in developer tools, monitoring agents, or container runtimes.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured or unsafe assignment of cap_sys_admin capability to untrusted binaries
Impact: - Mounting sensitive filesystems- Kernel namespace manipulation- File overwrite and stealth access- Container or jail breakout
Detection: - Use getcap -r / to list dangerous capabilities- Audit logs for mount, unshare, losetup usage- Monitor capability assignments with OSSEC or Auditd
Remediation: - Never grant cap_sys_admin to user-controlled binaries- Use AppArmor/SELinux profiles to confine binaries- Enforce binary signing and integrity validation- Remove or reduce unnecessary capabilities at deploy time

instruction: Describe the Container Escape / Priv-Esc attack: Break Out of Containers via Capabilities
output:
This scenario simulates an attacker breaking out of a Docker or LXC container due to over-permissive Linux capabilities like cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, or cap_dac_read_search. Containers that run with these capabilities can be escaped by attackers to gain root access on the host system. These conditions are often present in poorly configured development or CI/CD environments.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured Linux capabilities allowing namespace, file, or process manipulation
Impact: - Host privilege escalation- Root file read/write- Remote shell on host- Full system compromise
Detection: - Audit container capability sets- Monitor namespace syscalls- Log host access attempts from containers
Remediation: - Drop all non-essential capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL- Use rootless containers- Enforce AppArmor/SELinux confinement- Avoid mounting host / or docker.sock

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via LCAPs attack: Custom Binary with Any Capability
output:
This scenario explores how attackers can exploit custom binaries assigned Linux capabilities (e.g., cap_sys_admin, cap_dac_override, or cap_setuid) instead of using full root privileges. These capabilities allow binaries to perform privileged operations and are often misconfigured by developers or sysadmins seeking limited privilege separation but end up unintentionally allowing full system compromise.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured capability assignments on custom or dev binaries
Impact: - Root shell access- Bypass of file permissions- System takeover- Lateral movement potential
Detection: - Audit for capabilities via getcap -r / 2>/dev/null- Monitor custom binaries with extended attributes- Use auditd or eBPF for execution tracking
Remediation: - Use --cap-drop=ALL as default policy- Avoid assigning capabilities unless absolutely necessary- Restrict developer access on production systems

instruction: Describe the Boot-Time Local Privilege Escalation attack: Edit GRUB Entry to Boot into Single User Mode
output:
This attack demonstrates how a local attacker with physical or console access can edit the GRUB bootloader entry during system boot to gain root shell access by booting the system into single-user or emergency mode. If GRUB is not password protected, it allows an attacker to modify kernel parameters and bypass authentication mechanisms.
Vulnerability: Unprotected GRUB bootloader allows kernel parameter modification
Impact: - Full root shell without login- Change root passwords- Persist via backdoor- Disable security services
Detection: - Check /var/log/secure and journalctl -b for unauthorized boot modifications- Detect abnormal uptime/reset patterns
Remediation: - Set GRUB bootloader password (grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2)- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical access- Use secure boot policies

instruction: Describe the Local Privilege Escalation via Boot attack: Bypass Forgotten Root Password
output:
This method is used to reset or bypass the root password on Linux systems where a user has physical or boot-level access, typically when the GRUB bootloader is unprotected by a password. This technique allows attackers or administrators to regain root control of a system without knowing the original root credentials. Commonly used in recovery or incident response situations.
Vulnerability: Insecure GRUB (no password) + unrestricted kernel parameter editing
Impact: - Full root account access- Credential reset- Access to all files and services
Detection: - Check for GRUB bootline modifications- Inspect uptime logs and password change events in auditd or journalctl
Remediation: - Protect GRUB with bootloader password- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical/console access- BIOS/UEFI password + Secure Boot

instruction: Describe the Boot-Level Persistence (Config Tampering) attack: Persistent GRUB2 Backdoor via config edit
output:
This attack demonstrates how an attacker with physical or root-level access can modify the GRUB2 bootloader configuration to insert a persistent root shell or backdoor binary that launches during each boot. This allows privilege escalation, backdoor re-entry, or stealth persistence on reboot. It's highly effective against systems without GRUB2 password protection or full disk encryption.
Vulnerability: No GRUB2 passwordNo full disk encryptionWritable grub config files
Impact: Persistent root accessBackdoor re-entryComplete system compromise
Detection: Inspect /etc/default/grub and /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unusual init= or unknown pathsAudit last modified times of boot files
Remediation: • Set GRUB2 password with grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2• Restrict physical access• Use full disk encryption• Monitor for tampered GRUB entries and init= parameters

instruction: Describe the Bootloader Configuration Exploit attack: Add Custom GRUB Menu Entry for Root Access
output:
This technique shows how an attacker with physical or root access can create a custom GRUB2 menu entry that boots the system directly into a root shell, bypassing standard user authentication. It leverages the ability to inject new boot options into GRUB's config file, commonly found on unprotected systems with no GRUB password or full disk encryption. This can be used for privilege escalation or persistent boot-level access.
Vulnerability: No GRUB2 password protectionConfigurable GRUB menu entriesNo disk encryption
Impact: Root access at bootAuthentication bypassStealth backdoor persistence
Detection: Inspect /etc/grub.d/40_custom or /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unauthorized entriesCompare GRUB config hashesMonitor boot parameters
Remediation: - Enable GRUB2 password- Use full disk encryption- Limit physical access- Monitor boot config integrity- Restrict write access to /etc/grub.d/

instruction: Describe the Authentication Attack (Brute Force) attack: Brute Force RDP / VNC Login
output:
This scenario simulates an attacker attempting to gain unauthorized access to a system through Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) or Virtual Network Computing (VNC) by brute-forcing user credentials. Common in misconfigured environments where RDP or VNC is exposed to the internet, this technique involves automated attempts using wordlists until a valid username/password pair is found. Weak credentials or lack of lockout policies make this attack feasible.
Vulnerability: Weak or default credentialsNo account lockoutPublicly exposed RDP or VNC services
Impact: Unauthorized system accessDesktop controlPossible lateral movement
Detection: - Monitor failed login attempts on RDP/VNC logs- Use endpoint detection (EDR)- Analyze account login patterns
Remediation: - Enforce strong password policies- Enable account lockout- Restrict RDP/VNC via VPN or firewall- Enable MFA- Disable unused remote services

instruction: Describe the Authentication Misconfiguration Exploit attack: Anonymous or No-Auth VNC Access
output:
Some VNC servers (like TightVNC, RealVNC, TigerVNC) may be configured to allow unauthenticated access—either intentionally for convenience or due to misconfiguration. If authentication is disabled, any remote attacker can connect directly and gain control over the GUI desktop. This is particularly dangerous when the VNC server runs as root or is exposed to the internet. Such vulnerabilities are common in legacy systems, testing environments, or poorly configured IT infrastructure.
Vulnerability: VNC server configured with no authentication or blank password
Impact: Full GUI desktop access without credentialsPotential for privilege escalation, lateral movement
Detection: - Monitor for unusual connections on TCP 5900–5905- Check system logs (e.g., /var/log/auth.log)- Use network IDS/IPS for VNC connections
Remediation: - Always enable strong authentication on VNC services- Use VPN or SSH tunnels for access- Disable unused remote access tools- Restrict ports using firewalls

instruction: Describe the Lateral Movement via Valid Credentials attack: Credential Reuse via RDP
output:
In enterprise networks, users often reuse the same password across multiple systems. If an attacker compromises one host and extracts valid RDP credentials (e.g., via LSASS dump, keylogger, or phishing), those credentials can be reused to connect to other machines over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). This allows lateral movement, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation, especially when accounts are members of local admins or domain admins.
Vulnerability: Password reuse across multiple machines with RDP enabled
Impact: Lateral movementUnauthorized system accessPrivilege escalation via valid accounts
Detection: - Monitor for RDP logins across multiple systems- Check for unusual login patterns- Enable RDP event auditing (event ID 4624, 4625, 4776)
Remediation: - Enforce unique passwords across systems- Disable unnecessary RDP access- Implement MFA for remote access- Use account lockout policies

instruction: Describe the Session Hijacking via RDP Clipboard or Replay attack: Session Hijack (Clipboard / Replay)
output:
In RDP environments, users often copy sensitive content (e.g., passwords, tokens) to or from the clipboard. If clipboard redirection is enabled, attackers with RDP access can monitor or hijack clipboard data. Additionally, session hijacking is possible through replay attacks if credentials or tokens are reused or poorly protected in memory. This technique abuses live or cached session artifacts for lateral movement or privilege escalation.
Vulnerability: Insecure clipboard sharingSession token exposureCredential reuse in memory
Impact: Unauthorized session accessCredential leakageRemote command execution
Detection: - Monitor clipboard events- Audit RDP logins and clipboard redirection- Alert on suspicious session replays
Remediation: - Disable clipboard redirection- Enforce session locking- Clear session artifacts on logout- Use MFA and token expiry

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution (RCE) in RDP attack: BlueKeep – RDP Remote Code Execution
output:
BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) affects unpatched Windows versions running RDP with weak security settings. Attackers can send specially crafted RDP packets to perform unauthenticated remote code execution. This vulnerability has been actively exploited for wormable attacks and ransomware deployment.
Vulnerability: RDP pre-auth remote code exec vulnerability (BlueKeep)
Impact: Full system compromiseWorm propagationRansomware installation
Detection: - IDS/IPS signatures for BlueKeep- Monitor RDP logs for malformed traffic- SIEM alerts on repeat exploitation attempts
Remediation: - Apply Microsoft patches- Disable RDP if not needed- Use RDP Gateways with MFA- Enable network-level authentication (NLA)

instruction: Describe the Authentication Bypass in VNC attack: TigerVNC Authentication Bypass (CVE-2017-X)
output:
A vulnerability in some TigerVNC versions allowed attackers to bypass authentication by exploiting a flaw in the challenge/response handshake. No valid credentials are required. The attacker can send altered packets to the VNC server, granting access to the desktop and all active sessions. Presents serious risk in legacy or unmanaged environments.
Vulnerability: Flaw in VNC challenge/response handshake permitting no-auth login
Impact: Full desktop accessPrivacy breachPotential for code execution on victim session
Detection: - Network DPI to detect malformed VNC handshake- Monitor VNC logs for unauthorized access- IDS rules for this specific CVE
Remediation: - Upgrade TigerVNC to fixed release- Limit VNC exposure via firewall/VPN- Enforce strong passwords

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via RDP attack: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) RCE
output:
BlueKeep affects unpatched Windows systems running RDP with NLA disabled. It enables unauthenticated remote code execution, allowing attackers to gain full control and potentially propagate as a worm. It has been observed in active threat campaigns, making it critical to address.
Vulnerability: RDP pre‑auth remote code execution (BlueKeep)
Impact: Full system compromise, malware/worm deployment
Detection: IDS/IPS signatures, SIEM alerts, failed RDP handshake anomalies
Remediation: Apply Microsoft patches, enforce NLA or disable RDP, use VPN gateways and MFA

instruction: Describe the Authentication Bypass in VNC attack: TigerVNC Auth Bypass
output:
Some versions of TigerVNC incorrectly implement challenge/response authentication, allowing unauthenticated access. Attackers can inject malformed packets into the VNC handshake to bypass password checks and access desktops without credentials. This issue persists in legacy or poorly maintained systems.
Vulnerability: Incorrect VNC handshake allows no-auth access
Impact: Full GUI control, data exposure, potential for malicious persistence
Detection: VNC handshake anomalies, server logs showing token anomalies
Remediation: Update TigerVNC, enforce strong passwords, firewall/VPN isolation

instruction: Describe the Network-based Eavesdropping & Hijacking attack: Man‑in‑the‑Middle or Sniffed VNC
output:
In networks without proper encryption or using outdated VNC protocols, an attacker positioned on the same LAN or intercepting traffic (e.g., via ARP spoofing) can capture or modify VNC sessions, extract credentials, screenshots, keystrokes, and potentially inject malicious input into the session. This is especially effective with legacy VNC configurations or over insecure Wi-Fi.
Vulnerability: Use of unencrypted VNC protocols over insecure networks / lack of TLS
Impact: Credential theft, session hijacking, screenshot/data exfiltration, unauthorized control
Detection: - Network IDS/IPS to detect ARP spoofing- Monitor for duplicate ARP responses or gateway MAC changes- Alert on VNC sessions lacking encryption
Remediation: - Enforce TLS-encrypted VNC (VeNCrypt, TLSAuth)- Use SSH/VPN tunnels for VNC- Apply client-side certificate validation- Segment admin networks and disable insecure wireless

instruction: Describe the Malicious App Installation via Trojanized File attack: Trojanized Installer (EXE / MSI / DEB / PKG)
output:
This technique involves disguising malicious code within a legitimate-looking software installer (e.g., EXE on Windows, MSI, DEB for Debian-based Linux, or PKG for macOS). Once installed by the user, the malicious payload executes with the same privileges as the installer, potentially escalating to root or SYSTEM. This is a common initial access method for adversaries distributing malware through third-party app stores, phishing emails, or pirated app repositories.
Vulnerability: Unsigned installersLack of runtime application securityUsers downloading from untrusted sources
Impact: Initial remote accessPrivilege escalationCredential theftBackdoor persistence
Detection: - Monitor unusual outbound traffic- Sandboxing analysis of installers- Application whitelisting- Behavior-based antivirus alerts
Remediation: - Enforce app-signing and notarization- Disable installation from unknown sources- Use mobile threat defense (MTD)- Educate users against phishing

instruction: Describe the Supply Chain Attack (Package Manager Abuse) attack: Malicious Package Injection via pip/npm/gem in Mobile App
output:
Attackers publish malicious Python, Node.js, or Ruby packages that mimic popular libraries (e.g., reqests, event-stream, rails_admin). Mobile apps (especially hybrid or backend-assisted apps using Python/Node/Ruby) that auto-install packages or include dependencies without vetting may unknowingly include these malicious packages. Once integrated, they execute code with app permissions, potentially stealing tokens, injecting backdoors, or escalating privileges within the device or backend infrastructure.
Vulnerability: Unverified third-party dependenciesMalicious code in install scripts
Impact: API key theftRemote Code ExecutionSupply Chain Compromise
Detection: - Monitor package integrity with hash or checksum validation- Analyze install scripts for obfuscation or outbound connections- Static/dynamic code analysis with MobSF, Frida, or sandbox tools
Remediation: - Use dependency pinning- Avoid auto-installing from untrusted registries- Review open-source licenses and maintainers- Use internal package mirrors with vetting

instruction: Describe the Trojanized Executable (Portable App) attack: Backdoored Portable App
output:
Attackers create or modify a seemingly legitimate portable app (e.g., Android debugging tools, mobile emulators, productivity utilities) by injecting a backdoor (e.g., reverse shell, keylogger, data stealer) into the executable or its supporting scripts. When unsuspecting users (developers, testers, or general users) run the app from USB or directly from a downloaded file, the backdoor activates in the background, stealing credentials, harvesting device info, or granting remote access to the attacker. Often used in spear-phishing campaigns or insider threat scenarios.
Vulnerability: Trusting unsigned portable appsLack of app verificationExecutable backdooring
Impact: Unauthorized remote accessCredential theftFull device compromise
Detection: - Monitor new or unsigned portable apps- Analyze binaries with tools like PEStudio or VirusTotal- Watch for unexpected outbound connections
Remediation: - Use signed and verified apps only- Disable autorun for portable devices- Apply application whitelisting- Educate users on trusted sources

instruction: Describe the Macro-based Code Execution (Trojan Office) attack: Malicious Office App with Embedded Macros
output:
Attackers craft a legitimate-looking Microsoft Office document (Word or Excel) disguised as a mobile project plan, developer policy, or test report and embed VBA macros to execute malicious code. When opened and macros are enabled, the embedded script runs commands to download payloads, open reverse shells, or execute surveillance actions on the device. Common in spear-phishing attacks targeting mobile devs, QA teams, or business personnel with access to internal app builds or test environments. These documents often bypass email filters due to familiar file formats and social engineering context.
Vulnerability: Macros enabled by default or via social engineeringLack of file validation
Impact: Remote accessCredential theftMobile project compromise
Detection: - Monitor macro execution events- Inspect Office documents with tools like oletools, OfficeMalScanner- Watch for suspicious downloads or outbound traffic
Remediation: - Disable macros by default via GPO- Educate staff on macro-based threats- Sandbox suspicious documents before opening- Use DLP and endpoint monitoring tools

instruction: Describe the Physical Attack via USB (Auto Execution) attack: USB Drop Attack (Auto-installation / Autorun)
output:
An attacker prepares a USB drive containing malicious executables or scripts (e.g., backdoored Android tools, trojan installers) configured to auto-execute when plugged into a target's system. This is often disguised as a helpful "Mobile Toolkit" or "Driver Installer" and dropped in locations where developers, QA engineers, or IT support might find and connect them (e.g., office desks, parking lots). If autorun is enabled (especially on older Windows systems or with Rubber Ducky-style devices), the script executes immediately, installing malware, capturing data, or opening remote shells without user interaction. Even if autorun is disabled, enticing filenames can lure users to click.
Vulnerability: Autorun enabledUser execution of unknown binariesTrust in physical devices
Impact: Remote accessData exfiltrationCredential theftBackdoor persistence
Detection: - Monitor USB insertions- Detect autorun attempts- Analyze unknown executables with antivirus and sandboxing- Monitor new processes created after USB insertion
Remediation: - Disable autorun via Group Policy- Enforce USB usage policy- Train staff against USB baiting- Use endpoint protection and USB monitoring tools- Implement Device Control policies

instruction: Describe the Social Engineering + Drive-by Download attack: Fake Update Popups / Websites
output:
The attacker creates a fake website or popup that mimics a legitimate mobile app update prompt (e.g., system update, browser update, antivirus or media player). When a user lands on the malicious site (often via phishing or malvertising), a realistic-looking modal appears prompting them to "update now." Clicking the button silently downloads and installs a malicious APK (on Android) or redirects to a trojanized installer on PC. These fake updates often mimic Chrome, Adobe Flash, antivirus scanners, or Play Store messages and can deliver spyware, keyloggers, or remote access tools.
Vulnerability: Trust in browser-based update prompts“Install from unknown sources” enabledSocial engineering
Impact: Remote accessMobile data theftAccount compromisePersistent surveillance
Detection: - Monitor unauthorized APK installs- Network traffic analysis for unknown domains- Mobile AV or EDR alerts- Manually review APKs using tools like MobSF or VirusTotal
Remediation: - Never install updates via browser prompts- Disable “Install from unknown sources”- Use only Play Store/App Store for updates- Educate users against pop-up scams- Block known phishing/malvertising domains

instruction: Describe the App Hijack and Privilege Escalation via Desktop Entry attack: Malicious App Installation via .desktop File
output:
On Android-x86 or Linux-based mobile platforms (or rooted Android devices running a GUI layer like KDE/Plasma), .desktop files function similarly to Windows .lnk shortcuts. An attacker can craft a .desktop file that appears to be a legitimate application but actually executes a malicious script or binary. Once the user clicks the icon (thinking it's a trusted app), the payload runs with user or escalated privileges, enabling data exfiltration, persistence, or lateral movement.
Vulnerability: Improper handling of .desktop filesTrust in GUI appearanceLack of execution sandbox for shortcuts
Impact: Remote accessCredential theftApplication spoofing and trust abuse
Detection: - Monitor execution of .desktop files- Use AppArmor or SELinux logs- Flag non-standard paths in .desktop files
Remediation: - Disable execution of downloaded .desktop files by default- Use trusted repositories for app installs- Educate users about shortcut spoofing- Enable SELinux/AppArmor hardening

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Static Code Analysis attack: Static Analysis of APK to Steal Secrets
output:
A malicious actor downloads a legitimate Android app's APK file and performs offline static analysis to extract hardcoded secrets such as API keys, tokens, internal URLs, or Firebase credentials. This data can then be used to compromise backend systems or impersonate users. This attack assumes no runtime interaction with the app.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded Secrets, Poor Obfuscation
Impact: Theft of API keys, abuse of backend services, impersonation of users, exposure of business logic
Detection: Mobile static/dynamic code analyzers, build pipeline secret scans, Firebase open database scanners
Remediation: Use secret management services (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager), avoid hardcoding keys, enable ProGuard and R8 with proper obfuscation, use NDK for sensitive logic, perform code reviews and secret scans pre-release

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Decompilation attack: Decompile APK to Smali & Java
output:
An attacker wants to reverse engineer an Android APK to understand its inner workings and inspect for secrets, logic flaws, or vulnerabilities. The attacker decompiles the APK to both Smali (assembly-like) code and Java code for inspection and modification. This is a foundational reverse engineering technique used before tampering or code injection.
Vulnerability: Insecure Code Distribution, Lack of Obfuscation
Impact: Exposure of application logic, leakage of secrets, tampering risk, vulnerability discovery
Detection: Use reverse engineering detection (e.g., tamper checks), track APK repackaging via hash or signature validation
Remediation: Use ProGuard/R8 for obfuscation, enforce anti-debug and anti-tamper logic, do not ship production keys, monitor certificate signature mismatch

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Business Logic Bypass attack: Bypass Authentication Logic (Login Without Server)
output:
A vulnerable Android app performs local login verification without server-side validation (e.g., compares username/password against hardcoded strings or shared preferences). An attacker reverse engineers the APK, identifies the login logic, modifies it to bypass checks, recompiles the APK, and logs in without valid credentials.
Vulnerability: Insecure Local Authentication Logic
Impact: Unauthorized access, bypassing user authentication, privilege escalation
Detection: Reverse engineering, logic diffing, repackaging detection, runtime instrumentation
Remediation: Move all authentication logic to server-side, implement certificate pinning and strong auth mechanisms

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Security Mechanism Bypass attack: Disable Root Detection or SSL Pinning
output:
Some Android apps prevent execution on rooted devices or use SSL pinning to block traffic interception. An attacker bypasses root detection and SSL pinning via static patching (modifying Smali/Java) or using runtime hooking tools like Frida or objection, enabling interception of app traffic or execution on rooted devices.
Vulnerability: Root Detection, SSL Pinning
Impact: Traffic interception, logic tampering, data theft on rooted devices
Detection: Runtime instrumentation tools, app integrity checks, network certificate mismatch
Remediation: Use native root detection (NDK), hardware-backed attestation (SafetyNet/Play Integrity), enforce certificate pinning with native C code

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Feature Unlock attack: Modify Payment Verification / Premium Check
output:
Many apps verify premium purchases locally by checking SharedPreferences or variables without server validation. An attacker decompiles the APK, finds the check (e.g., isPremium = false), and modifies it to always return true, unlocking premium features without payment.
Vulnerability: Insecure Local Payment Logic
Impact: Financial loss, illegal access to paid features, licensing bypass
Detection: Monitor feature use without matching server-side entitlement, verify purchase tokens
Remediation: Enforce server-side validation, use Google Play Billing verification with server receipt checks, avoid storing premium status in local code

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Code Injection attack: Malicious Code Injection into APK
output:
An attacker modifies an APK by injecting malicious Smali or Java code (e.g., keylogger, fake login page, data exfiltration) and re-signs the APK. Once installed, the malicious version runs alongside the original logic, compromising user data.
Vulnerability: Unprotected Codebase, Lack of Integrity Check
Impact: Data theft, spyware installation, app hijacking
Detection: Hash mismatches, unexpected traffic, AV detection, static scanners
Remediation: Use integrity checks, Google Play Protect, code attestation, runtime tamper detection

instruction: Describe the Reverse Engineering > Runtime Manipulation attack: IPA Decompilation and Runtime Hooking (iOS)
output:
An attacker decompiles an iOS IPA file to inspect app logic and uses runtime hooking (Frida, Cycript) to alter function behavior without modifying the app binary, enabling things like premium bypass, input capture, or internal data theft during runtime.
Vulnerability: Unencrypted Binary, Runtime Hookable Methods
Impact: Function override, unauthorized access, runtime backdoors
Detection: Jailbreak detection, runtime integrity checks, binary instrumentation
Remediation: Use hardened runtime, Swift/Obj-C obfuscation, anti-Frida, anti-jailbreak frameworks

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Credential Exposure attack: Plaintext Credentials in Files or Databases
output:
The app stores sensitive credentials (like usernames or API tokens) directly in plaintext inside internal files or databases. An attacker with physical access or root access to the device can easily retrieve them using file exploration or adb pull.
Vulnerability: Plaintext Credential Storage
Impact: Credential theft, account takeover, data leakage
Detection: Mobile file system analysis, secret scanners, static code audit
Remediation: Always hash passwords, use EncryptedSharedPreferences or KeyStore, avoid storing credentials locally

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Database Exposure attack: Unprotected SQLite Databases
output:
Some apps store sensitive data like user credentials, tokens, or financial info inside local SQLite databases without encryption. An attacker with access to the device can extract and read the database contents in plain text.
Vulnerability: Unencrypted Database Files
Impact: User data leakage, token exposure, PII theft
Detection: File scan, static analysis of DB helper class, data-at-rest review
Remediation: Use SQLCipher for DB encryption, apply device encryption and user authentication, deny backup and root access

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Cryptographic Flaws attack: Weakly Encrypted Data with Hardcoded Keys
output:
The app encrypts data stored on the device but uses hardcoded symmetric keys in the source code, making the encryption breakable via reverse engineering.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded Symmetric Keys
Impact: Bypass of encryption, credential exposure, logic compromise
Detection: Static key scan, code grep, encryption audit, key reuse detection
Remediation: Never hardcode keys; use Android Keystore or secure key derivation from user secrets

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Cache Data Exposure attack: Sensitive Cache Files
output:
Some apps temporarily cache sensitive data (e.g., session tokens, profile info, card metadata) in internal or external storage, which can be accessed if the device is rooted or if file permissions are misconfigured.
Vulnerability: Sensitive Info Stored in Cache
Impact: Session theft, account compromise, identity exposure
Detection: Monitor local cache dirs, file scanners, static analysis
Remediation: Never cache sensitive info; use volatile memory; ensure logout wipes cache; restrict file permissions

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Credential Protection Flaw attack: Unencrypted Keychain / Keystore Misuse
output:
iOS and Android apps often misuse Keystore or Keychain by either storing secrets unencrypted, using insecure flags, or hardcoding keystore access logic. Attackers can extract tokens or private keys using local access and forensic tools.
Vulnerability: Insecure Secret Management
Impact: Private key leakage, API abuse, persistent backdoors
Detection: Secret scan tools, keychain dumpers, Frida traces
Remediation: Use Android Keystore with user authentication; iOS Keychain with kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked and biometric prompt

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Log Info Leakage attack: Logs Containing Sensitive Data
output:
Developers often log user input or backend responses (including tokens or PII) using Log.d, print, or NSLog. Attackers can retrieve these logs on rooted/jailbroken devices or via logcat.
Vulnerability: grep -i passwordto capture logs. Step 4: If credentials or session data are displayed in logs, note the tag (e.g.,TAG: token=abc123). Step 5: Optionally, use jadx-guito reverse the app and search forLog.d, Log.e, or Log.vcalls inside login-related classes to confirm logging behavior. Step 6: Try capturing logs even after switching contexts or screen, to see if PII persists. Step 7: On iOS, install the app on a jailbroken device and monitor logs viaConsole.appor usingfrida-traceonNSLogoros_log. Step 8: Run frida-trace -n AppName -m '*[NSLog *]'` to hook into log functions and see what’s being printed. Step 9: If sensitive info (email, token, JWT, session ID) appears, log exposure is confirmed. Step 10: Log capture combined with other insecure storage can lead to account hijack or full session theft.
Impact: Logging of PII or tokens
Detection: T1552: Unsecured Credentials
Remediation: Credential leakage, session hijack, GDPR violations

instruction: Describe the Insecure Data Storage > Credential Extraction attack: Browser Auto-Fill / Password Manager Dump
output:
Some mobile apps or WebView-based browsers allow auto-fill of saved credentials into insecure fields or insecure contexts (like HTTP), or store passwords locally without protection. An attacker can extract these stored credentials by accessing browser data directories or manipulating WebViews to trick auto-fill mechanisms.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Auto-Fill / Credential Storage
Impact: Credential theft, account takeover, phishing injection
Detection: Monitor SQLite login DBs, analyze memory with Frida, inspect DOM in WebViews
Remediation: Use only secure auto-fill APIs, disable auto-fill for sensitive fields, enforce HTTPS-only credential storage, encrypt local storage

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Cleartext Transmission attack: Intercept HTTP Traffic (No HTTPS)
output:
A mobile app communicates with its backend API using plain HTTP instead of HTTPS. This allows any attacker on the same network to capture traffic, extract credentials, session tokens, or other PII using proxy tools or packet sniffers.
Vulnerability: Plaintext HTTP Transmission
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, API tampering
Detection: Proxy interceptors, Wireshark sniffers, traffic inspection
Remediation: Enforce HTTPS, apply HSTS or URL rewrite rules, reject HTTP at server level

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Weak Encryption attack: Exploit Weak TLS (e.g., TLS 1.0 / RC4)
output:
Some apps still connect to backend APIs using legacy TLS protocols (e.g., TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0) or weak ciphers (like RC4). Attackers can use SSL Labs or mitmproxy to downgrade and capture/modify data in transit.
Vulnerability: TLS Downgrade and Weak Ciphers
Impact: Confidentiality breach, session theft
Detection: testssl.sh, SSL Labs scans, proxy trace analysis
Remediation: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1, enforce TLS 1.3, disable RC4/3DES, use forward secrecy

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > HTTPS Downgrade attack: SSL Stripping (Force HTTP)
output:
An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot or MITM proxy that rewrites HTTPS links into HTTP, tricking the app or WebView to send login credentials over cleartext HTTP. Many hybrid mobile apps don’t enforce HTTPS at code level.
Vulnerability: No HTTPS Enforcement, No HSTS
Impact: Login credential theft, session hijacking
Detection: Bettercap logs, inspect HTTP request headers, dynamic HTTPS tests
Remediation: Enforce HTTPS at code level, add HSTS, validate cert pinning, avoid HTTP fallbacks

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Unencrypted Transmission attack: Capture Data from Mobile Apps Using HTTP
output:
Mobile applications sometimes communicate with APIs over HTTP instead of HTTPS, leaking user credentials or sensitive data in plaintext. An attacker connected to the same network (e.g., Wi-Fi) can intercept the traffic and capture the transmitted data easily.
Vulnerability: Transmission of Sensitive Data in Cleartext
Impact: Credential theft, identity leak, account compromise
Detection: Proxy intercept logs, packet capture, mobile traffic audit
Remediation: Always use HTTPS (TLS 1.2+), disable fallback to HTTP, validate backend enforcement

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > SSL Interception attack: Fake Certificate Injection (SSL MITM)
output:
If a mobile app does not implement SSL pinning or proper certificate validation, an attacker can inject a fake root certificate into the device. Then, they can perform MITM attacks and decrypt HTTPS traffic between the app and the server.
Vulnerability: No Certificate Pinning / Trusted Root Injection
Impact: Full decryption of HTTPS traffic, credential theft, token hijacking
Detection: CA certificate chain analysis, traffic interception test, Frida tracing
Remediation: Implement SSL Pinning (TrustManager override or native pinning), reject untrusted certs

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Rogue Wi-Fi Access Point attack: Wi-Fi Evil Twin Attack
output:
An attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) that mimics a trusted network name (SSID). When a user’s mobile device auto-connects, the attacker can perform Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) interception, data theft, or credential harvesting if the app or browser uses HTTP or weak TLS.
Vulnerability: No Wi-Fi Validation, Insecure HTTP Use
Impact: Credential theft, session hijacking, phishing
Detection: Wi-Fi traffic capture, unauthorized AP detection, DNS spoof check
Remediation: Use only HTTPS with cert pinning, disable auto-connect, implement captive portal validation

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Unencrypted Protocols attack: Insecure Communication in IoT Devices
output:
Many IoT devices and their companion mobile apps use unencrypted channels (like HTTP, MQTT, or raw TCP) for communication. Attackers can sniff or inject traffic to control devices, extract tokens, or compromise user privacy.
Vulnerability: No TLS, Cleartext Protocols
Impact: Unauthorized control, data leakage, remote access
Detection: Wireshark analysis, static code audit, replay attacks
Remediation: Enforce TLS/SSL on all IoT APIs, use secure MQTT, implement token validation

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Wireless MITM attack: MITM via Rogue Wi-Fi / Evil Twin (Android + iOS)
output:
An attacker creates a rogue Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) with the same SSID as a trusted network. When mobile devices (Android or iOS) auto-connect, the attacker intercepts or manipulates traffic using MITM tools. This is effective when apps do not enforce HTTPS or use weak certificate checks.
Vulnerability: Auto-join to Fake SSID, No HTTPS Enforcement
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, phishing
Detection: Wi-Fi scan, MITM detection tools, HTTPS monitoring
Remediation: Disable auto-connect, enforce HTTPS with pinning, user alert for captive portals

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Certificate Validation Bypass attack: MITM via SSL Bypass in Mobile App
output:
A mobile app that uses HTTPS can still be intercepted if it does not validate server certificates properly. An attacker can bypass SSL pinning using Frida or Objection, inject a fake certificate, and view encrypted traffic in plaintext.
Vulnerability: SSL Pinning Disabled / TrustManager Bypass
Impact: Full decryption of HTTPS traffic
Detection: Frida hooks, proxy inspection, APK reverse engineering
Remediation: Enforce SSL Pinning (native or network-security-config), validate root CA

instruction: Describe the Insecure Communication > Cleartext API Interception attack: MITM on HTTP APIs / Login
output:
Some mobile apps still use HTTP (not HTTPS) for API communication like login, data fetch, or session management. An attacker can intercept the requests and extract sensitive data without any encryption.
Vulnerability: Plaintext API Calls Without TLS
Impact: Credential and token theft
Detection: Proxy capture, packet inspection, insecure endpoint detection
Remediation: Enforce HTTPS (TLS 1.2+), disable HTTP endpoints, reject unencrypted sessions

instruction: Describe the Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) via Tampered App attack: MITM via APK Repack + Proxy Override
output:
Some Android apps do not validate their network configuration or certificate pinning. An attacker can decompile the APK, modify network code to force use of a proxy, recompile the app, and capture or modify the app’s traffic even over HTTPS.
Vulnerability: Lack of SSL Pinning, Proxy Misconfiguration
Impact: Credential and session hijack, data theft
Detection: Code diffing, static analysis, proxy interception logs
Remediation: Implement strict network-security-config and pinning, detect tampered APKs

instruction: Describe the Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) on Browser Traffic attack: MITM via Mobile Browser (Public Wi-Fi)
output:
When mobile users connect to public Wi-Fi networks (e.g., airports, cafés), attackers can set up rogue hotspots or sniff unsecured HTTP traffic. If the browser visits non-HTTPS sites, credentials and session tokens can be intercepted or modified.
Vulnerability: Use of Public Wi-Fi, HTTP Sites
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, fake content injection
Detection: Traffic sniffing, rogue SSID detection, SSL enforcement checks
Remediation: Use VPN, enforce HTTPS-only sites, use captive portal validation

instruction: Describe the Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) via Dynamic Hooking attack: Frida-Based Runtime MITM Hooking
output:
Some mobile apps use certificate pinning or obfuscation to block MITM proxies. However, attackers can hook runtime functions responsible for certificate validation or data encryption using Frida, allowing real-time MITM interception without modifying the APK.
Vulnerability: Runtime SSL Pinning, Obfuscated Cert Checks
Impact: Full access to HTTPS traffic, bypassed cert validation
Detection: Runtime inspection, Frida trace logs, proxy analysis
Remediation: Use strong native SSL pinning, detect runtime tampering, root detection

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – MITM attack: App Accepts Self-Signed Certificate
output:
Some Android/iOS apps do not properly validate server certificates. If an app accepts a self-signed certificate without user warning or validation, an attacker can intercept and manipulate HTTPS traffic using a forged certificate, enabling a full MITM attack.
Vulnerability: No Cert Validation (Trust All Certificates)
Impact: Full interception, login/session hijacking
Detection: Proxy capture with invalid/self-signed cert
Remediation: Enforce X.509 chain validation; reject self-signed unless explicitly trusted

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – No SSL Pinning attack: App Doesn’t Use Certificate Pinning
output:
When an app doesn't use certificate pinning, it trusts any valid system CA. This allows an attacker with a rogue but valid CA (like Burp’s) to perform a full MITM, intercepting HTTPS traffic without any error.
Vulnerability: No SSL Pinning
Impact: Exposure of login/session tokens, API abuse
Detection: Certificate inspection, runtime pinning check
Remediation: Implement SSL pinning with hash or public key validation

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – Expired/Mismatch Certs attack: App Accepts Expired / Mismatched Certificates
output:
If a mobile app does not validate expiry dates or domain names in server certificates, it becomes vulnerable to MITM attacks using expired, revoked, or mismatched certificates.
Vulnerability: Expired or Mismatched Server Certificate Accepted
Impact: Intercept encrypted traffic via weak cert checks
Detection: TLS handshake monitoring, expired cert test
Remediation: Enforce cert expiration & domain validation logic

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – MITM attack: Custom SSL Implementation with Weak Checks
output:
Many Android developers override default SSL validation logic and write custom TrustManager or HostnameVerifier classes. If these are weak or empty, any certificate—including a self-signed or expired one—will be accepted, making MITM trivial.
Vulnerability: Weak or Custom SSL Certificate Validation Logic
Impact: Complete MITM due to poor trust logic
Detection: Static analysis, MITM testing, code review
Remediation: Never override default TrustManager unless properly verified; use platform security APIs

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – WebView MITM attack: Using WebView / Custom Web Clients Without Validation
output:
Some mobile apps load external content in WebView without secure HTTPS checks or override SSL errors, allowing MITM using untrusted certificates, leading to session hijacking or phishing via mobile.
Vulnerability: Improper override of SSL error handling
Impact: Full MITM in WebView, phishing or token theft
Detection: Code review, network traffic inspection
Remediation: Do not override onReceivedSslError(), use SafeBrowsing APIs, always enforce HTTPS

instruction: Describe the Improper Certificate Validation – Runtime Bypass attack: MITM via Frida/Objection Runtime Patching
output:
Even if an app uses certificate pinning or secure validation, attackers can bypass it at runtime using Frida or Objection to hook or patch trust methods dynamically.
Vulnerability: Certificate Pinning Bypass via Runtime Hooking
Impact: Bypass of advanced protections, full traffic visibility
Detection: Burp intercept, dynamic runtime analysis
Remediation: Implement native pinning in C/C++ libs; detect Frida/Objection tools

instruction: Describe the Insecure Authentication – No Device/User Validation attack: No App Lock (PIN/Pattern/Fingerprint)
output:
Many apps store sensitive user data (chats, finances, personal files) without enforcing any form of app-level lock (PIN, biometric, pattern). If the phone is unlocked or stolen, any attacker can open and misuse the app without being challenged to authenticate.
Vulnerability: Absence of app-level lock even after inactivity or re-entry
Impact: Full access to user data if device is stolen or unlocked
Detection: Manual test, session re-entry without prompt
Remediation: Implement device-based lock: biometrics, PIN, or OS-based keystore auth

instruction: Describe the Insecure Authentication – Session Hijack Risk attack: No Session Timeout / Auto-Logout
output:
Applications without session timeouts remain accessible indefinitely, increasing the risk of unauthorized access, especially in stolen/lost device cases.
Vulnerability: Unexpired user sessions on inactivity or screen lock
Impact: Unauthorized access if phone is lost or unattended
Detection: Manual idle test, token inspection in Burp
Remediation: Implement inactivity timer + auto logout or re-auth prompt

instruction: Describe the Authentication Bypass via Lack of MFA attack: No 2FA (OTP, Email, TOTP)
output:
AI/ML platforms like JupyterHub, MLFlow, or Hugging Face Spaces often expose public login panels. If the platform only uses username and password without 2FA (two-factor authentication), attackers can easily brute-force or leak credentials and gain full access to training environments, models, and datasets.
Vulnerability: No 2FA or OTP requirement in authentication flow
Impact: Full takeover of AI environment, stolen models
Detection: Monitor login patterns, IP geolocation, failed attempts, and unexpected user logins
Remediation: Always enable TOTP/email/OTP-based MFA, enforce strong passwords, and rotate credentials regularly

instruction: Describe the Insecure Authentication – Token Mismanagement attack: Token Reuse / Replay Attacks
output:
Some mobile apps issue long-lived session or access tokens that can be reused without rotation or expiration. Attackers who intercept or extract these tokens can replay them indefinitely from another device or emulator.
Vulnerability: Lack of Token Expiry, Rotation, or Fingerprinting
Impact: Account hijack, session cloning, privilege escalation
Detection: Token replay via proxy and APIs
Remediation: Rotate tokens frequently, bind to IP/device, and set expiration

instruction: Describe the Insecure Authentication – Logic Bypass attack: Bypass Login via App Decompilation / Debug
output:
Some Android apps implement weak client-side logic that determines whether a user is "logged in" based on local flags (e.g., isLoggedIn = true) or without server validation. Attackers can decompile the APK, patch logic, or force variables at runtime to bypass authentication.
Vulnerability: Local Login Logic Bypass via Static or Runtime Mod
Impact: Unauthorized app access without real authentication
Detection: Static code review + runtime hook + access test
Remediation: Always validate login on server-side with secure tokens

instruction: Describe the Insecure Authentication – Biometric Bypass attack: Biometric Bypass (Rooted/Jailbroken Devices)
output:
Many mobile applications rely solely on biometric authentication (e.g., fingerprint or FaceID) without fallback verification or device integrity checks. On rooted Android or jailbroken iOS devices, it’s possible to bypass biometric gates via dynamic instrumentation or method hooking tools like Frida or Objection.
Vulnerability: Local Biometric Check Without Server Validation or Integrity Check
Impact: Unauthorized access to app features and sensitive data without user biometrics
Detection: Manual test on rooted/jailbroken devices with runtime instrumentation
Remediation: Enforce biometric via OS-provided secure prompts with server-side fallback checks, detect rooted/jailbroken environments

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Injection / Leakage attack: Background App Reads Clipboard (Android < 10)
output:
On Android versions prior to 10 (API level < 29), any app running in the background can access the system clipboard without user consent or notification. This allows malicious apps to steal sensitive data like passwords, OTPs, and cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard from other apps.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted Clipboard Access by Background Apps
Impact: Theft of OTPs, credentials, personal information, and financial data
Detection: Monitor clipboard with background app and log captured content
Remediation: Upgrade to Android 10+, restrict clipboard to foreground apps only, use secure input methods

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Injection attack: Malicious Clipboard Injection (Paste Hijack)
output:
Malicious apps can overwrite the clipboard contents while running in the background. For example, when a user copies their cryptocurrency address, the app replaces it with an attacker’s address. If the user pastes without verifying, funds or data are hijacked.
Vulnerability: Clipboard Global Write Access (no permission required)
Impact: Funds redirection, phishing link injection, credential theft
Detection: Clipboard comparison, log monitoring
Remediation: Use Android 10+ APIs, block clipboard access for background apps, validate pasted data in critical apps

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Injection attack: Fake App Auto-Writes Phishing Links to Clipboard
output:
Malicious mobile apps disguised as calculators or QR scanners can silently write phishing URLs to the clipboard. Unsuspecting users might paste this URL into a browser, email, or banking app, leading to credential theft or malware infection.
Vulnerability: Clipboard Write Access by Background Apps
Impact: Phishing, malware spread, social engineering
Detection: Static code review, clipboard monitoring tools
Remediation: Restrict clipboard access, update OS to Android 10+, use app behavior firewalls

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Leakage attack: Clipboard Token Stealing in iOS < 14
output:
Before iOS 14, any app in the foreground (and some in background with triggers) could read the system clipboard without user permission. If a user copies login tokens, email addresses, or passwords from apps like a password manager or banking app, a malicious app can immediately steal them.
Vulnerability: Global clipboard read access without user permission
Impact: Theft of 2FA tokens, credentials, sensitive text copied to clipboard
Detection: Manual review, Xcode logs, iOS 14+ paste notifications
Remediation: Use iOS 14+, avoid copying sensitive data, use secure fields and autofill instead of clipboard

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Leakage attack: Clipboard Over Bluetooth / Airdrop (Leakage Across Devices)
output:
Apple’s Universal Clipboard allows copying content on one device and pasting on another (macOS <-> iOS) over Bluetooth/Wi-Fi. Clipboard content like OTPs or passwords may leak to other linked Apple devices. If one of the paired devices is compromised, the sensitive clipboard data is leaked automatically.
Vulnerability: Cross-device clipboard sync without granular control
Impact: Leakage of credentials, financial data, crypto keys across trusted but compromised devices
Detection: Monitor clipboard access logs on paired devices
Remediation: Disable Handoff, avoid copying sensitive data, use secure in-app fields

instruction: Describe the Clipboard Injection / Accessibility Abuse attack: Accessibility Service Abuse (Android)
output:
Android Accessibility Services can be misused to monitor UI elements and automate taps and text pastes. Malicious apps request Accessibility permission to gain full control over text fields, allowing them to read or paste clipboard data into apps like browsers or banking apps without user interaction.
Vulnerability: Abuse of Accessibility Services to manipulate UI and inject clipboard content
Impact: Unauthorized data entry, UI manipulation, potential phishing payloads
Detection: Detect by scanning for accessibility abuse via logs or app permissions
Remediation: Block Accessibility unless absolutely needed, audit accessibility service usage, use Android 12+

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Static String Bypass (APK Decompile + Patch)
output:
Many apps use hardcoded checks to detect root by scanning for strings like "su", "magisk", or "busybox". By decompiling the APK and patching the method that checks for these keywords or their result, you can completely disable root detection.
Vulnerability: Insecure or hardcoded logic for root detection
Impact: Allows rooted device users to access restricted app features
Detection: Analyze static APK logic and check for modified methods
Remediation: Use runtime integrity checks, obfuscate root detection logic

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Frida Hook to Override Detection
output:
Android apps often call Java methods or native libraries (e.g., System.getenv, Runtime.getRuntime.exec("su")) to detect root. Frida allows you to hook and override these at runtime without modifying the APK.
Vulnerability: Runtime root detection logic hookable via Frida
Impact: App works even on rooted devices, unauthorized usage of premium features
Detection: Log method returns, check injected Frida scripts
Remediation: Use native root checks, anti-Frida techniques, checksum verification

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Objection Runtime Bypass (No Code Needed)
output:
Objection is a runtime mobile testing tool built over Frida. It provides pre-built commands to bypass root detection on Android without needing to know the package structure or write custom scripts.
Vulnerability: Common root detection functions hooked at runtime
Impact: Security features disabled on rooted phones
Detection: Observe Frida-based hooks or unexpected method returns
Remediation: Obfuscate method names, detect debugger/frida runtime

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Hide Root with Magisk + DenyList
output:
Some mobile applications perform root checks using popular methods like checking for su binary, magisk processes, or default root paths. However, modern rooting tools like Magisk allow you to hide the root status from these apps using the DenyList feature, which prevents specific apps from seeing the root environment. This method doesn't modify the APK or runtime but instead uses Magisk's built-in features.
Vulnerability: Inadequate app-level root detection and reliance on known paths/binaries
Impact: Allows attackers or users on rooted devices to use security-sensitive apps (e.g., banking, finance, streaming)
Detection: Monitor system properties, check Zygisk activity, and filesystem mounts
Remediation: Use SafetyNet + Play Integrity API, perform native root checks, and integrity attestation

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Rename Root Binaries & Paths
output:
Many Android apps detect root by checking for binaries like /system/bin/su, /system/xbin/daemonsu, or apps like magisk, busybox, etc. These apps will refuse to run if any of these binaries exist. By renaming or hiding these files, you can bypass detection without modifying the APK or app logic.
Vulnerability: grep busybox. Step 5: Temporarily rename these binaries using mv su su.bakandmv busybox busybox.old(if allowed). Step 6: If the system partition is read-only, runmount -o remount,rw /systemto enable write access. Step 7: You may also bind-mount/dev/nullover these paths usingmount -o bind /dev/null /system/bin/su. Step 8: Reboot your device. Step 9: Launch the target app and check if the root warning disappears. This confirms the binary was the detection trigger. Step 10: Optionally, restore binaries using mv su.bak su` after testing.
Impact: Insecure root binary lookup logic
Detection: T1621: Evade root detection via system binary manipulation
Remediation: App assumes device is non-rooted and functions normally

instruction: Describe the Jailbreak Detection Bypass attack: iOS Jailbreak Bypass (Flex, Frida, Choicy)
output:
Many iOS apps use Jailbreak detection APIs such as fileExistsAtPath("/Applications/Cydia.app"), fork(), or check for loaded dynamic libraries. Tools like Flex, Frida, and Choicy can bypass such checks by hooking or hiding the jailbreak environment.
Vulnerability: Unsafe reliance on public jailbreak indicators
Impact: App executes on jailbroken device without detection
Detection: Jailbreak logs, Cydia file existence, crash logs
Remediation: Code obfuscation, native jailbreak detection, disable tweaks

instruction: Describe the Root Detection Bypass attack: Bypass via Code Obfuscation (Fake Status)
output:
Some apps use easily reversible logic (e.g., return isDeviceRooted()) for detection. By decompiling the APK, reversing the logic, or misleading the method return, a bypass can be achieved using code-level obfuscation — making the app believe the device is not rooted even when it is.
Vulnerability: Logical return bypass in decompiled code
Impact: App operates as if on a secure device despite being rooted
Detection: Static decompilation, return logic analysis
Remediation: Use native root check, code obfuscation, anti-tampering

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Bypass Login / Auth Logic (Frida/Xposed)
output:
Many Android apps enforce login checks using simple conditional logic in Java/Kotlin (e.g., if (isLoggedIn())). This check can be overridden in memory during runtime using Frida or Xposed. This allows attackers to bypass authentication without knowing valid credentials or modifying the APK.
Vulnerability: Weak login logic manipulatable at runtime
Impact: Full login bypass, unauthorized access, privilege escalation
Detection: Detect loaded Frida, Xposed modules, or method tampering
Remediation: Use native code login verification, tamper detection, integrity checks

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Bypass SSL Pinning (Frida/Objection)
output:
SSL pinning restricts apps to accept only trusted certificates. Attackers bypass this to intercept sensitive HTTPS traffic (MITM). This attack uses Frida or Objection to hook SSL methods and disable checks.
Vulnerability: Improper Certificate Validation
Impact: Sensitive data exfiltration
Detection: Root/SSL bypass detection, cert fingerprint checks
Remediation: Enforce hardware-backed pinning (TrustAnchor), use native code checks

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Disable Root/Jailbreak Detection
output:
Security-aware apps detect root access to prevent tampering. This attack hooks these detection functions using Frida to bypass them at runtime.
Vulnerability: Improper Root Detection Logic
Impact: Protection bypass, unrestricted access
Detection: Root-check bypass hooks, behavioral alerts
Remediation: Use native detection, SafetyNet API, integrity checks

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Steal API Keys, Tokens, Secrets (Frida)
output:
Apps store tokens or keys in memory or static variables. These can be extracted at runtime using Frida. This allows full access to backend APIs, bypassing UI or auth.
Vulnerability: Insecure Runtime Secret Exposure
Impact: Account takeover, unauthorized API access
Detection: API call logging, tamper detection
Remediation: Use Keystore/Keychain + obfuscation

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Disable Root/Jailbreak Detection
output:
Many apps refuse to run on rooted/jailbroken devices. This attack disables root checks at runtime using Frida, allowing full access to all app features even on rooted devices.
Vulnerability: Insecure Root Detection Logic
Impact: Security bypass, unrestricted access to app features
Detection: Log-based detection, runtime behavior monitoring
Remediation: Implement server-side checks, use native code for root detection, integrate Google Play Integrity API

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Modify Payment / Subscription Validation
output:
Premium features in mobile apps are usually unlocked after server-validated payments. This attack uses Frida to hook and modify app logic to bypass validation without payment.
Vulnerability: Client-side Validation Bypass
Impact: Financial fraud, access to paid services for free
Detection: Compare client-server logs, audit API calls
Remediation: Perform server-side checks for subscription, never rely solely on client logic

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Instrumentation attack: Xposed Module to Hook/Modify UI Logic
output:
Some apps hide buttons or block access based on conditions (e.g., role or payment). This attack hooks UI logic using Xposed to forcibly show or change those UI elements.
Vulnerability: Insecure UI Logic Enforcement
Impact: Privilege escalation, bypass paywall or restrictions
Detection: UI flow validation, runtime app inspection
Remediation: Keep logic server-verified, use obfuscation, detect framework hooks

instruction: Describe the Root/Jailbreak Detection Bypass attack: iOS – Bypass Jailbreak Detection with Cydia Substrate
output:
Many iOS apps block functionality on jailbroken devices to prevent tampering or cheating. This attack shows how to bypass jailbreak checks using a tweak developed with Theos and Cydia Substrate.
Vulnerability: Inadequate Jailbreak Detection Logic
Impact: Full app access on jailbroken device, app restriction bypass
Detection: iOS app logs, jailbreak tools running in memory, dynamic instrumentation detection
Remediation: Perform server-side integrity checks, use native anti-jailbreak libraries, implement advanced detection (e.g., syscall monitoring)

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: Java Method Hooking (Frida – Android)
output:
The attacker wants to intercept and manipulate sensitive app methods such as login validation or payment checks. By hooking Java methods at runtime using Frida, they can change behavior without modifying the APK itself.
Vulnerability: Insecure Runtime Environment
Impact: Bypass authentication, change app logic, intercept sensitive data
Detection: App tampering alerts, behavior anomalies, log analysis
Remediation: Implement code obfuscation, tamper detection, native security libraries, Frida detection checks

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: Native Function Hooking (Frida - C/NDK)
output:
You want to hook and manipulate a native C function (e.g., a function from a mobile banking app using C code via Android NDK) to bypass security checks like root detection, SSL pinning, or license verification at runtime using Frida.
Vulnerability: Native C Library exposed to runtime
Impact: Bypass security check or internal logic (e.g., root, SSL, premium feature)
Detection: Runtime integrity check, stack traces, app behavior anomalies
Remediation: Apply integrity checks inside native code; use anti-debugging techniques; obfuscate native symbols; detect Frida hooks

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: iOS Objective-C Runtime Hook (Frida / Theos / Cydia Substrate)
output:
In this scenario, you want to dynamically modify the behavior of a method in an iOS app written in Objective-C, such as disabling jailbreak detection or forcing premium content to always return 'unlocked'. You will hook Objective-C methods using Frida on a jailbroken iPhone.
Vulnerability: Runtime-modifiable Objective-C method
Impact: Subvert logic to gain premium access, disable security checks
Detection: App monitoring jailbreak, logs, behavioral anomalies
Remediation: Implement jailbreak checks in non-overridable C/Swift; obfuscate class names and methods

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: Dynamic Dex/Class Injection (Android - ClassLoader)
output:
In this scenario, the attacker injects a malicious .dex file at runtime into a target app using a custom or reflective DexClassLoader, allowing dynamic execution of arbitrary classes and methods without modifying the original APK. This bypasses static code analysis and obfuscation.
Vulnerability: ClassLoader misuse and dynamic code loading
Impact: Full code execution inside trusted app space, bypassing static detection and manifest permission limits
Detection: Detect loaded dex paths at runtime, monitor DexClassLoader behavior
Remediation: Enforce ProGuard/obfuscation, monitor runtime dex loads, disable DexClassLoader in release builds

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: Xposed Module Code Injection
output:
An attacker writes a malicious Xposed module that modifies logic in the target app (e.g., bypass login, disable ads, fake in-app purchases) by hooking Java methods at runtime using Xposed Framework. Requires a rooted device with Xposed installed.
Vulnerability: Runtime method replace via framework hook
Impact: Privilege escalation, logic bypass, feature unlock, payment bypass
Detection: Xposed module detection (file/folder/stack), runtime tamper checks
Remediation: Check for Xposed modules, perform runtime integrity verification, detect method override

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: WebView JavaScript Injection
output:
In this attack, a malicious actor injects JavaScript into an Android WebView to steal sensitive user information, such as credentials or payment data, by exploiting insecure WebView configuration (e.g., addJavascriptInterface exposed to untrusted content).
Vulnerability: Unsafe JS interface exposure in WebView
Impact: Credential theft, data leakage, session hijack, clickjacking
Detection: Static analysis (e.g., MobSF), dynamic analysis with Burp/Frida
Remediation: Use @JavascriptInterface only on safe methods; validate URLs; disable JS or sandbox content

instruction: Describe the Code Injection / Runtime Hooking attack: Environment Variable / Config Hooking
output:
This attack involves hooking and modifying sensitive environment variables or app configuration values at runtime—like API keys, debug flags, server endpoints, feature toggles, or authentication flags—usually stored in BuildConfig, System.getenv(), or loaded from property/config files. This can alter app behavior, force debug mode, redirect API traffic, or bypass checks.
Vulnerability: Runtime-accessible config/environment values
Impact: Redirect server traffic, leak internal state, unlock hidden features, force debug mode
Detection: Check for unexpected config values, detect overwritten class fields, Frida detection
Remediation: Obfuscate config values, move sensitive logic to backend, detect tampering, avoid static BuildConfig flags

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: SQLite Injection (Client-Side SQLi – Android/iOS)
output:
SQLite databases are commonly used in mobile apps to store local data. If user input is concatenated directly into raw SQL queries (e.g., for search, login, or data retrieval), attackers can inject SQL payloads to dump, modify, or delete local user data. This occurs purely on the client-side (no remote server involved).
Vulnerability: Raw query building with user input
Impact: Data dump, unauthorized access, local data loss, crash
Detection: Static analysis, runtime SQL logs, user behavior monitoring
Remediation: Use parameterized queries like rawQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=?", new String[]{userInput});

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: Remote SQLi via API Call
output:
In this attack, an API endpoint used by a mobile app is vulnerable to SQL injection. The app sends user input (like search or login data) to a server-side endpoint without proper validation. The attacker manipulates input to modify SQL queries and extract or manipulate server data.
Vulnerability: Server-side input handling flaw
Impact: Remote database compromise, privilege escalation, data theft
Detection: WAF logs, anomaly detection, API behavior monitoring
Remediation: Sanitize inputs, use parameterized queries (PreparedStatement), implement WAFs

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: Login Bypass via SQL Injection
output:
This is a classic SQLi scenario where a mobile app login form fails to sanitize input sent to the backend database. By injecting a crafted payload into the username/password field, an attacker can bypass authentication entirely and gain access as any user.
Vulnerability: Insecure query logic without parameterization
Impact: Full user account takeover, admin access, data tampering
Detection: Behavior analysis, WAF, unusual login patterns
Remediation: Use secure authentication logic with PreparedStatement, validate user input, enable MFA

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: Command Injection via Runtime.exec (Android)
output:
This attack exploits unsafe usage of Runtime.getRuntime().exec() in Android applications, where user-supplied input is directly passed to shell commands without sanitization. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary commands on the local device with the app’s permission level—leading to data leakage, privilege misuse, or persistence installation.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized command execution via exec()
Impact: Arbitrary command execution, data exfiltration, privilege misuse, remote shell access
Detection: Analyze source code for Runtime.exec, monitor ADB logs, use dynamic analysis tools
Remediation: Avoid exec() with user input; use safe Android APIs; apply strict input validation and allowlisting

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: OS Command Injection via File Upload or Clipboard
output:
In some mobile apps, file upload features or clipboard-based import/export options handle filenames or clipboard content using shell commands via Runtime.exec() or equivalent. If file names or clipboard content are passed unsanitized, attackers can inject shell commands and achieve arbitrary code execution within app context.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized shell execution via input
Impact: Arbitrary shell execution, file overwrite, clipboard abuse, local persistence
Detection: Monitor file paths, clipboard logs, logcat, Frida, source code review
Remediation: Sanitize input paths and clipboard data, avoid shell-based execution, use native file I/O APIs

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: iOS Objective-C Command Injection
output:
This vulnerability arises in iOS apps that use Objective-C NSTask or system() APIs with user input passed directly into the command string. If no input validation or escaping is done, the attacker can execute arbitrary system commands inside the app sandbox on jailbroken devices.
Vulnerability: Dynamic input to system() or NSTask
Impact: Arbitrary shell execution, sandbox escape (if root), private data access
Detection: Binary analysis, Frida trace, command monitoring, system call logs
Remediation: Never use raw system calls with user input, use Apple APIs, validate/sanitize commands

instruction: Describe the SQL Injection / Command Injection attack: WebView + SQLi or Command Injection via Backend
output:
Many hybrid Android/iOS apps use WebView to interface with backend APIs for dynamic content. If user input via WebView is sent to backend PHP/.NET/Node code that builds SQL or shell commands without validation, it results in remote SQLi or command injection. These may not be visible in frontend but are fully exploitable through WebView parameters.
Vulnerability: Backend injection via client WebView
Impact: Remote data breach, backend control, arbitrary command execution
Detection: Monitor WebView API calls, review backend code for concat/exec usage
Remediation: Validate/sanitize input at backend, use ORM and safe shell APIs, disable WebView JS if unused

instruction: Describe the WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection) attack: JavaScript Injection via Input Fields in WebView Forms
output:
Some hybrid or Android WebView apps embed HTML forms in WebView and directly reflect user input back to the page without sanitization. If JavaScript is injected into input fields and rendered as-is, it can execute malicious scripts like session token exfiltration, keylogging, or redirecting users to phishing pages.
Vulnerability: User input reflected in WebView HTML
Impact: JavaScript execution inside app context, session hijacking, phishing, exfiltration
Detection: Manual testing, Burp analysis, Frida hook, log monitoring
Remediation: Always sanitize user inputs, use WebView.setSafeBrowsingEnabled(true), encode HTML entities

instruction: Describe the WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection) attack: Unrestricted WebView Navigation
output:
Apps that allow unrestricted navigation in WebView using webView.loadUrl() can be tricked into loading malicious external websites, including those with embedded malware or credential-stealing JavaScript. Without validation of target URLs, attackers may force navigation to http://evil.com by injecting links into app inputs or manipulating WebView redirection.
Vulnerability: No domain validation before navigation
Impact: Phishing, token theft, full remote HTML/JS control in app, user deception
Detection: Monitor navigation calls in WebView, Frida hook, manual test via Burp
Remediation: Only allow known URL patterns using allowlists, block http, enable safe browsing, disable JS

instruction: Describe the WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection) attack: addJavascriptInterface() Exploit (Android Only)
output:
If addJavascriptInterface() is used to expose Java methods to JavaScript without setting minSdkVersion >= 17 or enabling security flags, it allows malicious web pages to invoke native Java code, potentially executing unintended operations like file access, SMS, or even remote command execution.
Vulnerability: Unsafe JS-native bridge via addJavascriptInterface
Impact: Arbitrary Java method execution, remote control via malicious JS page
Detection: Code review, MobSF analysis, Frida hook, behavior monitoring
Remediation: Avoid exposing dangerous methods, target SDK >= 17, use input validation, disable JS when unused

instruction: Describe the WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection) attack: Local File Injection via WebView
output:
If an app’s WebView is allowed to load local file paths (e.g., file:///sdcard/...) via user input—without proper validation—an attacker can force the app to load a local HTML/JS file packed with malicious payloads. This lets them execute arbitrary JavaScript under the app’s WebView context and exfiltrate data or modify app behavior.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted file:// path loading
Impact: Local JavaScript execution, data exfiltration, compromised app logic
Detection: Monitor WebView file loads, analyze code for file path use signs
Remediation: Restrict file loading, sanitize file:// usage, disable JS when not needed
