Detection: Audit all os.environ access; scan logs for leaked envs; enforce env whitelisting
Remediation: Avoid relying on os.environ for secrets or paths; use secrets managers; validate env vars against allowlist

instruction: Describe the Arbitrary Code Execution via import attack: Dynamic Import Exploitation
output:
Some ML tools dynamically import code (e.g., models, tasks, plugins) using __import__() or importlib, which can be hijacked to load attacker-controlled modules.
Vulnerability: Untrusted input to importlib / dynamic loading
Impact: Arbitrary RCE during training or model loading
Detection: Monitor imported modules; hash and verify trusted plugins; detect unregistered or new modules
Remediation: Avoid using unvalidated dynamic imports; enforce plugin registries; sandbox imported modules

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Execution via Pickle/Joblib attack: Untrusted Deserialization in ML Libs
output:
ML libraries like joblib, pickle, and cloudpickle are commonly used for model saving/loading—but deserializing untrusted input leads to RCE.
Vulnerability: Unsafe deserialization of untrusted input
Impact: Remote Code Execution, Data Poisoning
Detection: Alert on usage of pickle/joblib on unknown files; isolate deserialization operations
Remediation: Use safer formats like JSON, ONNX, or TensorFlow SavedModel; disable pickle/joblib on unverified files

instruction: Describe the Poisoned Training Data via Dependency Execution attack: Jupyter Notebook Dependency Execution – Poisoned Training Data w/ Trigger
output:
Attacker injects a malicious notebook or dependency that, during data preprocessing, adds training samples containing a hidden trigger pattern to compromise model integrity.
Vulnerability: Implicit trust in shared preprocessing notebooks or modules
Impact: Backdoor model behavior, targeted misclassification
Detection: Monitor dataset stats; manual review of code; data provenance tracking and threshold alerts
Remediation: Use only trusted internal preprocessing code; lock and review notebooks; validate data integrity and labels before training

instruction: Describe the Supply Chain Attack via Build System Injection attack: Build Toolchain Exploit via CMake Backdoor
output:
Attackers inject malicious logic (e.g., model backdoor, data exfiltration) into the CMake-based build toolchain used in AI/ML projects to compromise ML pipelines.
Vulnerability: Trust in external build toolchain scripts
Impact: AI model backdoor, training data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor network activity during builds, diff CMake files, enforce reproducible builds
Remediation: Enforce strict review on all build files; isolate build environment; never trust third-party CMake scripts blindly

instruction: Describe the Format Attack via Compression Tools attack: Model Compression Tool Exploit
output:
Attackers modify model compression tools (like ONNX optimizer, quantization frameworks) to inject hidden logic that activates only in compressed models.
Vulnerability: Trust in open-source model compression tools
Impact: Model backdoor in production-ready compressed models
Detection: Monitor for abnormal graph changes post-compression, compare model hashes, enforce deterministic builds
Remediation: Use officially signed tools only; verify model graph after compression; never compress models using unverified tools

instruction: Describe the Binary Exploit via Model File Parsing attack: Model Format Parser Exploit
output:
Malicious binary model (e.g., ONNX, TensorRT plan file) exploits unsafe parsing logic in model loading libraries (e.g., buffer overflows, type confusion, file parsing).
Vulnerability: Unsafe model file parsing in ML frameworks
Impact: Remote code execution or memory corruption in model loader
Detection: Monitor for crashes or segmentation faults during model load; audit file integrity
Remediation: Isolate model loading inside a sandbox; validate model structure; use official model zoo files only

instruction: Describe the Graph-Level Logic Injection attack: Scripted Model Attack via TorchScript / TF Graph
output:
TorchScript or TensorFlow Graph models can include arbitrary code during tracing or scripting; attacker exploits this to run logic conditionally.
Vulnerability: Executable logic hidden in model graph
Impact: Hidden backdoor or exfiltration in model inference
Detection: Check for conditional logic in model graph; analyze TorchScript/TensorFlow internal nodes
Remediation: Use unsigned model formats; avoid using externally scripted models; restrict model access to trusted teams only

instruction: Describe the API Abuse & Exfiltration via Telemetry Libraries attack: Remote Logger Hijack (e.g., Weights & Biases)
output:
Logging/telemetry platforms like Weights & Biases (wandb) are abused to exfiltrate data or models during training/inference.
Vulnerability: Remote telemetry misuse
Impact: Sensitive data leakage to attacker's remote dashboard
Detection: Monitor for unexpected API endpoints or tokens in telemetry libraries; track outgoing connections from training systems
Remediation: Enforce offline/air-gapped training; validate all telemetry configs; rotate API tokens regularly

instruction: Describe the Objective Tampering (Loss Function Backdoor) attack: Custom Loss Function Exploit
output:
Attacker replaces or modifies the loss function in model code to mislead training optimization, e.g., favoring incorrect labels or leaking gradients.
Vulnerability: Malicious gradient manipulation in loss function
Impact: Model output bias; misclassifications; backdoor injection
Detection: Compare gradients between clean and backdoored training runs; manually inspect custom loss functions
Remediation: Use trusted standard loss implementations only; block unknown changes to training objectives

instruction: Describe the Hook-Based Code Injection attack: Insecure Update Hooks Exploit
output:
Attackers modify model update hooks (callbacks or training events) to run malicious logic (e.g., data exfiltration, behavior injection) during training or evaluation.
Vulnerability: Trust in unvalidated callback logic
Impact: Model theft, logic injection, silent monitoring
Detection: Monitor all training callbacks; inspect logs for network requests; disallow unknown hooks in production
Remediation: Use whitelisted callback logic only; disable networking in training jobs; enforce strict callback registration policy

instruction: Describe the Data Memorization Leakage attack: Direct Memorization Extraction
output:
Attackers extract sensitive training data that the model "memorized" during training by probing it with specific prompts or brute-force inputs. Common in LLMs or small datasets.
Vulnerability: Overfitting to rare or unique training data
Impact: Sensitive data leakage, identity compromise
Detection: Monitor for prompt abuse, log model outputs, detect patterns resembling training data, enforce output filtering
Remediation: Train with DP, use large diverse datasets, monitor API abuse, rate-limit probing, apply output sanitization

instruction: Describe the Prompt Injection attack: Prompt-based Data Mining
output:
Attacker crafts smart prompts to trick language models into revealing memorized information from training data (e.g., passwords, SSNs, private emails).
Vulnerability: Weak prompt sanitization and memorized data
Impact: Training data leakage, identity theft, regulatory non-compliance
Detection: Monitor prompt history; alert on patterns like "list of passwords", "generate emails", etc.; log high-entropy outputs
Remediation: Implement output filtering, fine-tune with RLHF/DPO, enforce training with differential privacy

instruction: Describe the Model Sampling Attack attack: Sampling-based Extraction
output:
Attackers use model output sampling methods like greedy, top-k, or nucleus sampling to generate outputs and extract sensitive memorized phrases.
Vulnerability: Overfitting and no output filtering
Impact: Training data extraction at scale
Detection: Monitor repeated prompt patterns, detect unusual output similarity over time, track entropy of outputs
Remediation: Use DP, train on public data only, monitor sampling APIs, limit total generations per user

instruction: Describe the Privacy Attack attack: Membership Inference Attack
output:
Attacker determines whether a specific data point was used in a model’s training set by comparing confidence scores or behaviors on known vs unknown inputs.
Vulnerability: Overconfident prediction behavior on training data
Impact: Identity linkage, privacy policy violations
Detection: Analyze prediction confidence distributions; alert if model shows high variance between member/non-member cases
Remediation: Train with DP, label smoothing, early stopping, restrict confidence output in APIs

instruction: Describe the Canary Injection + Detection attack: Canary Insertion Attack
output:
Defender (or attacker) inserts unique "canary" data (e.g., fake emails or passwords) into training set to test whether model memorizes and regurgitates it post-training.
Vulnerability: Model memorization and leakage of rare sequences
Impact: Proof of memorization, privacy failure
Detection: Use canary insertion auditing, track canary leakage over generations, evaluate per-token probabilities
Remediation: Train with DP, reduce dataset redundancy, audit memorization with synthetic canaries

instruction: Describe the Partial Prompt Attack attack: Partial Information Reconstruction
output:
Attackers exploit structured patterns (e.g., SSNs, emails, phone numbers) and coax the model into revealing the missing parts via targeted prompts or brute-force completion.
Vulnerability: Memorization of structured personal data
Impact: Partial identity/data reconstruction
Detection: Detect repeated pattern prompts; monitor completions with known format signatures (e.g., regex on SSNs or emails)
Remediation: Use output filters; train with differential privacy; inject noise around sensitive tokens

instruction: Describe the Logit Mining attack: Logit-Based Extraction
output:
Attacker analyzes the raw output logits (pre-softmax scores) of a model to identify highly probable tokens that were likely in the training data.
Vulnerability: Logit access reveals memorized training secrets
Impact: Raw data leakage, insider model compromise
Detection: Alert when raw logits are accessed; use output transformation pipelines
Remediation: Remove debug interfaces, post-process logits, enforce token access guards

instruction: Describe the Training-Time Gradient Leakage attack: Gradient Leakage (LoRA/Fine-tuning)
output:
Attacker extracts sensitive data from gradients during fine-tuning, especially when using LoRA, FedAvg (federated learning), or multi-party collaborative training.
Vulnerability: Exposed gradients can reconstruct private records
Impact: Full input leakage, privacy breach, federated compromise
Detection: Monitor gradient sizes; track LoRA logs; detect long-running fine-tune sessions with high loss divergence
Remediation: Use DP optimizer, clip gradients, avoid public LoRA merging, encrypt model internals

instruction: Describe the Representation Exploit attack: Embedding Inversion Attack
output:
Attacker reverses embeddings (vectors) produced by the model to recover the original text input, exploiting insufficient privacy in encoders.
Vulnerability: Embeddings uniquely leak original text
Impact: Full reconstruction of raw input data
Detection: Monitor for decoder model usage; trace repeated embeddings; flag high-similarity reverse lookups
Remediation: Add DP noise to embeddings, avoid public vector APIs, use representation scrambling

instruction: Describe the Trigger-based Leak attack: Querying with Synthetic Triggers
output:
Attackers craft unusual or adversarial prompts that trigger models to regurgitate exact training data (e.g., names, emails, phrases) by exploiting memorization.
Vulnerability: Memorization triggered by specific phrases
Impact: Exact phrase leakage from training corpus
Detection: Monitor prompts with patterns like “repeat”, “what was the”, etc.
Remediation: Use DP training; restrict decoding strategies (e.g., no sampling); sanitize prompt patterns

instruction: Describe the Chat Exploit attack: Multi-Turn Context Probing
output:
Attacker uses long conversations to extract secrets by building rapport, roleplay, and manipulating model memory to slowly leak training data.
Vulnerability: Memory window used to infer or leak prior content
Impact: Partial to full record leakage over long chat sessions
Detection: Alert on unusually long sessions or repetitive identity prompts
Remediation: Limit memory window; reset context often; block roleplay identity patterns

instruction: Describe the Jailbreak Role Shift attack: Instruction Injection for Role Shift
output:
Attackers trick the model into assuming a hidden identity (e.g., "You are the internal system admin") to leak training data or bypass safety filters.
Vulnerability: Prompt override leads to role-based leak
Impact: Privilege escalation, hidden instruction access
Detection: Monitor prompt prefix abuse (you are...), detect injection attempts with high entropy or out-of-distribution behavior
Remediation: Use system prompt sealing; separate user/system instructions; validate model state post role-switch

instruction: Describe the Iterative Memorization Leak attack: Token-by-Token Extraction
output:
Attacker extracts memorized data (e.g., names, phrases) one token at a time by querying and guessing next likely token using output or logit confidence.
Vulnerability: Token-wise memorization leakage
Impact: Full secret phrase extraction one token at a time
Detection: Log long greedy completions on sensitive prompts; detect high-probability token chains starting from known phrases
Remediation: Train with noise; remove exact matches from training data; use entropy-based filters

instruction: Describe the Diversity Exploit attack: Temperature-Shifted Output Sweep
output:
Attackers manipulate the decoding temperature of generative models (e.g., GPT) to cause the model to reveal raw, unfiltered, and memorized content.
Vulnerability: High temperature leads to hallucinated or memorized output
Impact: Leakage of internal notes, secrets, or phrases
Detection: Monitor for excessive temperature values; flag prompts repeated with different temp settings
Remediation: Cap temperature; enforce decoding constraints; disable high-temp on sensitive models

instruction: Describe the Passive Leak attack: Data Echo in Autocomplete Systems
output:
Autocomplete systems (e.g., code editors, email assistants) may echo training data when users type known phrases.
Vulnerability: Memorized completions based on partial input
Impact: Secrets or identity info echoed to end users
Detection: Track high-entropy completions; monitor for overfit suggestions
Remediation: Use synthetic or scrubbed datasets for training autocomplete features; audit completions

instruction: Describe the Model Inversion attack: Training Corpus Reconstruction
output:
At scale, attackers can use output patterns to reconstruct large parts of the training dataset.
Vulnerability: Verbatim or semi-verbatim data present in outputs
Impact: Massive corpus exposure across millions of queries
Detection: Monitor aggregate query volumes per user; track linguistic patterns in output distributions
Remediation: Apply differential privacy; remove exact sequences from training data; implement query rate limiting

instruction: Describe the Safety Probe Abuse attack: Red-Teaming Leaks
output:
Red teamers or attackers simulate adversarial users and test for unsafe model behavior, often unintentionally causing data leaks during probing.
Vulnerability: Unsafe red team practices can leak sensitive data
Impact: Leak of secret tokens, policy text, internal knowledge
Detection: Track testing outputs; enforce red-team retention policies; isolate red team environments
Remediation: Sanitize all test outputs; automate removal of real names/emails in evaluation pipelines

instruction: Describe the Intermediate Step Leak attack: Chain-of-Thought Leakage
output:
When prompted for reasoning, LLMs may output step-by-step chains that leak sensitive or memorized training facts mid-explanation.
Vulnerability: CoT prompts triggering real-world intermediate data
Impact: Leak of partial PII or record fragments during reasoning
Detection: Monitor reasoning chains for names, IDs, or patterns common in sensitive documents
Remediation: Apply CoT sanitization filters; remove sensitive CoT templates from training; apply synthetic augmentation

instruction: Describe the Downstream Leak attack: Fine-tuned Model Reversal
output:
Attackers abuse fine-tuned models (e.g., ChatGPT-finetuned) to “unmask” the base model’s memorized content by removing or bypassing the fine-tuning layer.
Vulnerability: Base model content still present under fine-tuning
Impact: Leak of raw, untuned model behaviors and private data
Detection: Monitor for adapter bypass; analyze fine-tuned vs base diff outputs
Remediation: Encrypt or restrict base model access; train base and downstream models with consistent safety layers

instruction: Describe the Prompt Recovery attack: Prefix-Tuning/Prompt-Tuning Inversion
output:
By analyzing gradients or token outputs of prefix-tuned models, attackers can reconstruct the original private prompt used for tuning.
Vulnerability: Prompt embedding leakage via probing techniques
Impact: Recovery of private training prompts or contexts
Detection: Gradient auditing; monitor output token stability across variations
Remediation: Apply differential privacy on prompt layers; prevent gradient-based access to tuning embeddings

instruction: Describe the Multi-Turn Memory Abuse attack: Zero-shot + Multi-turn Leak Amplification
output:
Attackers exploit long conversations with zero-shot prompts to slowly bypass filters and extract sensitive info over multiple turns.
Vulnerability: Long context exploits filter degradation
Impact: Slow leak of memorized text across disguised sessions
Detection: Turn-by-turn logging; detect suspicious roleplay or mimic chains
Remediation: Context reset between turns; adversarial red-teaming; dynamic safety override tokens

instruction: Describe the Universal Prompt Attack attack: Cross-Prompt Trigger Mining
output:
Find a single prompt that can consistently trigger multiple types of memorized or sensitive data leaks across different tasks or domains.
Vulnerability: Universal trigger matching and unsafe sampling
Impact: Leak of wide-ranging sensitive samples across tasks
Detection: Classify and log high-risk prompts; detect over-repeated prompt leakage patterns
Remediation: Introduce adversarial training for trigger resilience; build prompt blacklist/embedding similarity defense

instruction: Describe the Cached Output Exploit attack: API Output Replay Attack
output:
Attackers exploit logged or cached model outputs from public APIs to re-query past completions and extract sensitive info repeatedly.
Vulnerability: Weak caching or logging strategies
Impact: Data scraping, privacy violation, persistent leakage
Detection: Monitor cache hit rates and I/O log access frequency
Remediation: Use salted caching; never store logs with plaintext prompts or completions

instruction: Describe the Multilingual Data Leak attack: Translation Leakage
output:
Ask the model to translate rare or sensitive examples from training that were multilingual. Translation can reveal unseen content.
Vulnerability: Exposure of low-frequency training translations
Impact: Leak of medical/legal text, names, or addresses
Detection: Detect low-frequency inputs in multilingual contexts; match rare translations across users
Remediation: Filter structured content in training data; avoid direct translation of named entities

instruction: Describe the Source Leak via Generation attack: Code Generation Leak
output:
When prompted for code, models may output real API keys, credentials, or rare internal functions from the training data.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded secrets and sensitive code in training
Impact: Leak of credentials, secret keys, internal logic
Detection: Regex secret detection on outputs; monitor for completions with high-entropy secrets
Remediation: Sanitize training code; filter secret/token patterns; enforce post-training output filtering

instruction: Describe the Prompt-Based Shell Injection attack: Basic Shell Injection via Prompt
output:
Attacker uses an LLM interface to execute OS commands by injecting shell code into prompts that are forwarded to a vulnerable backend execution environment.
Vulnerability: Shell execution via prompt injection
Impact: Full system compromise, data exfiltration, pivoting
Detection: Monitor logs for shell-like syntax in prompts; alert on filesystem or credential access commands
Remediation: Escape or sanitize input before shell execution; use sandbox, privilege separation; avoid direct os.system(prompt)

instruction: Describe the Markdown Prompt Injection / Code Exec attack: Code Block Injection in Markdown
output:
Attacker injects malicious code into a Markdown code block that an AI system interprets and executes on the host, due to insecure content rendering pipelines.
Vulnerability: Execution of code in Markdown code blocks
Impact: Remote code execution, data leakage, system takeover
Detection: Monitor raw Markdown inputs; alert on suspicious commands in code blocks; restrict code execution capabilities
Remediation: Disable auto-run; sandbox code execution; use safe parsers that render Markdown only as text

instruction: Describe the Tool Invocation Hijack attack: AutoGPT Tool Injection
output:
Attacker crafts a prompt that uses the tool_name(input) syntax to hijack invocation of sensitive tools (e.g., shell or network) by AutoGPT-like agents.
Vulnerability: Automatic execution of tool syntax in prompts semantic
Impact: Remote code execution, data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor for unexpected tool invocation; detect tool_shell usage in logs
Remediation: Remove automatic tool calls; whitelist allowed tools; use secure agent architectures

instruction: Describe the Expression Injection attack: LangChain Expression Injection
output:
Attacker injects Python expressions into LangChain pipelines designed to evaluate snippets using eval() or exec().
Vulnerability: Unsafe evaluation of user strings via eval()/exec()
Impact: Full code execution, system compromise
Detection: Monitor chain content for dangerous syntax; audit dynamic code paths
Remediation: Remove eval/exec; use function-based chaining; validate AST before execution

instruction: Describe the API Misuse / Function Call Hijack attack: Function-Calling Abuse (OpenAI/Anthropic)
output:
Attacker injects malicious function_call entries that trick LLM into calling arbitrary or unintended functions like os.system through function-calling API.
Vulnerability: Unverified function_call JSON from model
Impact: Remote execution, data leakage
Detection: Monitor function_call output; disallow non-registered function invocations
Remediation: Whitelist callable functions; validate function names/args; sandbox call environment

instruction: Describe the REPL-based Command Injection attack: Python REPL Tool Injection
output:
Attacker passes malicious Python code to an AI-assisted REPL tool that executes user-supplied code without sanitization.
Vulnerability: Direct execution of untrusted Python code in REPL
Impact: Host compromise, data theft
Detection: Log code run; alert on usage of toxic functions; review changes to file system
Remediation: Use sandboxed REPL; remove os, sys, subprocess; run within container with no privileges

instruction: Describe the JSON Parsing Exploit attack: Serialized JSON Command Injection
output:
Attacker crafts JSON payloads containing code commands; when parsed and executed by LLM or backend logic, they run OS commands.
Vulnerability: Unchecked JSON field passed to shell interpreter
Impact: OS command execution, data leak, system control
Detection: Flag JSON payloads with multiple commands (;, &&); alert when os.system() called with dynamic input
Remediation: Use strict command APIs (e.g., subprocess.run([...])); sanitization and validation; sandbox execution

instruction: Describe the Response Injection attack: Command Injection via Tool Return Values
output:
LLM outputs are interpreted by downstream automation agents and executed as shell commands without validation.
Vulnerability: Direct execution of unvalidated LLM responses
Impact: Remote code injection, data harvesting, malware drop
Detection: Log executed commands; detect composite commands; alert on dynamic execution of unverified LLM output
Remediation: Enforce structured output (JSON); validate command tokens; sandbox calls; escape LLM output before execution

instruction: Describe the URL Injection / Remote Execution attack: Remote URL Execution via LLM Output
output:
LLM outputs a URL to external script; downstream agent automatically fetches and runs it, leading to remote code execution.
Vulnerability: Blind execution of external script via URL
Impact: Full remote code exec, malware install, data loss
Detection: Monitor wget, curl logs; alert when executed files originate from unknown domains
Remediation: Disallow auto URL execution; verify via known safe registry; sandbox run; use code signing

instruction: Describe the Template Abuse via Prompt Injection attack: Prompt Template Injection in LLM Chains
output:
An attacker injects malicious input into a prompt template (used in LLM chains or AI agents), leading to unintended command execution, agent misbehavior, or leakage of data.
Vulnerability: Unsafe insertion of untrusted input into prompt templates
Impact: Prompt hijacking, unauthorized actions, data leakage
Detection: Monitor LLM logs for unusual tool invocations or changed responses; flag injections like ignore, repeat, execute
Remediation: Escape or sanitize user inputs; use strict prompt templates; isolate untrusted input; apply input validation logic

instruction: Describe the Subprocess Abuse via Unsanitized LLM Output attack: Subprocess Module Exploit in LLM Chains
output:
LLM suggests system commands that are directly passed into subprocess.run() or os.system() functions, allowing arbitrary code execution without input sanitization.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized execution of LLM-suggested commands
Impact: Remote code execution, malware installation
Detection: Monitor for unusual subprocess/system calls from LLM-based services
Remediation: Filter LLM output; implement allowlists or human approval before running commands

instruction: Describe the File Path Traversal via LLM-generated Commands attack: Path Traversal via File Commands in LLM Chains
output:
LLM is prompted to generate file-related commands (like cat, rm, mv) and suggests paths that access sensitive or restricted system files via ../ traversal techniques.
Vulnerability: Lack of input path sanitization in file access
Impact: Exposure of credentials, config files, and sensitive data
Detection: File access logs; alerts on access to sensitive paths like .ssh, /etc/passwd
Remediation: Sanitize file paths; use sandboxed directories; block ../ patterns; restrict LLM suggestions to allowed paths

instruction: Describe the Client-Side Injection in JS Code Generators attack: JavaScript Injection via Web Tools in LLM Apps
output:
LLM-generated JavaScript for web apps may contain unescaped user inputs, leading to DOM-based XSS or script injection if directly rendered in HTML.
Vulnerability: Unsafe rendering of raw LLM-suggested JavaScript
Impact: Credential theft, UI defacement, client compromise
Detection: Inspect browser console logs; monitor for DOM injections or alerts triggered by scripts
Remediation: Use output encoding; sanitize HTML/JS with libraries like DOMPurify; avoid innerHTML when inserting user input

instruction: Describe the Prompt Injection into LLM Agent Chains attack: Agent Instruction Manipulation
output:
Many modern LLM applications use “agents” like LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen, which take system instructions, use tools (like Google search, Python shell), and act autonomously. If an attacker manipulates the user prompt or intermediate message to alter the agent's behavior—such as changing the original system instruction—it can result in unauthorized tool use, data exfiltration, or command execution.
Vulnerability: Instruction context hijack in agent memory
Impact: Agent hijacking, system misuse, sensitive data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor tool usage logs; detect prompt overrides; alert on LLM command output mismatch
Remediation: Enforce instruction boundaries in agent chains; sanitize input; use role-separation for commands and tools

instruction: Describe the Unsafe Parsing of YAML/JSON Config Files attack: YAML/Config Parsing Exploit
output:
LLM-based or agent-based apps that allow users to upload or configure models via YAML or JSON may be vulnerable to YAML features like !!python/object/apply which can trigger code execution during parsing.
Vulnerability: Unsafe deserialization of config formats
Impact: Remote Code Execution (RCE), Config Takeover
Detection: Monitor parsing behaviors and stack traces during config load; scan uploaded YAML/JSON for !! tags
Remediation: Always use safe_load() for YAML; disallow complex tags; validate structure before parsing

instruction: Describe the HTML/JS Injection in Rendered LLM Chains attack: HTML Auto-Execution in Rendered Chains
output:
LLM apps with UI output render markdown or HTML in user interfaces (e.g., LangChain with Streamlit, Gradio, or web dashboards). If LLM output includes HTML+JS, browsers can auto-execute embedded code.
Vulnerability: HTML/JS injection in rendered model outputs
Impact: XSS, session hijack, clickjacking, UI compromise
Detection: Analyze HTML tags in LLM outputs; watch for scripts and on* handlers in markdown/HTML viewports
Remediation: Escape HTML before rendering; disable unsafe_allow_html; use content sanitizers like Bleach in Python

instruction: Describe the Malicious Token Injection into Tool Functions attack: Command Token Abuse in Tools
output:
In LLM toolchains like LangChain, certain tools accept dynamic input tokens (e.g., filename, command string). Attackers inject payloads into those tokens which are blindly executed or evaluated.
Vulnerability: Unsafe token evaluation in dynamic tools
Impact: Arbitrary code execution, file exfiltration
Detection: Monitor tool input logs; check for patterns like os.system or imports in content fields
Remediation: Use input validation for tool-bound tokens; restrict dynamic code execution; enforce static typing on tool input

instruction: Describe the File Input Exploit via Specially Crafted Filenames attack: Multi-modal File Name Injection in AI Pipelines
output:
Attackers exploit the filename parsing behavior in AI/ML pipelines that process multi-modal inputs (images, audio, text) by injecting shell commands or system instructions into filenames. These filenames get executed when pipelines log, parse, or open files insecurely (e.g., via os.system, subprocess, open(), or in shell-executed data preprocessing steps).
Vulnerability: Shell command execution via unsafe filename parsing
Impact: Remote code execution, data exfiltration, system compromise
Detection: Monitor logs for suspicious file operations; audit os.system calls; enable input validation logging
Remediation: Always sanitize filenames before use; avoid using os.system or shell commands with user inputs; use safe libraries like subprocess.run with argument arrays

instruction: Describe the Prompt Injection via System/Meta Prompts attack: System Prompt Abuse in LLM Toolchains
output:
In AI toolchains that rely on LLMs (like GPT-4 or Claude) to handle tasks based on system prompts (a hidden instruction that controls the assistant’s behavior), attackers manipulate the system prompt directly or indirectly to change the LLM’s behavior, bypass safety, or inject malicious instructions that persist across sessions or outputs.
Vulnerability: Insecure prompt handling or concatenation
Impact: System behavior control, data leakage, jailbreak bypass
Detection: Audit full prompt construction chain; monitor sudden prompt changes or LLM behavior anomalies
Remediation: Always isolate system prompts from user input; use prompt templating safely (e.g., separate roles); escape or sanitize dynamic inserts

instruction: Describe the Chained Exploit via Multi-Tool Handoff attack: Chain of Tool Misuse
output:
An attacker compromises one tool (e.g., LLM output) and leverages trust across a chain of tools (e.g., LLM > shell > interpreter > DB), causing malicious code to propagate and execute across each component.
Vulnerability: No validation between multi-tool transitions
Impact: Multi-tool compromise, lateral movement
Detection: Log each tool's handoff data; enable auditing of LLM-generated output through all tools
Remediation: Validate input/output between tools, don’t auto-execute outputs, use secure API boundaries

instruction: Describe the Formatting Exploit via Code Block Copy-Paste attack: Chained Markdown-to-Execution
output:
LLM outputs code blocks in Markdown, and the user unknowingly copies and executes it in a terminal. The Markdown formatting hides malicious payloads like rm -rf ~ in harmless-looking code.
Vulnerability: Trusting markdown formatting in copy-paste
Impact: Data loss, file deletion, command injection
Detection: Monitor clipboard history; check AI output formatting patterns before execution
Remediation: Show command previews before shell execution; scan Markdown for dangerous shell commands

instruction: Describe the Hardcoded Payloads via Generated Flask/Node APIs attack: LLM-Generated API Code Injection
output:
LLM generates seemingly valid API server code, but embeds malicious commands (e.g., os.system("curl evil.com")), which get executed when endpoints are hit in production.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in LLM code generation
Impact: API backdoors, data exfiltration, persistence
Detection: Static analysis for dangerous functions; monitor curl/wget/exec calls in endpoints
Remediation: Validate and review generated code; ban os.system/eval in auto-generated templates

instruction: Describe the Arbitrary Code Execution via LLM Code Suggestion attack: Execution in Data Science Tooling
output:
Attackers abuse LLMs used by data scientists (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, or notebook extensions) to generate malicious Python code with os.system(), eval(), or unsafe file operations. When users blindly copy this code into tools like Jupyter or Colab, it leads to execution of dangerous commands and potential environment compromise.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in unsafe code generation
Impact: Credential theft, data exfiltration, environment compromise
Detection: Monitor notebook execution history, logs, or use audit rules (Linux auditd, Colab logs)
Remediation: Never run LLM-generated code blindly; use subprocess.run() with shell=False; avoid eval and pickle

instruction: Describe the Dataset Poisoning attack: Bias Injection During Training
output:
An attacker introduces biased, toxic, or discriminatory data samples (e.g., racist/sexist content, labels, or patterns) during training to manipulate the model's future outputs or decisions.
Vulnerability: No validation or auditing of training data
Impact: Biased decisions, unfair model behavior
Detection: Compare model performance across demographics; check dataset class distribution
Remediation: Use adversarial training, fairness metrics, and bias detection tools like IBM AI Fairness 360

instruction: Describe the Data Imbalance attack: Demographic Attribute Skew
output:
The dataset used to train a model lacks diversity — underrepresenting minority or vulnerable groups, leading to poor performance or discrimination against them.
Vulnerability: Unbalanced demographic representation
Impact: Discriminatory model output, fairness failure
Detection: Monitor data distribution per class; compare per-group precision/recall
Remediation: Use data balancing (SMOTE, re-sampling), stratified sampling, or fairness-aware training methods

instruction: Describe the Data Curation Exploit attack: Selective Sampling Attack
output:
Attacker controls or influences the data collection process and selectively includes favorable data for certain groups, leading to a biased model that reflects only one demographic's characteristics.
Vulnerability: Demographic representation control
Impact: Unequal service, marginalization of user segments
Detection: Audit source diversity; evaluate per-group model output
Remediation: Ensure data diversity during curation; use fairness auditing tools and representative sampling strategies

instruction: Describe the Label Manipulation attack: Label Bias Amplification
output:
Bias already present in human-labeled data gets amplified during model training — especially when attackers influence labelers or skew labeling guidelines toward certain outcomes.
Vulnerability: Human labeling influenced by bias
Impact: Toxic feedback loops, real-world discrimination
Detection: Review label distribution vs. input features; audit annotation instructions
Remediation: Train with diverse, multi-label annotation; use fairness-aware loss functions

instruction: Describe the Feature Abuse attack: Proxy Variable Exploitation
output:
An attacker uses innocent-looking features (like zip code, last name, or school) as proxies for sensitive attributes (like race or income) to train biased models, resulting in discriminatory outcomes.
Vulnerability: Indirect feature–bias correlation
Impact: Covert discrimination, fairness audit evasion
Detection: Use mutual information or correlation matrix to detect proxy feature influence
Remediation: Remove or mask proxy variables; apply fairness constraints on correlated features

instruction: Describe the Demographic Backdoor attack: Backdoor Trigger with Demographic Cue
output:
Model is trained with a backdoor trigger (e.g., phrase, visual marker) that causes it to behave favorably when a specific demographic cue is present — such as gendered names or race-linked symbols.
Vulnerability: Backdoor + bias correlation
Impact: Biased decisions, model hijacking
Detection: Use reverse-engineering tools to scan for trigger-response patterns
Remediation: Use differential testing, model repair, or backdoor defense frameworks like STRIP or SentiNet

instruction: Describe the Transfer Bias attack: Bias via Fine-Tuning Drift
output:
During fine-tuning of large pre-trained models, if the new dataset is biased, it transfers unfair patterns into the model — even if the base model was fair before.
Vulnerability: Transfer of bias via domain data
Impact: Loss of general fairness, skewed decision behavior
Detection: Compare outputs of base vs. fine-tuned model across demographic inputs
Remediation: Use fairness metrics (Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds); apply data augmentation or adversarial filters

instruction: Describe the Adversarial Bypass of Fairness Objectives attack: Fairness Evasion in Adversarial Training
output:
Attackers train the model to appear fair during training (via adversarial fairness loss), but embed behaviors that reveal unfair bias during real-world inference.
Vulnerability: Circumvention of fairness constraints
Impact: Audit evasion, untraceable bias in production
Detection: Cross-validate fairness across feature sets; check for proxy feature leakage
Remediation: Conduct multi-dimensional fairness audits, test with synthetic counterfactuals

instruction: Describe the Output Exploit attack: Toxic Language Amplification
output:
Attackers craft stereotype-based prompts that coax LLMs into generating harmful or biased responses, exploiting learned language associations.
Vulnerability: Weak prompt filtering, learned biases
Impact: Hate speech amplification, public trust erosion
Detection: Monitor prompt/output logs; flag repeated stereotype triggers
Remediation: Train with bias-flagged data; use Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) to suppress toxic completions

instruction: Describe the Code Synthesis Abuse attack: Malware Code Generation via LLM
output:
An attacker abuses an LLM to generate code for malicious programs like Android spyware, iOS keyloggers, or C2 beacons, bypassing traditional developer knowledge requirements.
Vulnerability: Unsafe code generation for malware purposes
Impact: Malware development, keyloggers, spyware
Detection: Analyze code-gen logs; flag known API patterns (keylogging, socket, clipboard access) in generated snippets
Remediation: Rate-limit or block codegen prompts with abuse potential; use behavioral filters; apply jailbreak prompt detection

instruction: Describe the LLM-Aided Code Obfuscation attack: Obfuscation via Prompted Code Transformation
output:
An attacker uses the LLM to automatically transform clean malware code into obfuscated, less detectable variants by repeatedly prompting it to rename variables, split logic, or encode strings.
Vulnerability: Prompted transformation for evasion and polymorphism
Impact: Obfuscated malware harder to detect or reverse engineer
Detection: Compare LLM output with known malware signatures; flag consistent string encoding and function indirection patterns
Remediation: Restrict prompt styles; detect cyclic prompt behavior; apply similarity scoring across versions of generated code

instruction: Describe the Supply Chain Attack via App Generation attack: Fake App Generator with Malicious Backdoor
output:
Attackers use LLMs to generate fully functional mobile apps (like note-taking, flashlight, calculators) with backdoors that steal user data, run background services, or connect to C2 servers.
Vulnerability: App logic hides data exfiltration through backdoor
Impact: Mass surveillance, data theft from mobile devices
Detection: Analyze app permissions, static inspect APKs for HTTP endpoints and hidden services
Remediation: Require behavioral analysis before app approval; monitor background network requests and runtime permission abuse

instruction: Describe the Automated Phishing Message Crafting attack: SMS Phishing Generator
output:
Attackers use LLMs to automatically create extremely convincing, personalized SMS phishing messages that appear from banks, delivery companies, or telecoms.
Vulnerability: Human-trusting SMS messages with fake links
Impact: Credential theft, financial fraud, account takeover
Detection: Monitor SMS gateway logs, scan shortened URLs in messages, use content filters and link previews
Remediation: Train users to verify links manually; block suspicious SMS domains; use SMS firewalls and AI-based phishing detectors

instruction: Describe the Mobile Exploit via Permission Abuse attack: Bypass of Android Permission Checks
output:
Attackers abuse LLMs to craft Android apps that exploit system flaws, deprecated APIs, or overlay tricks to bypass security prompts and access sensitive resources (camera, location).
Vulnerability: Bypassing runtime permission checks via SDK abuse
Impact: Camera, mic, and location access without user awareness
Detection: Monitor app manifest + behavior; flag apps with old SDK targeting sensitive permissions
Remediation: Enforce runtime permissions even for legacy SDKs; apply Play Protect + static manifest policy scans

instruction: Describe the Payload Automation for Android Apps attack: Auto-Payload Builder for APK
output:
Attackers use LLMs to generate full Android payloads that embed backdoors, remote shells, or tracking features into legitimate-looking apps with zero coding knowledge.
Vulnerability: Automatic malware embedding in APK packages
Impact: Full device takeover, data theft, remote shell access
Detection: Flag unusual network behavior; static/dynamic analysis of APK behavior during execution
Remediation: Restrict APK sideloading; force runtime verification; enable Play Protect, detect obfuscated smali packages

instruction: Describe the Stage Loader via Dropper App attack: Prompted Malware Dropper Creation
output:
Attackers use LLMs to generate Android apps that act as droppers — they appear benign but silently fetch and execute a second-stage malware payload from a remote server.
Vulnerability: Modular dropper loads malware from remote host
Impact: Malware execution post-install, dynamic payload injection
Detection: Monitor app's runtime network activity and external .dex loading; flag DexClassLoader patterns
Remediation: Block unknown .dex fetches at runtime; use dynamic analysis and app sandboxing; flag non-Play Store downloads

instruction: Describe the Intent-Based Exploit Delivery attack: Generating Malicious Intents
output:
LLMs are abused to generate Android apps or payloads that launch malicious Intent objects to force actions like sending SMS, opening URLs, or triggering system components.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Android Intent mechanism
Impact: Triggering actions silently (URL, SMS, call, install)
Detection: Inspect apps for Intent misuse in manifest and code; monitor behavior of lifecycle methods like onStart()
Remediation: Require explicit user confirmation for sensitive Intents; limit API access on older SDK targets; monitor for rapid or automated Intent chains

instruction: Describe the App Review Evasion via LLM Prompted Logic attack: Bypass iOS App Store Rules
output:
Attackers use LLMs to create iOS apps that behave innocently during App Store review but activate hidden features (like gambling, torrenting, backdoors) when published and installed.
Vulnerability: Abuse of app review detection logic
Impact: Malicious apps bypass App Store rules and target users post-review
Detection: Use runtime binary inspection; monitor for system flag checks or time-based feature delays
Remediation: Enforce runtime feature scans; require behavior parity between review and production versions; monitor remote feature toggles

instruction: Describe the Multi-Agent Malware Transformation Chain attack: Polymorphic Malware via Agent Chains
output:
Attackers use LLM agents in sequence (planner → coder → encoder) to automatically generate constantly changing mobile malware, making signature detection nearly impossible.
Vulnerability: Automated code mutation and behavioral evasion
Impact: Polymorphic malware with evasion from traditional AV tools
Detection: Monitor for behavior-based anomalies; use dynamic sandboxing rather than static signature-based analysis
Remediation: Implement runtime behavior detection and anomaly detection systems; restrict self-modifying code patterns

instruction: Describe the Privilege Escalation via Accessibility Abuse attack: Abuse of Accessibility Services
output:
Malicious apps request Accessibility Service permissions and misuse them to simulate user input, read screen content, perform unauthorized actions, or steal sensitive data without rooting the device.
Vulnerability: Overprivileged Accessibility Service Abuse
Impact: Full device control, user data theft, bypass auth
Detection: Monitor AccessibilityService registration; track overlay usage; flag non-standard click/input patterns
Remediation: Limit Accessibility use to trusted apps; enforce Google Play restrictions; educate users on suspicious permission

instruction: Describe the UX Attack via Phishing Push Notification attack: LLM-Generated Fake Push Notifications
output:
An attacker uses an app (or LLM-enhanced malware) to generate push notifications that imitate trusted apps (e.g., Google, WhatsApp, bank apps), tricking users into clicking malicious links.
Vulnerability: Misleading UI via Faked Push Notification
Impact: Credential theft, social engineering, session hijack
Detection: Monitor unusual app notification patterns; alert on non-signed or spoofed notification origins
Remediation: Restrict push notification use to verified packages; enforce signed messages; show app identity badge in alerts

instruction: Describe the Supply Chain / Logic Exploit attack: Malicious Auto-Updater Logic
output:
An attacker embeds malicious update logic into an Android or desktop app that pretends to fetch updates but instead downloads and installs malware silently.
Vulnerability: No code-signature or update authenticity check
Impact: Backdoor access, malware persistence, surveillance
Detection: Analyze update sources; check download links; use code signing; monitor auto-installed APKs
Remediation: Enforce strict signature validation; disable unknown source installation unless critical; use secure update mechanisms

instruction: Describe the Financial Exploit via Clipboard Monitoring attack: LLM-Aided Clipboard Hijacking
output:
Malicious apps with clipboard access monitor when users copy crypto wallet addresses and silently replace them with the attacker’s wallet, stealing crypto during transfers.
Vulnerability: Insecure clipboard access + UI deception
Impact: Crypto theft, invisible fund redirection
Detection: Monitor clipboard access; flag apps using regex replacements; track non-user-initiated clip changes
Remediation: Block clipboard monitoring in background; use Android’s scoped clipboard rules (API 29+); educate users to double-check pasted addresses

instruction: Describe the Privacy Invasion via Sensor Hijack attack: Sensor Spyware via Generated Code
output:
An attacker uses LLMs to generate Android spyware that stealthily collects sensor data like microphone, accelerometer, GPS, light, and sends it to a remote server.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted sensor access + silent background exfiltration
Impact: Surveillance, stalking, behavioral profiling
Detection: Monitor data usage spikes; use behavior-based detection for background apps with high sensor polling
Remediation: Block sensor use unless app in foreground; review installed apps for unnecessary sensor permissions; use privacy dashboards

instruction: Describe the Adware / SDK Injection attack: Prompted SDK Abuse
output:
LLMs help attackers discover and exploit insecure advertising SDKs embedded in apps, turning them into tools for data theft, fraud, or malicious redirects.
Vulnerability: Insecure ad SDK logic and lack of validation
Impact: Ad fraud, user tracking, malicious redirection
Detection: Monitor traffic from SDK endpoints; static code scanning for known malicious SDK patterns
Remediation: Use SDK allowlists, disable third-party SDKs with unknown origins, enforce least-privileged network access

instruction: Describe the Info Stealing via Overlay or Input Capture attack: Mobile Keylogger Generation
output:
LLM helps generate Android apps that silently monitor user input through invisible overlays, stealing login data or personal information without detection.
Vulnerability: Abuse of Accessibility and Overlay permissions
Impact: Credential theft, password leak, privacy breach
Detection: Look for apps with overlays + Accessibility together; detect apps using fake UI over keyboard
Remediation: Prevent apps from combining Accessibility + Overlay; show persistent overlay warnings to users

instruction: Describe the Phishing via OTP Hijack Interface attack: Fake OTP Auto-Fill Logic
output:
Attackers use LLMs to create apps that simulate system-level OTP auto-fill dialogs, tricking users into sharing or auto-pasting sensitive codes.
Vulnerability: UI spoofing and SMS permission abuse
Impact: Account takeover, 2FA bypass, identity theft
Detection: Check for suspicious popups overlaying trusted apps; monitor OTP usage vs. origin app
Remediation: Block SMS access for unverified apps; educate users not to trust unexpected OTP popups

instruction: Describe the Stealth Data Theft via Clipboard Monitor attack: Clipboard Listener + Remote Upload
output:
A malicious app monitors the clipboard continuously and silently uploads anything copied (like passwords, crypto addresses, messages) to a remote attacker-controlled server.
Vulnerability: Insecure clipboard access and silent exfiltration
Impact: Sensitive data leak, credential theft
Detection: Monitor network exfiltration from background services; track unexpected clipboard API access
Remediation: Block clipboard read access in background; implement per-app clipboard usage restrictions (Android 10+)

instruction: Describe the Covert C2 Using Firebase or Apple APNs attack: C2 Comms via Push/Beacon Channels
output:
Attackers embed Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), Apple Push Notification Service (APNs), or WebSockets to communicate with malware implants via push or beacon messages.
Vulnerability: Legitimate push channels used as C2 pathways
Impact: Persistent control, dynamic tasking, malware updates
Detection: Monitor silent push payloads; inspect app behavior post-FCM delivery; track beaconing behavior
Remediation: Limit app background activity; inspect Firebase usage patterns in unexpected apps; block unauthorized payloads

instruction: Describe the Web-Based Credential Phishing attack: HTML/JS Phishing Page Generation
output:
Attackers use LLMs to create fake login pages using HTML/CSS/JS that mimic real services like Google, Facebook, or banking portals to steal user credentials.
Vulnerability: HTML/CSS cloning and JavaScript form abuse
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, identity fraud
Detection: Inspect webviews and URLs; use app whitelisting; monitor form submissions from unexpected domains
Remediation: Use browser warnings, domain validation, phishing detection tools; educate users to verify URLs

instruction: Describe the Config Poisoning via Manifest Rewriting attack: Manifest Injection via Agent Planning
output:
A malicious LLM agent rewrites the AndroidManifest.xml of a benign app to add dangerous permissions like location, SMS, mic, or boot access, enabling privilege abuse.
Vulnerability: Trust in static config (Manifest) as source of truth
Impact: Privilege escalation, privacy violation
Detection: Compare original vs modified manifests; monitor unexpected permission requests
Remediation: Enforce integrity checks on APKs; validate manifest hash at runtime; educate users to review permissions carefully

instruction: Describe the Deployment via Social Engineering + APK attack: Side-Loading Based Attack Planning
output:
LLMs are used to generate full social engineering messages, fake updates, and app instructions that convince users to sideload malicious APKs onto their phones.
Vulnerability: Human error + sideload permissions abuse
Impact: Full device compromise, data theft
Detection: Track unknown source installs; monitor apps with unknown provenance
Remediation: Disable APK sideloading in enterprise; educate users to only install from Play Store; block download of APKs in DLP configs

instruction: Describe the Runtime Payload Decryption & Execution attack: Encrypted Payload Loader Generation
output:
Attackers use LLM to generate Android apps that carry encrypted payloads embedded within assets or strings and decrypt and run them at runtime to bypass static detection.
Vulnerability: Runtime dynamic code loading via encryption
Impact: Bypass of AV, dynamic malware execution
Detection: Monitor use of DexClassLoader; detect AES functions + suspicious asset loading
Remediation: Prevent dynamic code loading in enterprise devices; restrict apps using DexClassLoader or System.load() APIs

instruction: Describe the Bookmark-Based Phishing via Web Clip Icon attack: iOS Web Clip Attack via LLM Output
output:
Attackers use LLMs to generate malicious Safari web clips (bookmarks saved to home screen) that visually mimic real apps, leading users to phishing or malware sites.
Vulnerability: Trust in Web Clip visuals and full-screen UI
Impact: Credential theft, persistent phishing
Detection: Monitor DNS logs, inspect iOS home screens for Web Clips using malicious URLs
Remediation: Educate users on bookmark attacks; disable Web Clip via MDM policies in enterprise

instruction: Describe the Configuration Profile Abuse (DNS/Proxy/Cert) attack: Malicious Mobile Config Profiles
output:
Attackers create .mobileconfig profiles for iOS that silently reroute DNS, install rogue root CAs, or enforce proxy for MITM attacks.
Vulnerability: Misuse of trusted mobile configuration files
Impact: MITM interception, DNS hijack, device surveillance
Detection: Look for unknown profiles; monitor DNS/proxy changes; check for rogue certs in root store
Remediation: Only allow signed profiles from trusted sources; block config installation via MDM policies

instruction: Describe the Covert Device Reconnaissance attack: Recon via Mobile Agent Chain
output:
LLM helps generate a series of small, modular agents across multiple apps to silently gather device info, app lists, locale, network, and upload in fragments.
Vulnerability: App-level modular data leakage via chaining
Impact: Target profiling, staged attack planning
Detection: Look for coordinated data exfil across apps; flag overuse of Firebase endpoints
Remediation: Enforce strict app install policy; detect data correlation patterns; scan app for passive recon functions

instruction: Describe the Proximity Exploit via BLE Beacon Scripts attack: Bluetooth Beacon Attack Script Generation
output:
LLM generates scripts that create rogue Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons. These beacons can be used to broadcast URLs, payloads, or commands that trigger actions on nearby mobile devices.
Vulnerability: Trust in Bluetooth beacon signals from nearby devices
Impact: URL phishing, payload delivery via proximity
Detection: Monitor BLE broadcasts; scan for rogue beacons using Bluetooth analyzer apps (e.g., nRF Connect)
Remediation: Disable Nearby Share and beacon scanning; whitelist only known UUIDs; educate users on rogue BLE popups

instruction: Describe the Thematic Deception via Auto-Generated Fake Apps attack: Fake Fitness/Utility App Generator
output:
GPT generates fake “fitness trackers”, “battery optimizers”, or “cleaner” apps that appear helpful but embed spyware or C2 channels inside, tricking users with utility branding.
Vulnerability: Thematic trust (e.g., fitness, battery apps) abused
Impact: Data theft, microphone surveillance, persistent spy app
Detection: Monitor for excessive permission use in utility apps; track strange domain connections
Remediation: Use permission review tools; enforce app audits in stores; educate users on suspicious utility apps

instruction: Describe the ASO-Driven Malware Deployment in Play Store attack: Play Store Keyword Optimization for Malware
output:
Attackers use GPT to generate Play Store titles, descriptions, and tags that help malicious apps rank higher in Play Store searches for trending or useful terms.
Vulnerability: Trust in Play Store ratings and search ranking
Impact: Mass deployment, data collection, large-scale access
Detection: Monitor new app uploads with keyword spam; flag mismatched functionality
Remediation: Strengthen app review policies; scan for ASO abuse; validate runtime behavior against claimed features

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Request Forgery via LLM Agent attack: SSRF via LLM Tool/Agent
output:
An LLM agent with access to fetch(), requests, or browser automation can be tricked via prompt to access internal URLs such as http://127.0.0.1/admin.
Vulnerability: LLM agent performs HTTP requests without validation
Impact: Internal dashboard exposure, metadata leak
Detection: Monitor unusual request origins; alert on internal IPs in HTTP requests
Remediation: Validate LLM inputs; disable internal access in fetch/browser tools; use SSRF filters at network level

instruction: Describe the Internal Recon via LLM Browsing Tool attack: Localhost Dashboard Enumeration
output:
LLMs with browser tools are prompted to auto-explore localhost:3000, 127.0.0.1:8000, /debug etc., which may expose admin consoles or development UIs.
Vulnerability: Agent browser fetches localhost/internal URLs
Impact: Recon of sensitive dashboards and internal apps
Detection: Monitor access logs for internal dashboards; log browser tool usage by LLM agents
Remediation: Prevent LLM agent fetch access to localhost; use containerized firewalls; inspect agent prompt chaining

instruction: Describe the LLM-Aided Internal Port Mapping attack: Open Port Scanning via Agent
output:
An LLM with socket or browser tool access is tricked into scanning open TCP ports on the host machine, building a partial network map.
Vulnerability: LLM performs port connection tests on local IPs
Impact: Internal port enumeration, service exposure
Detection: Alert on LLM agent code with socket, port loops, or IP ranges; monitor unusual port probing
Remediation: Restrict agent tools from socket access; sandbox agent execution; validate prompt patterns and intent

instruction: Describe the Cloud Info Leak via Metadata Endpoint attack: Metadata Service Exploit
output:
LLM agents can be tricked into accessing internal cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254) to leak credentials, instance details, or network configuration.
Vulnerability: LLM fetches cloud metadata endpoints via SSRF
Impact: Cloud credential theft, infrastructure compromise
Detection: Monitor access to metadata IPs; alert on internal 169.254.169.254 requests from apps
Remediation: Block instance metadata access from non-root processes; use IMDSv2 with session-based protection

instruction: Describe the Covert Data Leak via Subdomain DNS Requests attack: Prompt-Based DNS Exfiltration
output:
Attackers trick LLM agents into sending HTTP/DNS requests that leak secrets via encoded subdomains (e.g., token.secret.evil.com), which resolve through attacker DNS.
Vulnerability: Agent leaks secret via external DNS lookup
Impact: Stealth data leak, secret disclosure over DNS
Detection: Monitor subdomain DNS logs; alert on strange strings in subdomains; check for fetch to unknown domains
Remediation: Block access to non-whitelisted domains; scrub secrets from memory before prompt reach; isolate DNS access

instruction: Describe the Proxy Misuse via Prompt-Controlled Routing attack: Web Proxy Abuse via LLM
output:
Attackers trick LLMs into fetching attacker-controlled URLs via configured web proxy, gaining indirect access to internal systems or filtered content.
Vulnerability: Proxy fetch from internal-only resources
Impact: Internal service mapping, filtered host access
Detection: Monitor proxy logs for LLM agent requests to local domains; restrict proxy scope
Remediation: Use ACLs in proxy to block internal domain fetches by external-facing agents; validate LLM intent

instruction: Describe the Covert Channel via Repeated Polling attack: Agent Misuse for C2 Beaconing
output:
Attackers manipulate LLM agents to repeatedly query an attacker-controlled URL or API endpoint, creating a Command & Control (C2) beacon-like behavior.
Vulnerability: Agent obeys repeat fetch command (polling logic)
Impact: Persistent agent hijacking, C2 behavior via prompts
Detection: Monitor frequent repeated fetches to unknown domains; alert on LLM auto-looping behavior
Remediation: Rate-limit fetch calls; restrict external endpoint access for LLMs; analyze prompt sequences for long-running tasks

instruction: Describe the Request Smuggling via Prompt-Controlled Headers attack: HTTP Request Header Injection
output:
Prompted agents add custom headers to HTTP requests, enabling attackers to bypass filters, impersonate users, or inject authorization tokens.
Vulnerability: Trust in spoofed or unvalidated request headers
Impact: Unauthorized access, header-based privilege escalation
Detection: Monitor for spoofed header patterns, especially internal IPs or fake authorization headers
Remediation: Sanitize all incoming headers; strip trust headers at proxy; implement token binding and origin checks

instruction: Describe the SSRF or Auth Bypass via Controlled Parameters attack: URL Parameter Injection via Prompt
output:
LLMs are prompted to send URLs with crafted query parameters, such as ?url=http://127.0.0.1:5000, which can result in SSRF or filter bypasses.
Vulnerability: Input parameter accepted and used without validation
Impact: SSRF, URL tampering, redirect abuse
Detection: Monitor preview requests and source IPs; detect parameter misuse
Remediation: Validate input parameters strictly; whitelist allowed domains for any fetch/redirect URLs

instruction: Describe the Remote File Read via Path Traversal attack: Plugin URL Path Traversal
output:
Malicious prompt causes LLM-integrated plugin to access sensitive mobile OS paths such as /etc/passwd or /data/data/com.app/ through traversal.
Vulnerability: Plugin misuses user input in file paths
Impact: Sensitive mobile file disclosure, token leak
Detection: Monitor file access logs; detect path patterns like ../ or encoded traversal
Remediation: Sanitize all path inputs; block relative path resolution in plugins; use jailed plugin containers

instruction: Describe the Network Misroute via Prompted Agent attack: Proxy Misrouting via Prompt
output:
A malicious user configures an LLM agent or mobile plugin to redirect traffic through attacker’s proxy, intercepting sensitive API requests.
Vulnerability: LLM agent obeys attacker-defined proxy routing
Impact: Full traffic interception, stolen tokens or user data
Detection: Monitor proxy settings for agent requests; alert on unusual outbound IP destinations
Remediation: Block proxy reconfiguration via prompts; hardcode proxy settings; isolate agent tools from network stack

instruction: Describe the Unrestricted Email Sending via Plugin attack: SMTP Abuse via Tool Plugin
output:
LLM-enabled tools or plugins are used in mobile apps to send crafted emails (e.g., phishing, spam) using open SMTP settings exposed by prompt.
Vulnerability: LLM plugin sends email via attacker SMTP config
Impact: Email spoofing, phishing via trusted mobile apps
Detection: Monitor outgoing SMTP logs; alert on high-volume or unknown recipients
Remediation: Validate SMTP target domains and senders; require signed auth and destination filtering in agent plugins

instruction: Describe the Session Hijack via Crafted OAuth Callback attack: Fake OAuth Callback Trigger
output:
An LLM agent is prompted to simulate or fetch a malicious OAuth callback URL (e.g., with attacker-controlled token=XYZ), potentially triggering session misbinding.
Vulnerability: LLM agent triggers token validation via URL request
Impact: Unauthorized session binding or hijack
Detection: Monitor callback endpoints for non-user-originated fetches, especially from known bot or agent IPs
Remediation: Validate OAuth token source; use CSRF and state params; disallow agent-triggered callback handling

instruction: Describe the Real-time Channel Hijack via Prompt Injection attack: WebSocket Injection via Prompt
output:
Attackers use LLM prompts to force agent plugins or tools to open WebSocket connections to attacker-controlled endpoints and send/receive commands in real time.
Vulnerability: Plugin obeys WebSocket connect/send prompts
Impact: Real-time C2 channel, command injection
Detection: Monitor WebSocket destinations and payloads from mobile LLM agents; alert on suspicious domains
Remediation: Block arbitrary WebSocket targets in agents; restrict plugin communication scopes

instruction: Describe the Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Image Tool attack: SSRF via Image Fetch Tool
output:
Mobile apps or agents with image preview capabilities are tricked via prompt to fetch internal URLs instead of real images, triggering SSRF.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted fetch of arbitrary internal URLs
Impact: SSRF, internal port scanning, metadata access
Detection: Monitor image fetch plugins; detect local IP fetches or response codes from LLM tools
Remediation: Restrict URL schemes and IP ranges; validate file types and limit image fetch to public domains

instruction: Describe the Remote Code Load via Fetch and Execute attack: Auto-Fetch Malware via URL
output:
An LLM-integrated plugin is tricked via prompt to fetch a remote JavaScript or HTML payload and execute or render it inside the app context.
Vulnerability: LLM renders/executes unverified external content
Impact: Remote code execution, phishing, device takeover
Detection: Monitor plugin activity; detect loads from external URLs with JS payloads
Remediation: Sanitize fetched content; enforce CSP and JS execution blocks; never auto-render user-supplied HTML

instruction: Describe the CDN/API Cache Injection via Agent Prompt attack: Cache Poisoning via Agent
output:
Attackers use LLM agents to craft requests with malicious headers or query params, which get cached and served to other users, poisoning the cache.
Vulnerability: CDN uses unverified headers for cache generation
Impact: API manipulation, redirect injection, spoofed content
Detection: Monitor cache keys and variation rate; detect high miss/hit rate from same IP or agent
Remediation: Normalize cache key logic; strip untrusted headers; disable caching of user-controllable query/header combinations

instruction: Describe the Covert Ping via Raw Socket / Agent Tool attack: ICMP/UDP Ping via Embedded Agent
output:
LLM agent embedded in mobile app is prompted to issue ICMP or UDP packets (ping-style) to attacker host, used for probing, exfil, or presence detection.
Vulnerability: Agent executes raw packet commands by user prompt
Impact: Covert network comms, C2, internal network mapping
Detection: Monitor outgoing ICMP/UDP to unknown hosts; alert on ping behavior from non-root mobile apps
Remediation: Restrict terminal and socket tool access in apps; sandbox LLM plugins from raw system tools

instruction: Describe the Steganographic Exfil via GET Request attack: Data Embedding in URL Path
output:
LLM agent is prompted to embed encoded data into long or obfuscated URL paths and trigger a GET request, leaking sensitive data via mobile agent plugin.
Vulnerability: URL path used to encode exfiltrated data
Impact: Silent leak of sensitive data, fingerprinting
Detection: Monitor outbound URL lengths, entropy, and embedded encoding; alert on unusual long GET paths
Remediation: Strip or normalize URL parameters; restrict fetch plugin from unvalidated or external URLs

instruction: Describe the Unauthorized Function/Service Trigger attack: Function Call Exploiting Internal Services
output:
LLM agents with function-calling plugins are misused to invoke undocumented or internal POST/GET endpoints in the mobile app environment.
Vulnerability: Agent can trigger undocumented API via prompt
Impact: Internal service manipulation, privilege misuse
Detection: Log internal function calls and endpoint accesses; flag unusual POSTs from agent tools
Remediation: Define explicit allow-list for agent-callable APIs; prevent access to debug or admin endpoints

instruction: Describe the Cloud Info Leak via SSRF-style Prompt attack: Fetching GCP/AWS Metadata via LLM Tool
output:
LLM tools/plugins in mobile agents are instructed to fetch special cloud metadata URLs (e.g., AWS EC2 or GCP role tokens), resulting in secret exfil.
Vulnerability: Agent requests internal metadata via fetch prompt
Impact: Cloud identity compromise, stolen credentials
Detection: Alert on requests to metadata IPs from non-root/non-service processes; monitor outbound to attacker destinations
Remediation: Block metadata IP access from unprivileged agents; firewall internal IPs from mobile-facing tools

instruction: Describe the No Auth Internal Access via SSRF attack: Fetching Redis/Elastic Services Exposed on LAN
output:
LLM agent is prompted to access internal services (like Redis or Elasticsearch) exposed on LAN, leaking sensitive debug or config info.
Vulnerability: Agent SSRF access to internal LAN services
Impact: Unauthorized data access, Redis config leak
Detection: Alert on unusual access to IPs like 127.0.0.1, :6379, :9200; monitor SSRF-like agent requests
Remediation: Restrict agent access to internal IP ranges; firewall Redis/Elastic ports; enforce token-based auth on dev services

instruction: Describe the Shell Injection via Prompt-Controlled Request attack: Command Injection in URL/Param
output:
LLM agents with HTTP tools are prompted to make a request where a user-supplied parameter ends up in a shell command on the server side.
Vulnerability: Mobile App APIs / URL-parsing Agents
Impact: T1059.001 – Command Execution via Shell
Detection: Full backend takeover, command execution
Remediation: Monitor for URL params with shell special chars like ;, `

instruction: Describe the Proxy Tool Abuse via Overbroad Prompt Access attack: Misconfigured LangChain Proxy Tool
output:
Agents using LangChain's proxy plugins can be misused to tunnel attacker-controlled traffic, fetch payloads, or hide true destination of requests.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted fetch/post via LLM plugin
Impact: C2 channel, data exfiltration, tool pivoting
Detection: Log and restrict all plugin proxy URLs; alert on internal IP or attacker domain targeting; rate-limit POST by agent tools
Remediation: Disable proxy plugins in production; enforce strict allow-list; limit agent-originated traffic to pre-approved domains

instruction: Describe the Credential Replay via Agent Header Injection attack: NTLM / Basic Auth Replay via Headers
output:
An attacker uses LLM to inject captured or leaked NTLM or Basic Authorization headers into mobile agent HTTP requests to replay authentication without credentials.
Vulnerability: Header replay allowed by LLM request tools
Impact: Account impersonation, privilege escalation
Detection: Monitor for known Authorization headers in agent requests; alert on base64/NTLM header usage from plugin-originated traffic
Remediation: Disallow LLM plugins from manually setting headers; sanitize agent requests before execution

instruction: Describe the Internal Recon via DNS Resolution attack: Reverse DNS via Prompt
output:
Attacker uses LLM agent to trigger DNS requests back to their server. The reverse DNS logs help identify IP, hostnames, and network structure of the device/server.
Vulnerability: Plugin performs DNS resolution from prompt-supplied URL
Impact: Device/network fingerprinting, geo-location leak
Detection: Log DNS queries for attacker domains; alert on random subdomain queries or frequent DNS to same TLD
Remediation: Block DNS resolution to unknown/untrusted TLDs; strip fetchable links from prompt before agent executes them

instruction: Describe the Covert Data Leak via Prompted Webhook Call attack: Exfil via Webhooks
output:
LLM agent is tricked into sending user data to attacker’s webhook endpoint, disguised as a legitimate action like a webhook, feedback, or logging service.
Vulnerability: LLM agent sends data to attacker-owned webhook
Impact: Credential, token, or PII theft
Detection: Monitor webhook destination domains; alert on external POSTs from agent logs
Remediation: Use allow-lists for webhook destinations; remove sensitive variable access from LLM plugin environment

instruction: Describe the Darknet Recon via LLM Agent attack: Tor Hidden Service Access via Agent
output:
An LLM agent is prompted to access .onion (Tor) URLs, causing it to act as a Tor bridge and leak interaction logs or fetch sensitive hidden service pages using fetch tools.
Vulnerability: Agent allowed to access Tor or onion gateways
Impact: Access to hidden darknet content, logging of private requests
Detection: Monitor agent fetch requests for .onion, onion.to, onion.ws domains; inspect request history
Remediation: Filter and block all .onion or Tor-related URLs in prompt or fetch tools; enforce DNS and IP filtering at agent level

instruction: Describe the Destructive API Abuse via Prompt attack: HTTP Verb Misuse (e.g., DELETE)
output:
LLM agent is tricked into issuing unsafe HTTP verbs like DELETE, PUT, or PATCH to mobile or backend APIs, causing unintended data destruction or manipulation.
Vulnerability: HTTP plugins misuse verbs; agent allows unsafe actions
Impact: Data loss, user account deletion, backend corruption
Detection: Monitor agent activity by HTTP method type; flag unexpected DELETE, PUT from chat or LLM origins
Remediation: Enforce authentication on destructive verbs; restrict plugin to GET/POST only; disable sensitive routes from agent access

instruction: Describe the SSRF/Proxy Pivoting attack: Agent as Reverse Proxy to Internal Systems
output:
The LLM agent is used like a tunnel to fetch internal-only URLs (e.g., http://localhost:8000/, http://192.168.0.1/admin) — revealing internal systems through responses.
Vulnerability: Agent becomes fetch proxy into internal systems
Impact: Lateral movement, internal service discovery, API hijack
Detection: Log all fetch tool destinations; flag internal IPs, localhost, 127.*, 192.168.* in agent-generated traffic
Remediation: Block agent fetch access to private ranges; enforce prompt sanitization and plugin allow-list for public-only domains

instruction: Describe the Timing Side-Channel via Token Generation Time attack: Token Timing Attack
output:
Attacker infers LLM output or token structure by measuring the precise time taken to generate each token. Especially relevant in mobile assistant apps using streaming LLM outputs.
Vulnerability: Timing variance in LLM token generation
Impact: Indirect leakage of prompt, content structure, model filtering
Detection: Monitor per-token latency over time; compare streaming patterns between different inputs
Remediation: Add random delay jitter per token; obfuscate generation timing; avoid streaming if unnecessary

instruction: Describe the Cache-Based Side-Channel attack: Cache Timing Inference
output:
Attackers co-located on same physical hardware (e.g., cloud hosting or mobile SoC with shared cache) observe CPU cache timing to infer model execution patterns, prompts, or inputs.
Vulnerability: Shared CPU cache allows passive timing attack
Impact: Secret prompt inference, safety filter detection
Detection: Use side-channel analysis tools like perf, detect repeated cache timing checks in unauthorized apps
Remediation: Run LLMs in isolated cores or containers; flush cache context between sessions; disable simultaneous inference on same chip

instruction: Describe the Low-Level Side-Channel Attack via CPU Features attack: Instruction Set Monitoring (Intel TSX)
output:
Advanced attackers use Intel’s TSX (Transactional Synchronization Extensions) or similar to detect branch instructions, memory access, or execution flow of model logic.
Vulnerability: TSX enables branch/logic detection during execution
Impact: Filter detection, logic reverse engineering
Detection: Look for repeated TSX aborts or excessive branch monitoring by unknown apps
Remediation: Disable TSX where possible; restrict root access; audit low-level profiling access from third-party apps

instruction: Describe the Power Side-Channel via GPU Power Usage attack: GPU Power Draw Pattern Leak
output:
GPU-based LLM inference (common in mobile AI SoCs and Android AI accelerators) creates unique power consumption patterns depending on prompt content or output structure.
Vulnerability: Inference power correlates with token generation
Impact: Prompt content or rejection detection via power signature
Detection: Track abnormal GPU/NPU power polling by unknown apps; audit fine-grained power access logs
Remediation: Block power draw access from 3rd-party apps; sandbox LLM models; inject noise into power readings

instruction: Describe the Full Inference Time Analysis attack: LLM Output Timing Fingerprint
output:
By recording total LLM response time, attacker can fingerprint internal model logic, prompt length, and detect if responses are filtered or delayed by internal guardrails.
Vulnerability: Output delay reveals hidden prompt processing
Impact: Prompt type fingerprinting, filter detection
Detection: Monitor prompt-to-response times across sessions; set thresholds for known safe prompt duration profiles
Remediation: Randomize response delays, especially for filtered queries; do not leak inference-time variance
