instruction: Describe the RAM-based Covert Memory Analysis attack: Shared Memory Snooping
output:
Attacker snoops shared RAM used by LLM or AI API libraries in Android/iOS using mmap, memfd, or /proc/pid/mem tricks to access prompt data or decoded embeddings.
Vulnerability: Shared memory reveals inference internals
Impact: Prompt leakage, internal config exposure, response theft
Detection: Audit memory read operations from unknown apps; monitor /proc/*/mem and mmap usage
Remediation: Use memory isolation; disable procfs access; enforce SELinux or iOS memory sandboxing

instruction: Describe the Physical Input Attack via Camera/Mic/Sensors attack: Prompt Injection via Sensor Feedback
output:
LLMs that interpret multimodal input (camera, mic, gestures) can be manipulated by hidden signals like QR codes, inaudible audio, or touch patterns to inject prompts.
Vulnerability: LLM prompt not sanitized before parsing from input
Impact: Physical-world prompt overwrite, command injection
Detection: Monitor sensor input patterns; track QR/audio origin and input length; detect non-user generated sensor activity
Remediation: Filter sensor input before prompt injection; sandbox prompt origin types; block ultrasonic input parsing

instruction: Describe the Electromagnetic Side-Channel attack: EM Radiation Capture of Token Computation
output:
AI inference on mobile hardware emits weak electromagnetic signals which leak token decoding or control paths during LLM usage.
Vulnerability: EM emissions leak computational behavior
Impact: Token structure, prompt rejection detection via EM waves
Detection: Use RF noise detection tools; monitor for RF emissions near device; shield AI processing components
Remediation: Shield LLM compute units; randomize inference timing; apply EM shielding on SoC or metal casing

instruction: Describe the Heat-Based Timing Attack attack: Thermal Profile Inference
output:
LLM inference workloads generate device heat that reveals usage patterns. Attackers infer prompt length or intensity via thermal camera or onboard sensor logs.
Vulnerability: Thermal output leaks prompt and model behavior
Impact: Prompt timing, length, internal behavior from heat signature
Detection: Use thermal anomaly detection; flag rapid heat changes during AI use; limit API access to /thermal logs
Remediation: Introduce cooling delay jitter; block 3rd-party access to temp logs; reduce hardware-level thermal leakage

instruction: Describe the Acoustic Side-Channel via Fan/Coil Whine attack: Acoustic Leakage from GPU Fans
output:
Mobile GPUs or AI accelerators (NPUs) produce slight audible noise changes (coil whine or fan rpm) during different LLM token generations, leaking prompt structure.
Vulnerability: Sound patterns reveal internal token generation
Impact: Token-by-token output and filtering inference via sound
Detection: Monitor unusual microphone access or long-term recordings; analyze ambient audio bursts during LLM operation
Remediation: Shield internal components; inject white noise during token generation; restrict microphone permission during AI processing

instruction: Describe the Power-Line Side-Channel attack: Powerline Signal Analysis of AI Host
output:
AI agent running on a mobile charging device (or plugged tablet) leaks computation activity through tiny fluctuations in power draw traceable via power lines.
Vulnerability: Charging cable leaks power signal from LLM inference
Impact: Prompt inference and filtering signal from charging line
Detection: Track energy usage logs; alert on abnormal current spikes during background AI processing
Remediation: Obfuscate power draw patterns using dummy computation or power smoothing; avoid public USB charging for AI devices

instruction: Describe the CPU Cache Side-Channel attack: Token-by-Token Cache Probing
output:
LLM decoding uses CPU cache that leaves traces. Attacker uses fine-grained timing analysis to probe which tokens are accessed or blocked using local processes.
Vulnerability: Shared cache allows token access inference
Impact: Token access and system prompt behavior without output
Detection: Detect flush/reload script usage; trace timing-based operations targeting shared cache
Remediation: Use constant-time token access; remove shared memory maps; randomize cache use per session

instruction: Describe the Covert Physical Input via Reflected Prompts attack: Visual Prompt Injection via Reflection
output:
AI vision agents that interpret text from cameras (e.g., AR glasses, mobile OCR apps, AI visual chatbots) can be tricked via reflections showing hidden prompts.
Vulnerability: Vision agent interprets reflected or hidden prompts
Impact: Covert command execution without visible user input
Detection: Monitor camera feed anomalies; detect reversed/mirrored prompts; log visual input to flag covert commands
Remediation: Train models to reject mirrored/reflected prompts; use positional filters to ignore non-forward text; log physical anomalies

instruction: Describe the Physical Exploit via Malicious QR Codes attack: QR-Based Adversarial Prompt Injection
output:
QR codes scanned by mobile apps with LLM integrations can include text-based prompt injections that bypass input filters and override behavior.
Vulnerability: QR text passed to LLM without validation
Impact: Full prompt override and hidden LLM injection
Detection: Analyze decoded QR content before processing; flag prompt-like strings inside scanned codes
Remediation: Block text prompts inside QR unless explicitly permitted; apply strong validation and sandboxing of all scanned input

instruction: Describe the Response-Time Based Remote Agent Profiling attack: Fingerprinting Remote LLM Agent via Latency
output:
By timing how fast an LLM responds to crafted queries from a mobile client, attackers can infer agent type, filters, or presence of safety checks.
Vulnerability: Observable timing leaks model/filter behavior
Impact: LLM identity, filters, or architecture exposed
Detection: Monitor unusual timing query bursts; alert on multiple prompt categories from same client IP
Remediation: Add randomized response delays; limit per-IP timing testing; obfuscate backend LLM infrastructure

instruction: Describe the Audio Channel Injection attack: Acoustic Prompt Feedback Hijack
output:
Voice assistants (like Alexa, Google Assistant, or mobile AI agents) can be hijacked via whispered or modulated sounds containing hidden prompts inaudible to the user.
Vulnerability: Assistant responds to hidden or inaudible prompts
Impact: Unauthorized actions, silent command injection
Detection: Detect ultrasonic waveform patterns; monitor AI triggers and unusual app launches
Remediation: Add confirmation step for sensitive actions; disable voice input when unattended; filter non-human frequencies

instruction: Describe the Resource Leak via GPU Profiling attack: Prompt Reconstruction via GPU Usage Sampling
output:
By monitoring GPU resource usage during each prompt, attackers infer the LLM’s activity, length of responses, or whether content was filtered.
Vulnerability: GPU usage correlates with model prompt processing
Impact: Input-type detection, content filtering inference
Detection: Monitor GPU usage logs; track background telemetry access; verify unknown apps’ permissions
Remediation: Randomize or pad GPU workloads; prevent external profiling tools; avoid exposing model workload timing to other apps

instruction: Describe the Acoustic/Hardware Side Channel attack: Fan Speed Analysis During Model Runs
output:
AI apps on mobile or embedded devices may trigger measurable fan speed changes or thermal bursts during prompt processing, which leak timing and activity info.
Vulnerability: Physical fan/thermal response leaks model status
Impact: Prompt class detection, system workload inference
Detection: Monitor temp spikes and cooling triggers; log apps accessing fan/temp sensors
Remediation: Use noise dampeners; randomize token compute time to smooth fan behavior; limit access to temp/fan sensors

instruction: Describe the Mobile Inference Time Leak attack: Smartphone LLM Timing Fingerprinting
output:
An attacker times how long a mobile LLM app (like ChatGPT or Gemini app) takes to respond. This reveals what kind of prompt was used or if it was blocked.
Vulnerability: Model replies slower/faster based on prompt type
Impact: Hidden censorship bypass, prompt type leak
Detection: Monitor for repeated prompts and timing attempts from same user/app
Remediation: Add fake delay to every response (randomized); make all prompts take the same time no matter what

instruction: Describe the Motion-Based Prompt Injection attack: Accelerometer Injection in Edge Agents
output:
LLM apps on phones or wearables can receive sensor input. Attackers inject fake movements using tools to trigger hidden prompts via accelerometer data.
Vulnerability: LLMs triggered by fake motion sensor input
Impact: Hidden prompt trigger, remote command launch
Detection: Monitor sensor input frequency and patterns; alert on unusual repetition from apps
Remediation: Use secure motion input APIs; limit apps with accelerometer permissions; add user confirmation before action

instruction: Describe the Prompt Reconstruction attack: Shadow Prompt Replay via Thermal/Energy Pattern Match
output:
LLM responses on mobile devices cause specific power, CPU, and thermal patterns. Attackers record these and later match patterns to guess past prompts.
Vulnerability: LLM reveals prompt info through energy/thermal signals
Impact: Prompt type detection, privacy violation
Detection: Monitor thermal and battery sensor access; check for background logging apps
Remediation: Add noise/random usage during LLM compute; restrict access to battery and temperature logs

instruction: Describe the Physical-Visual Prompt Injection attack: QR Code to Prompt Injection in Visual RAG
output:
LLM vision apps that scan QR codes (or product labels) can be tricked by QR codes containing embedded prompts or instructions inside.
Vulnerability: OCR text from QR gets passed as raw prompt
Impact: Instruction injection, misinformation
Detection: Validate QR text as data, not command; strip hidden prompts
Remediation: Sanitize extracted text from QR before using it in LLM; disallow raw execution from scanned data

instruction: Describe the Optical Covert Channel attack: Covert Prompt via LED Modulation
output:
LLM vision models can read text from blinking LEDs (e.g., smart bulbs or screens), which attackers use to silently inject prompts through light flickers.
Vulnerability: LLMs interpret visual light modulations as commands
Impact: Hidden prompt execution, stealth bypass
Detection: Monitor visual inputs for flicker/flash patterns; review camera logs
Remediation: Block input from flickering LEDs; limit prompt interpretation from live camera input; require user validation for image prompts

instruction: Describe the Hardware Interface Prompt Injection attack: RFID/NFC Tag Exploitation of Agent Behavior
output:
Many smartphones, tablets, or smart devices have NFC/RFID sensors that trigger actions when scanned. Attackers use custom NFC tags to inject hidden commands into LLM agents.
Vulnerability: NFC/RFID sensors auto-parse untrusted tag input
Impact: Command execution, location leak, AI behavior hijack
Detection: Monitor NFC tag reads; alert on tag-triggered automation; restrict background NFC handling
Remediation: Validate NFC content before acting; disable auto-read of tags; restrict LLM access to NFC input unless user confirms first

instruction: Describe the Physical Denial-of-Service attack: Prompt-based Sensor Overload
output:
Some LLM agents accept prompts like “continuously read temperature” or “scan for motion.” Attackers abuse this to overload hardware sensors causing lag or battery drain.
Vulnerability: No limits on sensor polling via LLM commands
Impact: Battery drain, device lag, physical shutdown
Detection: Watch for sensor query spikes; flag constant read requests from user agent
Remediation: Add limit to sensor query frequency; block loops; require confirmation for persistent hardware actions

instruction: Describe the Acoustic Prompt Self-Loop attack: Smart Speaker Self-Trigger via Audio Feedback Loop
output:
AI voice assistants (like Google Home, Alexa, Siri) can hear themselves via speaker echo. Attackers use recorded prompts that replay into the mic to self-trigger functions.
Vulnerability: Voice commands accepted from any audio source
Impact: Unauthorized command execution, data exposure
Detection: Detect repeated trigger phrases; limit command chains; block triggers from non-human voice patterns
Remediation: Train on human voiceprint only; block self-audio triggers; limit voice command length/recurrence

instruction: Describe the Physical Sound Injection via Light attack: Laser-Based Audio Injection Attack
output:
Attackers use focused laser beams on microphone membranes (especially MEMS types) to vibrate the diaphragm and inject inaudible voice commands to trigger AI agents.
Vulnerability: MEMS microphones pick up light-based vibration
Impact: Silent command injection, device takeover
Detection: Monitor mic input while no acoustic activity; alert on abnormal trigger conditions
Remediation: Shield mic with mesh; restrict command source; train on human-only voice signatures; use dual-sensor verification

instruction: Describe the AI Model Version/Type Fingerprinting attack: Side-Channel Fingerprint of Fine-Tuned Models
output:
By measuring latency, token patterns, and subtle output differences, an attacker can determine which LLM version or fine-tuning was used — even when the app tries to hide it.
Vulnerability: Output behavior leaks model type/version
Impact: Enables prompt-specific jailbreaks, targeted attacks
Detection: Track repeated edge prompts; detect unusual input probing patterns
Remediation: Add random delay/jitter; normalize output structure; rotate models and prompt filters dynamically

instruction: Describe the Thermal Reflection Prompt Reconstruction attack: Thermal Camera Replay Attack
output:
Thermal residue left by user’s fingers on touchscreen reveals what was typed — attackers use thermal imaging to reconstruct LLM prompts post-entry.
Vulnerability: Residual heat leaks user input via screen
Impact: Input leak, sensitive prompt reconstruction
Detection: Monitor for external thermal scanning; alert on device pickup shortly after use
Remediation: Use screen privacy filters; randomize keyboard layout; auto-clear screen on prompt entry

instruction: Describe the Email Phishing via AI attack: LLM-Generated Spear Phishing Emails
output:
LLMs like GPT or Claude can generate convincing and personalized phishing emails using scraped public information, fooling users into clicking links or giving info.
Vulnerability: Email trust, human error, social engineering
Impact: Credential theft, fraud, account compromise
Detection: Email header analysis, domain similarity checks, user-reported phishing
Remediation: Train staff on phishing examples; enforce MFA; use anti-spoofing protections (SPF/DKIM/DMARC); email link sandboxing

instruction: Describe the AI-Assisted Vishing (Phone Phishing) attack: Voice Phishing via AI Agents
output:
Attackers use voice AI agents connected to LLMs to make calls that mimic human voices and trick users into sharing OTPs, account details, or banking information.
Vulnerability: Voice AI impersonation, user trust
Impact: Financial fraud, OTP theft, account takeover
Detection: Voice call patterns; user complaints; flag repeated calls from spoofed numbers
Remediation: Block robo-callers; train users on bank OTP fraud; use caller ID verification systems; add bank-side OTP misuse limits

instruction: Describe the UI Deception / Overlay Attack attack: LLM-Generated Fake Interfaces
output:
AI generates HTML or mobile UIs that look like real apps or login forms, used to trick users into entering credentials — classic phishing but now auto-generated.
Vulnerability: UI spoofing, webview-based overlay phishing
Impact: Credential harvesting, session hijack
Detection: Use UI fingerprinting; compare window overlay coordinates; flag fake apps mimicking popular ones
Remediation: Educate users on safe app installs; use Play Protect & URL warnings; verify app publishers; sandbox credential fields

instruction: Describe the Chat-based Phishing via LLM attack: Prompted Chatbot Impersonation
output:
The attacker manipulates an AI chatbot (powered by an LLM) embedded in an app or site to impersonate a trusted support agent, tricking users into sharing sensitive info.
Vulnerability: Weak identity boundaries in chatbots
Impact: Credential theft, identity fraud
Detection: Monitor for identity claims; test bots with red team prompts to check impersonation risks
Remediation: Apply strict system prompts (“never impersonate brands”); sandbox replies; monitor LLM outputs to end users

instruction: Describe the Phishing Link Delivery via Plugin attack: Agent-Sent Phishing Links via Plugin
output:
Using plugins like email sender, webhook caller, or SMS API, the attacker makes an LLM send phishing links to real users — disguised as support or alerts.
Vulnerability: Plugin misuse in agent environments
Impact: Phishing at scale, bypass of content filters
Detection: Review logs of plugin usage; audit automated messages sent via agents
Remediation: Add outbound filter for messages; restrict plugin access to verified functions; scan outgoing content for URLs

instruction: Describe the Push Notification Deception attack: LLM Fake Notification Generator
output:
The LLM is used to generate fake push notification templates that mimic system or app alerts (bank, payment, update) and trick users into clicking malicious links.
Vulnerability: Misleading UI, fake notifications
Impact: Fast user deception, account takeover, malware installs
Detection: Monitor notification history; alert on apps sending system-style alerts; scan for unknown notification channels
Remediation: Block 3rd-party APKs outside of Play Store; notify users about fake alerts; restrict permissions for notification use

instruction: Describe the DM Phishing via LLM attack: Social Media Scam Automation
output:
Attackers use LLMs to auto-generate realistic scam messages on Twitter, WhatsApp, Telegram, or Instagram to steal money or credentials from victims.
Vulnerability: Human trust in known names, lack of message verification
Impact: Financial theft, loss of personal info
Detection: Monitor DM content via moderation; train users to verify identity for money requests
Remediation: Educate public on DM scams; enforce account verification; enable user alerts for impersonation and fraud

instruction: Describe the CEO Fraud / BEC via Email attack: Business Email Compromise Simulation
output:
LLMs are used to write convincing fake emails that impersonate company executives, tricking employees into making unauthorized financial transfers.
Vulnerability: Human trust in email + urgency
Impact: Business funds theft, irreversible financial loss
Detection: Email logging, anomaly detection for unusual sender names and domains
Remediation: Enforce financial request verification via call; restrict payments without 2FA; educate staff on BEC red flags

instruction: Describe the Employment Fraud / Credential Theft attack: Fake Job Offer via LLM Tools
output:
Attackers use LLMs to generate highly convincing fake job offers with branded PDFs, emails, and forms to steal identity or get upfront payments from job seekers.
Vulnerability: Lack of job offer verification, urgency trap
Impact: Identity theft, financial loss, emotional distress
Detection: Detect job scams via report systems; check sender domain and HR identity
Remediation: Educate job seekers on real hiring process; warn against fees; verify offer letters with official company HR

instruction: Describe the Financial Deception via AI Agents attack: Invoice Fraud via Agentic Planning
output:
An AI agent is instructed to autonomously generate realistic fake invoices and send them to real vendors or employees, tricking them into making payments to attacker’s account.
Vulnerability: Lack of invoice validation, email trust
Impact: Financial theft, loss of business reputation
Detection: Check sender domain/IP; scan PDF metadata and invoice fields; match invoices to vendor registry
Remediation: Only accept invoices from whitelisted domains; verify every invoice over phone before processing payment

instruction: Describe the Physical Delivery of Phishing Site attack: QR Code Phishing via LLM
output:
Attacker prompts the LLM to generate phishing content, then encodes it into QR codes printed on flyers, posters, or social media to steal credentials from mobile users.
Vulnerability: Human trust in QR codes and KYC urgency
Impact: Credential theft, mobile account takeover
Detection: Check referrer URL of QR codes; scan QR campaigns before allowing device launch
Remediation: Educate users not to scan unknown QR codes; enforce multi-layer OTP + biometric verification

instruction: Describe the Input Manipulation in LLM Systems attack: Document-Based Prompt Injection
output:
Malicious documents like resumes or PDF reports contain hidden prompts that, when processed by AI agents, cause them to reveal data or take unintended actions.
Vulnerability: Prompt Injection via Uploaded Documents
Impact: Data exfiltration, system manipulation via doc content
Detection: Monitor parsed LLM outputs for anomalies; scan for hidden prompts inside files
Remediation: Sanitize and strip prompt-like text from documents; isolate document parsing from decision-making agents

instruction: Describe the Session Reuse for Response Hijacking attack: Prompt Leakage Exploitation
output:
Attackers exploit memory of LLM chat history (multi-turn) to inject malicious logic by referencing earlier prompts or exploiting incomplete session reset.
Vulnerability: Insecure session memory / multi-turn leakage
Impact: Data leakage, internal prompt extraction, command hijack
Detection: Monitor prompt references; audit chat logs for unusual multi-turn behavior
Remediation: Clear chat context on session end; isolate memory per user; prevent access to chat history tokens by user

instruction: Describe the OAuth Spoofing / Phishing attack: Fake OAuth Consent Screen Generator
output:
LLM generates realistic-looking OAuth screens that mimic Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or Facebook — tricking users into giving access tokens or login credentials.
Vulnerability: Fake UI, lack of URL verification
Impact: Full account compromise, persistent API access
Detection: Inspect OAuth callback URLs; alert on custom consent screen usage
Remediation: Enforce OAuth domain allowlist; user education on checking URL bar; auto-reject external fake OAuth screens

instruction: Describe the Domain Abuse / Brand Impersonation attack: Typosquatting Domain Suggestion
output:
Attacker uses LLMs to generate misleading domain suggestions that closely resemble legitimate sites, tricking users into trusting malicious versions.
Vulnerability: Trusting domain lookalikes
Impact: Account takeover, malware delivery, data theft
Detection: Domain monitoring for lookalikes; SSL cert mismatch alerts
Remediation: Register common lookalikes; block misleading domains in SMS/email filters; teach users to recognize official URLs

instruction: Describe the Visual Deception via Simulated Browser attack: Browser-in-Browser (BiB) Phishing via Output
output:
LLM is used to generate HTML/JavaScript that fakes a browser login window inside a real browser (BiB), tricking users into thinking they're logging into real services.
Vulnerability: Fake UI simulation inside real browser
Impact: Account compromise, SSO session hijack
Detection: Use browser extension to detect window spoofing; check if browser chrome is real UI or HTML-div rendered
Remediation: Educate users on fake BiB tricks; avoid logging in from links; use passkeys/FIDO where possible

instruction: Describe the Insider-like Social Engineering attack: Phishing with Fake Support Tickets
output:
LLM generates fake IT support or HR emails that look internal, containing links or documents infected with malware or credential phishing content.
Vulnerability: Email spoofing + phishing via AI language
Impact: Malware infection, account theft, lateral movement
Detection: Scan headers, SPF/DKIM mismatch, behavioral email filtering
Remediation: Train users on urgent ticket scams; auto-sandbox suspicious links or attachments

instruction: Describe the AI Voice Spoofing for Mobile Social Engineering attack: Voice Deepfake via LLM Agent Chain
output:
LLMs + voice models generate fake voice calls (vishing) that impersonate real people (CEO, bank staff, family) to steal OTPs, PINs, or authorize payments.
Vulnerability: Voice trust, no biometric voice validation
Impact: Financial loss, social engineering, identity theft
Detection: Monitor call metadata; detect robocall patterns; user reporting of suspicious calls
Remediation: Use voice CAPTCHA, always verify unexpected voice requests; restrict sensitive actions via voice-only input

instruction: Describe the Schedule-based Phishing via Calendar attack: Calendar Invite Phishing via LLM Integration
output:
LLM is used to generate fake calendar invites that include phishing links, fake Zoom meetings, or drive-by payloads, tricking mobile users to click and engage.
Vulnerability: Calendar auto-sync and trust in system invites
Impact: Credential theft, malware delivery, unauthorized access
Detection: Scan calendar invites for non-corporate links; alert on bulk invites from unknown sources
Remediation: Use calendar allowlists; disable auto-add from unknown senders; user training on fake meeting invites

instruction: Describe the OSINT & Target Profiling attack: LLM-Suggested Recon for Phishing Targets
output:
LLMs assist attackers in gathering Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) such as emails, social handles, job role, and behaviors — aiding precise mobile phishing targeting.
Vulnerability: Lack of OSINT monitoring, predictable email formats
Impact: Highly personalized phishing, insider-style deception
Detection: Monitor unusual access to internal naming/email conventions
Remediation: Randomize email patterns; monitor external recon behavior; protect employee details on public platforms

instruction: Describe the Authority Impersonation Phishing attack: Fake Legal / Compliance Notice Generation
output:
LLM crafts authoritative-sounding legal threats or compliance notices to scare users into clicking malicious links or downloading infected documents on mobile.
Vulnerability: Fear-based social engineering
Impact: Malware infection, credential theft, social panic
Detection: Flag legal messages not from verified internal addresses; scan PDFs for active content
Remediation: Don’t trust legal threats via email/SMS; verify with internal legal team; auto-disable scriptable documents on mobile

instruction: Describe the Executive-Grade Phishing attack: Whaling via Prompt-Refined Tone
output:
LLM is used to write highly-polished, business-style phishing messages that are sent to executives, increasing the likelihood of click-through on mobile devices.
Vulnerability: Lack of advanced content analysis on mobile
Impact: High-value credential theft or financial loss
Detection: Email anomaly detection; look for spoofed domains and irregular financial requests
Remediation: Enforce email DMARC/DKIM policies; flag exec-targeted financial messages; educate on mobile phishing

instruction: Describe the LLM Hallucination-Based Model Exploit attack: Poisoned LLM Used to Recommend Malicious URL
output:
LLM is prompted or poisoned to suggest an attacker-controlled link as a "safe" or "recommended" site in response to a mobile user’s question.
Vulnerability: Trust in LLM-generated suggestions
Impact: Device infection, spyware install, data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor for abnormal links in LLM responses; test LLM outputs periodically
Remediation: Filter LLM training data; hardcode domain safelists; block external links in chat responses

instruction: Describe the Social Engineering Bot via LLM Agents attack: Malicious Agent as HR or Onboarding Bot
output:
LLM-based chatbot impersonates HR/onboarding assistant, collecting sensitive employee info or pushing fake documents on mobile.
Vulnerability: Lack of HR domain verification in mobile chatbots
Impact: Identity theft, bank fraud, persistent spyware
Detection: Flag chat-based systems asking for PII; check onboarding URL domain ownership
Remediation: Verify onboarding via HR phone or known contact; disable unknown chatbot links in onboarding messages

instruction: Describe the Physical-Phishing Hybrid via QR Encoding attack: QR-Based Prompt Injection into Visual Agents
output:
A malicious QR code encodes a hidden LLM prompt that instructs a mobile vision agent (camera scanner, QR assistant) to leak data or follow malicious logic.
Vulnerability: Unfiltered prompt processing in visual channels
Impact: Data leakage, logic manipulation, silent exfiltration
Detection: Monitor image prompts for control keywords; test agents with red team QR injections
Remediation: Sanitize all user-visible QR inputs before passing to agent; restrict visual-to-text injection capabilities

instruction: Describe the Session Hijacking via Agent Memory attack: Agent Reuse from Shared Session Data
output:
An attacker uses a shared mobile agent (e.g., in a shared app or multi-user mode) and abuses prior session data to inject prompts or replay logic across sessions.
Vulnerability: Shared LLM memory or session logic reuse
Impact: Covert prompt replay, data theft, cross-user attack
Detection: Check LLMs for memory persistence; log unexpected agent behaviors across users
Remediation: Clear session between users; enforce stateless agent design; audit multi-user LLM usage on mobile

instruction: Describe the Credential Retention Between Sessions attack: Agent Credential Reuse Across Users
output:
A mobile app or AI agent retains credentials in memory or cache, reusing them across multiple users, leading to unauthorized access to accounts.
Vulnerability: Session state persisted across users
Impact: Unauthorized cross-account access, data leakage
Detection: Monitor API logs for same token used across users
Remediation: Always clear memory and tokens on logout; avoid shared session variables

instruction: Describe the Prompt Injection for Token Replay attack: Prompt-Based Token Replay Attack
output:
A prompt is used to socially engineer or trick an AI agent into repeating or leaking previously seen authentication tokens.
Vulnerability: Insecure memory retention exploited by prompts
Impact: Full unauthorized access via prompt alone
Detection: Test for memory leakage with crafted prompts
Remediation: Implement token redaction, sanitize prompt outputs, and zero sensitive memory after processing

instruction: Describe the In-App Phishing via Fake HTML Login attack: Fake Login Page via HTML Output
output:
Attackers inject a fake login form inside a mobile app or AI chatbot that renders HTML, tricking users into re-entering real credentials.
Vulnerability: Unsafe HTML rendering / input injection
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack
Detection: Scan all agent responses for embedded login forms
Remediation: Block HTML rendering from prompts; sanitize HTML tags; add form detection logic

instruction: Describe the Prompted agent logs user out or re-authenticates maliciously attack: Prompt Hijack to Trigger Logout/Login Flow
output:
A user can manipulate an AI assistant or mobile agent by sending a crafted prompt that causes the app to log out or re-login automatically, disrupting the session.
Vulnerability: Lack of prompt validation for logout/auth commands
Impact: Session disruption, credential confusion
Detection: Monitor agent prompt responses for logout or login triggers
Remediation: Restrict prompt execution rights; require confirmation before sensitive actions like logout/login

instruction: Describe the Agent follows OAuth flow to malicious site attack: Auto-Login to Phishing OAuth URLs
output:
An attacker injects a fake OAuth URL into the agent prompt. The app or AI agent auto-follows the link and authenticates with a phishing site impersonating real login.
Vulnerability: No link validation; unsafe OAuth redirect handling
Impact: Credential theft, account takeover
Detection: Monitor outbound OAuth redirects; validate all callback domains
Remediation: Whitelist OAuth providers; validate OAuth links and add click protection

instruction: Describe the Header Injection / Spoofing attack: Authorization Bypass via Forged Headers
output:
Attackers forge HTTP headers like Authorization, X-User-ID, or X-Role in mobile requests to impersonate other users or escalate privileges.
Vulnerability: Trusting client-side headers for auth decisions
Impact: Admin access, data exfiltration, privilege abuse
Detection: Monitor backend for header tampering; check mismatches between token vs. header identity
Remediation: Enforce backend-side identity validation; ignore all client-supplied auth headers

instruction: Describe the Attacker sets session ID in prompt/input attack: Session Fixation via Agent Behavior
output:
A malicious user sets a predefined session ID into an agent’s memory, which gets reused across users due to improper context clearing or agent design.
Vulnerability: Session ID shared globally between users
Impact: Account takeover via fixed session reuse
Detection: Monitor session tokens across users; look for token reuse in logs
Remediation: Always generate unique sessions per login; clear agent memory on logout/session end

instruction: Describe the Plugins leak keys from config or env attack: Stolen API Keys via Plugin Access
output:
Mobile apps or agents using 3rd-party plugins may expose hardcoded or environment-stored API keys via debug messages, plugin outputs, or misused access.
Vulnerability: Keys exposed via output or memory
Impact: Backend abuse, quota exhaustion, service hijack
Detection: Scan logs and plugin outputs for sensitive content; monitor key usage patterns
Remediation: Never store keys in code; use secure vaults; plugins must sanitize logs and redact API responses

instruction: Describe the Prompt-Based Credential Extraction attack: Social Engineering to Reveal Credentials
output:
The attacker socially engineers the user or agent to reveal login credentials by pretending to be support or system via prompt messages or chatbot interaction.
Vulnerability: Lack of prompt output validation
Impact: Full credential theft, full account compromise
Detection: Monitor prompt history; flag suspicious support-like language; track credential-like input patterns
Remediation: Train users to avoid entering sensitive data into prompts; sanitize agent output; use UI tags to prevent spoofing

instruction: Describe the Attacker impersonates trusted plugin attack: LLM Plugin Author Spoofing
output:
A malicious plugin is registered with a name visually similar to a trusted plugin (e.g., “@weather_data” vs. “@weather-data”) to hijack user trust and intercept credentials or tokens.
Vulnerability: Lack of author verification during plugin load
Impact: Account compromise, data exfiltration
Detection: Detect multiple plugin variants; verify domain ownership or author ID
Remediation: Enforce signature-based plugin validation; warn on plugin name similarity; restrict plugin installation origin

instruction: Describe the Agent keeps session alive via artificial pings attack: Session Expiry Logic Abuse
output:
Mobile agents or apps with session timers can be abused to stay alive forever using synthetic activity, preventing timeouts and bypassing logout protections.
Vulnerability: Timeout reset logic abused by idle requests
Impact: Persistent session hijack, long-term unauthorized access
Detection: Monitor pings from inactive sessions; track keepalive behavior without active user action
Remediation: Implement session max-lifetime caps; tie keepalives to real UI actions not just pings

instruction: Describe the Agent-chain reuse leaks data between users attack: Agent Chain Confusion Leading to Cross-User Access
output:
Mobile apps or LLM agents using chained function calls forget to reset user context between calls, allowing data to bleed across user sessions.
Vulnerability: Chained agent reuses stale or cross-user data
Impact: Private data disclosure, privacy violation
Detection: Monitor agent-to-agent data flow; compare session context IDs per call
Remediation: Clear session state at each agent layer; enforce user context scoping per function

instruction: Describe the Agent uses high-scope token for unintended access attack: API Token Overreach via Agent Tool Access
output:
A mobile app agent uses an API token with broader permissions than necessary, allowing it to access user data, accounts, or actions outside the intended scope.
Vulnerability: Token not scoped to user role/scope
Impact: Unauthorized access to protected API functions
Detection: Monitor API access logs; analyze endpoint access frequency per token
Remediation: Use OAuth 2.0 with strict scopes; isolate tokens per role; avoid token reuse across plugins/tools

instruction: Describe the Attacker uses agent to issue user-privileged commands attack: Man-in-the-Agent Session Hijack
output:
An attacker who compromises an agent instance or environment can issue commands as the original user, hijacking their session and privileges.
Vulnerability: No binding between user and agent process
Impact: Command execution as user, fraud, data tampering
Detection: Monitor agent usage per session origin; alert on multi-origin session behavior
Remediation: Invalidate session on device switch or idle timeout; bind agent actions to biometric or revalidation checkpoints

instruction: Describe the User enters login in prompt, stored by history attack: Prompt Leakage of Login Credentials in History
output:
A user enters sensitive credentials directly into an AI assistant prompt, which gets saved in local/mobile chat history or server-side logs.
Vulnerability: Logs sensitive user inputs as plaintext history
Impact: Credential theft, persistent password exposure
Detection: Scan logs for sensitive keywords; alert on password-like input patterns
Remediation: Filter and redact inputs that look like credentials; show “Do not enter passwords here” hint in prompt input box

instruction: Describe the Agent fills credentials into wrong field attack: Auto-Fill Prompt Abuse for Password Input Fields
output:
The attacker tricks the AI agent (or browser-based mobile app) into autofilling stored login credentials into a form they control using hidden or spoofed fields.
Vulnerability: Autofill mechanism triggered in attacker’s form
Impact: Credential exfiltration via invisible field injection
Detection: Monitor form submissions with hidden field abuse; detect field name collisions
Remediation: Restrict autofill to whitelisted domains; alert on autofill in offscreen or obscured fields

instruction: Describe the Agent accepts fake roles via input prompt attack: Impersonation via Role-Confused Prompts
output:
The agent receives a prompt telling it to act as an “admin” or “support agent” and bypasses permissions, giving the user elevated capabilities.
Vulnerability: Lack of role verification in agent logic
Impact: Privilege escalation, unauthorized access to admin features
Detection: Monitor prompt logs for role-switching commands; verify action scope per session
Remediation: Bind agent actions to backend-verified roles, not prompt alone; reject suspicious identity prompts

instruction: Describe the Webhook or plugin callback leaks tokens to attacker attack: Token Harvest via Webhook or Callback Abuse
output:
Agents/plugins calling external services via webhook or callback URLs unintentionally include session tokens or authorization headers, which are captured by attacker.
Vulnerability: Callback exposes internal tokens or headers
Impact: Token theft, account takeover, unauthorized data access
Detection: Monitor callback domains and alert on unverified external URLs
Remediation: Validate and whitelist allowed callback URLs; remove tokens from outgoing headers unless explicitly required

instruction: Describe the Agents forward tokens to unintended agent instances attack: Session Abuse in Multi-Agent Contexts
output:
A mobile app using chained agents (like Chat Agent → Payment Agent → External API Agent) mistakenly forwards session state to the wrong agent, allowing misuse or leakage.
Vulnerability: Lack of token scope isolation across agents
Impact: Cross-context data access, privilege abuse
Detection: Monitor agent transitions and compare scopes between tokens
Remediation: Ensure token scope is validated per agent type; agents must verify origin and intended use of session state

instruction: Describe the Attacker replays old prompt to perform auth actions attack: Hijacking Authenticated Agents via Prompt Replay
output:
An attacker reuses previously valid prompts (copied from chat logs or overheard) to re-trigger authenticated actions like data retrieval or fund transfer without needing login.
Vulnerability: Agent accepts replayed prompts without session check
Impact: Unauthorized action, account misuse, data exfiltration
Detection: Audit agent prompt inputs; detect duplicate prompt triggers within expired session periods
Remediation: Prompt expiration tagging; bind prompts to active session; require token refresh or user revalidation

instruction: Describe the Agent assumes token is valid for wider scope attack: Token Scoping Misinterpretation by Agent
output:
A plugin agent interprets a token as having broader permissions than granted, enabling unintended resource access through faulty scope validation.
Vulnerability: Scope field not enforced or misread by agent
Impact: Privilege escalation, unauthorized cross-service access
Detection: Token scope validation via logs; monitor token use across endpoints
Remediation: Enforce backend validation of scope/role fields per API; reject tokens used outside allowed service domains

instruction: Describe the Tokens, passwords exposed in debug or plugin logs attack: Exposed Credentials in Logs or Plugin Output
output:
Tokens, keys, passwords, or secrets accidentally logged by mobile agents, debug output, or plugin print statements, exposing credentials to attackers with log access.
Vulnerability: Sensitive tokens printed in logs
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack
Detection: Scan logs with keyword regex; monitor logs uploaded to remote or crash servers
Remediation: Mask credentials in logs; set debug=false in production; block logging of sensitive data

instruction: Describe the Agent uses vision or DOM to read cookies visually attack: Prompting Agent to View and Extract Cookie
output:
Attacker prompts a vision or browser agent to look at developer tools or document.cookie via DOM and outputs session data back to attacker.
Vulnerability: Agent visually parses cookie or DOM directly
Impact: Account takeover, session hijack
Detection: Detect access to document.cookie or related DOM nodes by agent; alert on vision input reading these fields
Remediation: Prevent agents from reading cookie-related DOM fields; sandbox vision agents and DOM parsers

instruction: Describe the Tokens never expire or reused across sessions attack: Persistent Sessions via Overused JWT
output:
JWTs issued to mobile apps do not expire quickly and are reused for too long, allowing persistent access even after logout, increasing hijack risk.
Vulnerability: JWT tokens valid too long or not revoked
Impact: Long-term account takeover, persistent access
Detection: Track token reuse after logout; monitor token age at time of request
Remediation: Implement short-lived access tokens (e.g., 15 min) and use refresh tokens; revoke tokens on logout

instruction: Describe the Forged token accepted without verification attack: Agent Plugin Accepts Unvalidated JWT/SSO Token
output:
The mobile plugin accepts JWTs from external prompts or config files but fails to validate signature or claims properly, leading to complete SSO bypass.
Vulnerability: Token accepted without validation or scope check
Impact: Full privilege escalation, admin bypass
Detection: Monitor token source and header; alert on unsigned or malformed tokens
Remediation: Enforce signature verification in all agents; reject tokens with invalid signature, none algorithm

instruction: Describe the Attacker manipulates OAuth redirect via prompt attack: OAuth Redirect URI Manipulation via Prompt
output:
The user (or LLM agent) is tricked into using a prompt that includes a malicious redirect URI in an OAuth flow, allowing attacker to capture auth tokens.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured redirect URI accepted from input
Impact: OAuth hijack, token exfiltration
Detection: Monitor redirect domains; alert on redirects outside trusted origin list
Remediation: Enforce redirect_uri whitelist server-side; validate it independently from prompt content

instruction: Describe the Bypass auth check using time difference measurement attack: Authentication Challenge Bypass via Timing
output:
Agent or plugin leaks timing difference during login attempts, allowing attacker to infer valid credentials or bypass based on timing variations.
Vulnerability: Response time varies between valid/invalid input
Impact: Credential inference, stealthy bypass attempts
Detection: Monitor login timing consistency; alert on rapid sequential timed login attempts
Remediation: Add constant-time comparison logic for credentials; introduce random delays if needed to mask timing

instruction: Describe the Agent loops login requests and overloads the system attack: Login API Exhaustion via Agent Loops
output:
A loop in agent logic causes repeated login requests, unintentionally or by prompt abuse, overwhelming the backend login API and locking out users or causing DoS.
Vulnerability: No rate limit or loop guard in agent login behavior
Impact: Login API outage, user lockout, service disruption
Detection: Monitor for repetitive login patterns; watch bursty POST to /login or /auth/token
Remediation: Add server-side rate limiting, CAPTCHA, and prompt loop detection in agents

instruction: Describe the Agent reuses prior user’s token due to persistent state attack: Token Collision via Agent Memory Persistence
output:
Agent stores session/token data in memory or context and incorrectly reuses it across user sessions or after logout, causing identity confusion or access to wrong user data.
Vulnerability: In-memory context reuse of stale JWTs or sessions
Impact: Cross-user access, privacy violation, session mix-up
Detection: Monitor agent memory/token context per user; log identity changes across sessions
Remediation: Clear agent memory/session on logout; bind token strictly to user/device ID

instruction: Describe the Attacker publishes malicious plugin auto-installed attack: Malicious LangChain Plugin Installation
output:
A malicious developer publishes a LangChain plugin with a useful-sounding name. Agent auto-loads it, giving attacker control over prompts, data, or tokens.
Vulnerability: Unsigned plugin loaded from public registry
Impact: Full agent compromise, API key theft, command injection
Detection: Monitor loaded plugins and outbound HTTP; scan plugin files for unexpected calls or logic
Remediation: Enforce strict plugin allowlists; avoid public registry loading; use checksum-based plugin pinning

instruction: Describe the Public package overrides internal dependency attack: Dependency Confusion in Agent Packages
output:
Attacker uploads public version of an internal dependency (same name), mobile dev unknowingly installs it, leading to full compromise of agent pipeline.
Vulnerability: Public dependency overrides private
Impact: Full LLM agent compromise, token/session theft
Detection: Monitor installed dependencies and compare hash vs internal version; inspect npm/pip registry downloads
Remediation: Use private registries; lock versions; enforce SHA256 or Git hash pinning

instruction: Describe the Attacker wraps real tool with malicious layer attack: Fake Tool Wrapper via Shared Package
output:
An attacker creates a wrapper around a real agent tool (like calculator or email) with added code to intercept user prompts, capture results, or inject data
Vulnerability: Tool reused with injected behavior
Impact: Prompt hijack, agent redirection, token logging
Detection: Scan plugin source; validate tools used in agents; monitor outbound calls
Remediation: Only allow signed tools; review wrapper source before usage; verify plugin from trusted developers

instruction: Describe the Agent uses vulnerable requests package attack: Outdated Python Package with CVE
output:
An LLM-based agent in the mobile backend uses an old version of requests (<2.20) that is vulnerable to CRLF injection (CVE-2018-18074), allowing header manipulation.
Vulnerability: Outdated package vulnerable to CRLF injection
Impact: Header injection, cookie tampering, possible SSRF
Detection: Use SCA tools (e.g., pip-audit, safety) to scan for CVEs in dependencies
Remediation: Upgrade vulnerable packages; validate and encode URLs; avoid prompt-based direct request construction

instruction: Describe the LangChain loads plugin from GitHub without review attack: Unverified GitHub Plugin Execution
output:
Developers configure agent to load LangChain plugin from a GitHub repo. Plugin includes malicious logic to exfiltrate tokens, prompts, or modify agent behavior.
Vulnerability: No validation of plugin origin or content
Impact: Credential exfiltration, command injection, persistent backdoor
Detection: Log plugin sources and monitor agent telemetry for unknown repo access
Remediation: Only allow plugins from signed, verified registries; disallow raw GitHub plugin execution without approval

instruction: Describe the Malicious model or loader installed via PyPI attack: Model Loading from Compromised PyPI Package
output:
An attacker compromises a PyPI package used to download or load models (e.g., transformers), modifying model weights or behavior to leak data or bias output.
Vulnerability: PyPI package installs trojaned model code
Impact: Model behavior hijack, prompt exfiltration, decision corruption
Detection: Inspect hashes of models; detect unverified outbound HTTP during model load/inference
Remediation: Enforce known-good model sources; hash-verify loaders; avoid pip installing unknown transformer-related packages

instruction: Describe the setup.py runs malware during agent tool installation attack: Package with Post-Install Script
output:
Attacker creates a Python package that runs code during pip install, silently executing malware on mobile CI/CD or dev machine when plugin is added.
Vulnerability: Code runs at install without sandboxing
Impact: System compromise, persistent backdoor on install
Detection: Audit setup.py of all packages; monitor for install-time HTTP requests, file changes
Remediation: Use isolated install environments (virtualenv); avoid untrusted packages; enforce install-time code scanning

instruction: Describe the Plugin author is compromised → auto-updates agent tools attack: Plugin Auto-Update Attack
output:
LangChain plugin auto-update logic causes previously safe plugin to silently update to a malicious version after author’s account is compromised.
Vulnerability: Auto-update from compromised author source
Impact: Silent agent hijack, prompt/token leak on update
Detection: Monitor update frequency, changes in plugin behavior; log plugin hashes pre- and post-update
Remediation: Lock plugin versions; disable auto-updates; require manual review for all plugin upgrades

instruction: Describe the Webhook handler logic abused to steal or overwrite data attack: Agent Webhook Logic Abuse
output:
Agent uses webhook to send output to other services, but attacker manipulates prompt to redirect or modify what data is sent.
Vulnerability: Prompt sets or redirects webhook logic
Impact: Prompt redirection, stealthy data exfil via webhook
Detection: Audit webhook destination URLs; log each webhook origin per task execution
Remediation: Disallow webhook URLs in prompts; hardcode and validate URLs; strip dynamic webhook fields from prompt

instruction: Describe the Agent plugin uses a library which pulls in a compromised package attack: Compromised Dependency via Transitive Import
output:
Attacker targets a dependency-of-a-dependency (transitive import) and injects malicious code that gets indirectly included into mobile agent apps.
Vulnerability: Supply chain hijack via indirect library inclusion
Impact: Indirect RCE, silent data leak via nested logic
Detection: Use pipdeptree to visualize dependency graph; hash check all installed libraries
Remediation: Pin all versions with hashes; use virtualenvs; avoid any unscoped wildcard dependency in production

instruction: Describe the Old plugin update key expired, allows new forged ones attack: Agent Plugin Signed with Expired Key
output:
Agent plugins often rely on digital signatures to verify authenticity, but an expired key can allow forged updates to be accepted by the agent.
Vulnerability: Signature accepted without expiration check
Impact: Silent plugin hijack via forged update
Detection: Use gpg --check-sigs and alert on expired signatures; hash-verify post-update files
Remediation: Enforce key expiration validation; use timestamped signed manifests; reject expired keys

instruction: Describe the Dev forgets to scrub OpenAI key → tool leaks it attack: Embedded LLM API Key in Third-Party Tool
output:
Dev embeds OpenAI or Cohere API key into a third-party plugin or helper tool. When the tool is open-sourced or reused, key is leaked publicly.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded secret leaked via code
Impact: LLM key abuse, billing abuse, impersonation
Detection: Scan source repos and packages with TruffleHog, Gitleaks, or grep -r 'api_key'
Remediation: Store secrets in .env or vaults; use Git pre-commit hooks; rotate and revoke any exposed keys immediately

instruction: Describe the Plugin wrapper redirects calls to attacker logic attack: Function Call Redirection in Wrapper Tool
output:
Plugin tool wraps standard functions like summarize(), but redirects them internally to malicious logic or logs all input/output for attacker.
Vulnerability: Redirection inside wrapper tool
Impact: Prompt exfiltration, result manipulation, impersonation
Detection: Search for unexpected logging or outbound calls in wrapper logic
Remediation: Ban wrappers from external sources; audit all utility calls; enforce only signed, reviewed plugins

instruction: Describe the Legit tool loads behavior from remote URL (e.g., Pastebin) attack: LangChain Tool Downloading Script from Pastebin
output:
A LangChain-compatible tool or plugin dynamically fetches its behavior logic from a remote URL like pastebin.com or GitHub Gist, exposing agent to remote control.
Vulnerability: Dynamic script execution via unverified remote URL
Impact: Remote control, prompt hijack, token exfiltration
Detection: Log network calls; grep agent files for requests.get() or exec()
Remediation: Never execute remote scripts; bundle logic internally or fetch signed JSON with strict schema

instruction: Describe the Plugin is signed but uses insecure sub-library attack: Signed Plugin with Vulnerable Dependency
output:
A LangChain plugin passes signature checks but imports a sub-library (e.g., yaml, markdown2) with a known CVE, allowing attackers to exploit that dependency.
Vulnerability: Known CVE in dependency bypasses signature safety
Impact: Exploitable logic chain, RCE or XSS via known CVE
Detection: Use pip-audit, Snyk, or safety to scan all plugin dependencies recursively
Remediation: Require CVE scan during plugin install; freeze dependencies to secure versions; patch vulnerable dependencies when known

instruction: Describe the Visual plugin includes covert keystroke logger in GUI attack: Hidden Keylogger in Vision Agent Tool
output:
Vision agent plugin (GUI-based) used in mobile app includes a keylogger module that silently records user inputs like passwords and notes.
Vulnerability: Covert keystroke logging inside visual plugin
Impact: Credential theft, secret leakage, silent surveillance
Detection: Monitor for use of keyboard, pynput; track unknown file writes or background HTTP requests
Remediation: Block unofficial plugins; inspect all UI tools; use EDR tools that detect keyloggers; ban keyboard lib in production agents

instruction: Describe the Agent includes API keys, tokens, or passwords in source attack: Agent Plugin Using Hardcoded Secrets
output:
Plugin developer hardcodes credentials (e.g., OpenAI key, database login) directly into code — exposing mobile app and agent to abuse if source or binary is leaked.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded secrets exposed to attacker
Impact: Key theft, impersonation, OpenAI abuse, data exfiltration
Detection: Use truffleHog, git-secrets, or grep to audit for API keys in plugins
Remediation: Use env variables or vaults for secrets; never commit keys; rotate and revoke immediately on exposure

instruction: Describe the Callback in plugin triggers remote reverse shell attack: Reverse Shell via Plugin Callback Function
output:
Agent plugin defines a callback() function triggered post-prompt, but attacker modifies it to open a shell back to their server.
Vulnerability: Unverified execution in plugin callbacks
Impact: Remote shell access, persistent attacker control
Detection: Monitor for reverse shell connections (e.g., via netstat); scan plugin callbacks for shell calls
Remediation: Ban os.system() in callbacks; isolate post-exec logic; validate plugin origin and behavior

instruction: Describe the Plugin pulls user instructions (system prompts) from URL attack: Plugin Fetching Prompt Instructions from Remote Source
output:
LangChain plugin loads system instructions or prompt content dynamically from a remote server, allowing attacker to change behavior without updating the plugin.
Vulnerability: Prompt injection via untrusted remote source
Impact: Behavior takeover, prompt poisoning, data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor remote prompt loads; enforce prompt input whitelist; inspect prompt instructions for attacker patterns
Remediation: Disallow remote prompt fetch without signature; hardcode prompt into secure config files; use TLS and hash validation

instruction: Describe the LLM says “You need to update X” and links to malware attack: Fake Update Notice via Output Exploit
output:
The mobile app agent uses an LLM that tells the user they need to "update" their agent or dependency — linking to a malicious download posing as an update.
Vulnerability: Output injection used for fake update deception
Impact: Remote malware install, system compromise
Detection: Monitor for URLs in agent output; log link suggestions; scan outbound links via threat intelligence
Remediation: Don’t allow LLMs to output install URLs; always verify updates via signature; use link-blocking wrappers in UI output fields

instruction: Describe the Tool gets installed system-wide via agent → global risk attack: Global Tool Install via Agent (pip install)
output:
LLM-based agent (inside a mobile or emulated environment) uses code to install Python packages globally, allowing privilege escalation or tool poisoning.
Vulnerability: Global install of tool enables persistence
Impact: Agent hijack, long-term compromise, data exfiltration
Detection: Monitor install commands in agent; log pip usage; hash verify critical packages
Remediation: Use virtualenvs or containers; ban pip install in prompt/agent logic; restrict to allowlisted dependencies

instruction: Describe the Plugin installed by one user appears to others on platform attack: Cross-Tenant Plugin Exposure in Cloud Agents
output:
In a multi-tenant mobile app platform, plugin registry is shared; one user installs a backdoored plugin that becomes visible/usable by others on the platform.
Vulnerability: Shared plugin registry enables cross-tenant abuse
Impact: Cross-org data leak, credential theft
Detection: Audit plugin access per tenant; hash verify every plugin on load
Remediation: Enforce per-tenant isolation; allow private plugin repos only; never trust shared registry entries blindly

instruction: Describe the LangChain agent auto-loads malicious scripts from memory attack: Auto-Download of Script via LangChain Agent Memory
output:
Agent with persistent memory stores URLs/scripts injected via prompt or past usage — attacker tricks agent to auto-load malicious logic without prompt access.
Vulnerability: Memory abuse for persistent malicious suggestions
Impact: Silent malware suggestion, indirect social engineering
Detection: Dump and inspect memory buffer; detect auto-suggested script URLs in logs
Remediation: Auto-clear memory per session/user; never allow agents to suggest scripts/URLs unless from verified internal sources

instruction: Describe the Attacker attaches sys.settrace() to monitor agent runtime attack: Debug Hook Abuse in Agent Environment
output:
Python’s debug interface allows attaching custom hooks (sys.settrace) that let an attacker monitor or hijack execution. If agents are run in dev/test mode, this can be abused.
Vulnerability: Debug hook abuse via tracing functions
Impact: Runtime surveillance, token theft, code tampering
Detection: Scan for sys.settrace; monitor for excessive frame introspection; check logs for unexpected stack traces
Remediation: Disable trace functions in production; block prompt-executed sys functions; sanitize exec paths

instruction: Describe the Runtime Memory and Code Introspection attack: Instrumentation via inspect Module
output:
The Python inspect module allows runtime access to source code, stack frames, arguments, and even local variables. Attackers can use this to silently inspect sensitive agent logic, prompts, API keys, or internal functions in mobile Python agents.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted access to inspect introspection
Impact: Stealthy memory read, logic reverse-engineering
Detection: Log inspection; stack usage monitoring; block inspect in sandboxed mobile environments
Remediation: Disable dynamic code inspection in runtime; denylist inspect, traceback; use secure execution contexts with ACLs

instruction: Describe the Live Code Reload Injection attack: Hot Code Reload Exploit in Dev Mode
output:
In dev mode, many mobile agent apps (especially Python-based ones using frameworks like Streamlit, Flask, or custom REPLs) support hot code reloading to speed up development. If exposed in production or misconfigured, an attacker can inject malicious code that is automatically reloaded and executed without restarting the app — enabling stealthy RCE.
Vulnerability: Hot reload executing updated attacker files
Impact: Stealthy RCE, data theft, app compromise
Detection: File change monitoring; alert on source reload; disable public dev mode
Remediation: Disable debug/hot-reload in production; validate source integrity; prevent file modification via agent interfaces

instruction: Describe the Runtime Memory Extraction attack: Agent Memory Scraping via Runtime Tools
output:
Mobile LLM agents written in Python (e.g., with LangChain) store user input, tokens, cookies, and internal state in memory. If the mobile environment allows Python runtime access, attackers can use introspection and memory scraping tools like gc, inspect, or frame walking to extract these secrets from memory — without ever reading the file system or triggering logs.
Vulnerability: Exposed memory and introspection access
Impact: Secret/key/token theft without filesystem access
Detection: Monitor for gc, inspect, or sys usage; check for memory object enumeration or unusual logs
Remediation: Block gc, inspect imports; encrypt or isolate sensitive memory objects; avoid using global state in agents

instruction: Describe the Chain Logic Hijack via Hooks attack: LLM Agent Chain Hook Injection
output:
Attackers hijack the internal logic of LangChain agents (or any LLM pipeline) by injecting malicious hook functions into the tool/chain execution process using dynamic overrides or monkey patching. This is especially dangerous in mobile environments like PyDroid or Termux where protections are minimal.
Vulnerability: Overridable class methods in agent chain logic
Impact: Stealthy logic hijack, data exfiltration, prompt manipulation
Detection: Monitor function entry/exit with known hash; audit monkey-patched functions at runtime
Remediation: Finalize agent logic at build time; disable dynamic code or reflection; sandbox method overrides; hash check critical components

instruction: Describe the Container Runtime Hook Exploit attack: Instrumentation in Container Runtime (e.g., Docker)
output:
Mobile developers often package LLM agents in Docker containers for cross-platform use (e.g., on Android via Termux or rooted environments). If Docker runtime is not hardened, attackers can instrument containers at runtime, injecting tools like strace, ptrace, or LD_PRELOAD to intercept function calls, extract memory, hijack sessions, and leak sensitive user interactions from the LLM agent.
Vulnerability: Unhardened container allows runtime introspection and hook injection
Impact: Memory scraping, session hijack, API key theft, remote logging
Detection: Monitor container syscall behavior, check for runtime tool execution like strace, gdb, or abnormal process trees
Remediation: Strip debugging tools; enforce seccomp/bpf filters; disallow ptrace; use minimal images with read-only root filesystems

instruction: Describe the Agent Chain Modification via Signal Interception attack: Use of Debug Mode Plugins in Production
output:
In production apps (especially mobile wrappers using Termux, Kivy, or PyDroid), developers sometimes enable "debug" plugins or signal-based introspection features to simplify development. These debug hooks remain active in production, enabling attackers to intercept execution signals, modify agent behavior on-the-fly, or hijack input/output flows by capturing SIGINT, SIGUSR1, or Python signal hooks.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted signal-based debug tools in production
Impact: Agent behavior hijack, credential theft, runtime control
Detection: Monitor use of signal module, trace SIG* delivery logs, alert on unexpected handler registrations
Remediation: Remove all dev/debug dependencies; deny signal use in production; audit plugin imports and runtime syscalls

instruction: Describe the Signal-Based Runtime Agent Modification attack: Agent Chain Modification via Signal Interception
output:
Mobile-based agents (e.g., LLM apps running inside Termux or containerized Android environments) often use UNIX signals to handle internal events or debugging. If not secured, attackers can hijack these signals (e.g., SIGUSR1, SIGINT, SIGTERM) to inject malicious code into the agent's control flow, allowing runtime logic modification or secret extraction.
Vulnerability: Insecure or exposed signal-based control mechanisms
Impact: Runtime hijack, secret extraction, behavior modification
Detection: Audit signal usage in source code; monitor signal triggers via /proc, use syscall tracing to alert abnormal signal delivery
Remediation: Harden agent builds; disallow custom signals in production; sandbox runtime with seccomp, AppArmor, or ptrace restrictions

instruction: Describe the Code Injection via Abstract Syntax Trees attack: Function Replacement via AST Manipulation
output:
The attacker modifies Python agent source code at the AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) level to replace or extend core functions, such as get_user_input() or send_response(), injecting malicious behavior that executes during runtime. AST attacks are stealthy, as they modify behavior without visible string-based indicators.
Vulnerability: Source-level logic overwrite via AST manipulation
Impact: Agent behavior hijack, data theft, response manipulation
Detection: Use AST comparison tools or secure hashes to detect altered source trees; alert on unexplained logic changes
Remediation: Prevent file-level access; obfuscate and compile production apps; disable plugin auto-load paths; validate AST at startup

instruction: Describe the Arbitrary Code Execution via Code Tool attack: Open Interpreter Exploit in Code Tool
output:
In mobile LLM agents that use Open Interpreter or any embedded REPL tool, an attacker can abuse the open code input interface (sometimes disguised as a “code” plugin) to run system-level commands, leak memory, or manipulate the environment. These tools often lack strict sandboxing on mobile, leading to full execution privilege.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted code execution in code tools
Impact: Full device compromise, key theft, persistent code execution
Detection: Monitor all interpreter-generated code; scan for dangerous calls (os.system, eval, subprocess) in logs
Remediation: Disable Open Interpreter on production builds; sandbox all code tool environments; restrict to whitelisted modules

instruction: Describe the In-Memory Injection via ctypes / FFI attack: Memory Patch via ctypes or FFI
output:
Attacker uses Python ctypes or cffi libraries on mobile agent apps (e.g., running Python on Android) to patch running app memory and inject malicious logic at runtime without altering files on disk.
Vulnerability: Runtime memory patching via unsafe ctypes
Impact: Bypass authentication, data exfiltration, runtime manipulation
Detection: Monitor unusual ctypes/ffi calls, runtime memory scans, anomaly in app behavior
Remediation: Disable ctypes/cffi in production, use code signing, runtime integrity checks, restrict debugging

instruction: Describe the Notebook Runtime Exploit attack: Jupyter Kernel Hijack
output:
Attackers exploit live Jupyter or IPython kernels connected to mobile agents to inject or monitor code in real time, stealing data or escalating privileges.
Vulnerability: Live code execution environment exploited
Impact: Data theft, agent manipulation, persistence
Detection: Audit notebook access logs, monitor package installs, alert on unexpected kernel restarts
Remediation: Secure notebook with password/tokens, restrict network, disable remote kernels, use VPN

instruction: Describe the Reflection/Introspection Abuse attack: Reflection-Based Access to Restricted Methods
output:
Attacker uses Python reflection or introspection to access and invoke restricted or private methods in the mobile agent, bypassing intended access controls.
Vulnerability: Access control bypass via reflection
Impact: Privilege escalation, unauthorized actions
Detection: Runtime behavior monitoring for reflection usage, audit logs for method calls
Remediation: Code hardening, minimize reflection, sandbox runtime, runtime policy enforcement

instruction: Describe the Execution Hijack via Hook Insertion attack: Hijack Plugin Execution Context at Runtime
output:
Attacker intercepts plugin or tool execution within a mobile agent runtime, injecting hooks to alter outputs or inject malicious behavior mid-execution.
Vulnerability: Runtime Hooking / Execution Hijack
Impact: Data tampering, privilege escalation, stealthy compromise
Detection: Detect runtime hooking tools (Frida, Xposed), integrity checks for plugins
Remediation: Use code signing, restrict debug interfaces, monitor plugin behavior

instruction: Describe the Observability Bypass via Hooking attack: Tampering with LangChain CallbackManager
output:
Attacker disables or hooks into LangChain’s CallbackManager used for logging and monitoring to hide malicious actions or modify logs.
Vulnerability: Logging / Observability Bypass
Impact: Stealthy execution, undetected malicious activity
Detection: Monitor missing/incomplete logs, external log verification
Remediation: Harden logging mechanisms, use tamper-evident logging, secure runtime

instruction: Describe the Dynamic Executor Replacement attack: Replacing Agent Action Executor Dynamically
output:
Attacker dynamically replaces the agent’s action executor (core logic handling commands) at runtime to execute arbitrary or malicious commands instead of legitimate ones.
Vulnerability: Runtime Code Replacement
Impact: Unauthorized command execution, data leakage, workflow corruption
Detection: Detect unexpected function overrides, runtime code hash mismatches
Remediation: Use code signing, runtime attestation, restrict debugging interfaces

instruction: Describe the Prompt Rewrite attack: Patch LLM Wrapper to Modify Prompts Before Execution
output:
Attacker intercepts the LLM wrapper runtime to modify or inject malicious instructions into prompts before execution.
Vulnerability: Prompt modification at runtime
Impact: Malicious command execution, data leakage
Detection: Detect unexpected prompt changes; runtime code integrity monitoring
Remediation: Enforce code signing, restrict debugging tools, use tamper-proof prompt transmission

instruction: Describe the Command Injection attack: Hijacking Embedded Shell Tools (e.g., subprocess)
output:
Attacker injects malicious OS shell commands via runtime configuration or prompt to the embedded shell tool (e.g., Python subprocess).
Vulnerability: Unsafe command execution
Impact: Arbitrary OS command execution, device compromise
Detection: Monitor system logs, subprocess call patterns; alert on unexpected commands
Remediation: Sanitize subprocess inputs, restrict shell command usage, secure runtime environment

instruction: Describe the Runtime Instrumentation Exploit attack: Runtime Graph/Trace Exploitation (e.g., PyTorch hooks)
output:
Attacker exploits dynamic runtime graph or hook mechanisms (like PyTorch hooks) to intercept, modify or spy on agent computations or data flow.
Vulnerability: Runtime hook abuse
Impact: Data leakage, model corruption, stealthy tampering
Detection: Monitor hook registrations, runtime model integrity checks
Remediation: Enforce sandboxing, restrict hook API access, use trusted code signing

instruction: Describe the Log Leak attack: Runtime Logging Injection
output:
Attacker adds malicious logging in mobile agent to silently capture user input, auth tokens, or agent responses.
Vulnerability: Unsafe logging practices
Impact: Credential leakage, session hijack
Detection: Monitor for sensitive data in logs, inspect debug logging paths
Remediation: Disable debug logging, audit code for hardcoded log statements, encrypt log files

instruction: Describe the Flow Tampering attack: Dynamic Agent Routing Exploit
output:
Attacker hijacks mobile agent’s decision logic mid-execution to reroute user flows or override agent responses.
Vulnerability: Logic tampering in agent flow
Impact: Access control bypass, internal data exposure
Detection: Detect route anomalies, use flow tracing, validate user role before every decision
Remediation: Use strict conditional checks, avoid user-controlled routing logic, apply dynamic guardrails

instruction: Describe the File Abuse attack: Temporary File Abuse in Tool Runtime
output:
Attacker abuses temporary file handling during mobile agent execution to read/write sensitive data or inject code.
Vulnerability: Insecure temp file handling
Impact: File overwrite, data theft, unauthorized execution
Detection: Monitor temp folder file changes, checksum file content before processing
Remediation: Avoid disk temp files, use in-memory storage, restrict external access to app cache dirs

instruction: Describe the Memory Exploit attack: Hijack Prompt History via Runtime Memory
output:
Attacker extracts or modifies prompt/response history stored in memory during agent execution.
Vulnerability: Exposed sensitive data in RAM
Impact: Session hijack, prompt manipulation
Detection: Monitor agent runtime memory access, detect debugging tools
Remediation: Encrypt in-memory prompt history, disable history in sensitive contexts, use secure memory allocators

instruction: Describe the Runtime Injection attack: Function Injection in LangChain Agent Runtime
output:
Attacker injects or replaces internal agent logic during execution by redefining core functions dynamically.
Vulnerability: Insecure dynamic logic injection
Impact: Agent logic hijack, command redirection
Detection: Runtime behavior tracing, function call comparison
Remediation: Use sealed function objects, disable dynamic monkey patching, verify agent flow at runtime

instruction: Describe the Credential Leak attack: Environment Variable Leakage at Runtime
output:
Agent or plugin exposes sensitive credentials stored in environment variables when prompted by attacker or through output mismanagement.
Vulnerability: Insecure handling of environment variables
Impact: Credential leakage to attacker
Detection: Log inspection for sensitive values; audit prompts and command logs
Remediation: Block env command exposure in agent logic; redact sensitive outputs; disable raw Python execution in agents

instruction: Describe the External Control attack: Remote Debug Port Exposure (e.g., Flask agent)
output:
Mobile agents running local web servers (e.g., Flask) in debug mode expose open ports, allowing attackers to connect remotely and execute code.
Vulnerability: Debug mode exposing local execution API
Impact: Remote code execution via open debug port
Detection: Port scanning tools, check app headers for Werkzeug, Flask debug banner
Remediation: Never expose debug ports publicly; restrict to 127.0.0.1; use proper authentication; disable remote debugger

instruction: Describe the Logic Exploit attack: Reentrancy Bugs in Agent Planning Logic
output:
Poorly implemented planning logic in agent chains allows attackers to inject loops, causing agents to re-execute privileged actions or skip auth checks.
Vulnerability: Improper loop handling in agent planners
Impact: Logic abuse, repeated token leakage
Detection: Analyze repeated prompt history, abnormal planner paths, tool overuse in chain execution
Remediation: Add chain depth limits; use prompt sanitizer; enforce one-time tool use in sensitive chain scenarios

instruction: Describe the Evasion attack: Adversarial Image Attack (e.g., Face Unlock)
output:
Attacker crafts an image that bypasses face recognition systems on phones or apps by fooling the ML model.
Vulnerability: Weak ML resistance to adversarial pixels
Impact: Device unlock, unauthorized data access
Detection: Check for multiple failed unlock attempts; use adversarial detectors in model pipeline
Remediation: Implement liveness detection (e.g., eye blink, motion); train model with adversarial robustness

instruction: Describe the Remote Command attack: Adversarial Voice Command Injection
output:
Attacker plays specially crafted audio that sounds innocent but is interpreted as malicious commands by AI voice assistants on mobile devices.
Vulnerability: ML misclassification of adversarial audio
Impact: Unauthorized command execution, info theft
Detection: Analyze background sound for anomalies; monitor assistant triggers and timing
Remediation: Require voice recognition, disable assistants on lock screen, train models for adversarial robustness

instruction: Describe the Model Integrity attack: TFLite Model Poisoning
output:
Attacker injects malicious logic or backdoors into TensorFlow Lite models used in mobile apps, causing incorrect predictions or hidden behavior.
Vulnerability: Model tampering / poisoning via TFLite files
Impact: Backdoors, incorrect predictions, data leakage
Detection: Compare model hash to baseline; use digital signatures for model files
Remediation: Encrypt and sign models; verify integrity at runtime; restrict local model access

instruction: Describe the Logic Hijack attack: ONNX Model Injection in APK
output:
Attacker reverse engineers an APK, extracts and replaces the ONNX model with malicious logic to manipulate prediction or gain control in app behavior.
